lessons.notes_html:
A thought experiment is a hypothetical scenario in which a hypothesis, theory or principle is presented to consider its consequences. It is a mental laboratory: instead of physically mixing chemicals or using tools, you imagine a scenario related to a scientific principle and apply logical reasoning to it.

How It Works

  • Imagine a specific scenario linked to a principle or theory.
  • Apply logical reasoning to predict the outcome if the principle is valid.
  • Use it to predict possible outcomes, understand how a process may work, and identify issues or unexpected results.

Thought experiments act as mental tools for testing hypotheses and understanding concepts, such as Avogadro's hypothesis and the mole, without requiring physical experiments. A teaspoon of water, for example, actually contains trillions of molecules — thought experiments help chemists understand such huge numbers through the mole concept.

Key Points

  • A thought experiment is a hypothetical situation used to think through the consequences of a hypothesis, theory or principle.
  • It needs no physical experiment or laboratory apparatus.
  • It works by imagining a scenario and reasoning logically about it.
  • It helps predict outcomes and find unexpected results or issues.
  • It is the mental tool behind ideas like Avogadro's hypothesis and the mole.
lessons.title: Thought Experiment

lessons.notes_html:
This section shows a step-by-step thought experiment on gases that leads to Avogadro's hypothesis.

Steps of the Thought Experiment

  • 1. Identify the question: Why do equal volumes of different gases, such as hydrogen and chlorine, at the same temperature and pressure have different masses?
  • 2. Define assumptions: Gases consist of tiny particles (atoms or molecules); temperature and pressure affect gas volume, so they must be kept constant.
  • 3. Construct the scenario: Imagine two containers, one of hydrogen and one of chlorine, with the same volume, same temperature and same pressure — and then suppose both contain the same number of gas particles.
  • 4. Predict the outcome: Gases react in simple volume ratios, e.g. one volume of hydrogen + one volume of chlorine → two volumes of hydrogen chloride. The mass difference is because hydrogen and chlorine molecules have different sizes and weights, not because there are more or fewer molecules.
  • 5. Analyse the implications: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, whatever the gas. Gases consist of molecules (like H2), not just single atoms (like H).
  • 6. Relate back to reality: This supports the mole concept, Avogadro's number (6.022 x 10^23 particles in one mole) and the ideal gas law PV = nRT.

Conclusion (Avogadro's hypothesis): Equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain an equal number of molecules.

Key Points

  • Avogadro's hypothesis: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
  • Different masses of equal gas volumes come from different molecular masses, not different numbers of molecules.
  • The experiment assumes gases are made of tiny particles and that temperature and pressure are constant.
  • It supports the mole, Avogadro's number (6.022 x 10^23 per mole) and PV = nRT.
  • Gases exist as molecules such as H2, not only as single atoms.
lessons.title: Avogadro's Hypothesis: Thought Experiment

lessons.notes_html:
Many things in chemistry — electrons, atoms, molecules, orbitals and energy levels — cannot be observed directly. Thought experiments enable chemists to construct mental models of these invisible systems to explain their properties and behaviour.

Example

Chemists visualise electrons as probability clouds surrounding a nucleus, even though electrons cannot be directly observed. This visual representation supports understanding of atomic orbitals, molecular shapes and reactivity. The book's figure of an atom with electron clouds, surrounded by molecular structures, is itself an example of visualising atomic orbitals and shapes through a thought experiment.

Key Points

  • Electrons, atoms, molecules, orbitals and energy levels cannot be seen directly.
  • Thought experiments build mental models of these invisible systems.
  • Mental models explain the properties and behaviour of atoms and molecules.
  • Electrons pictured as probability clouds around the nucleus help explain orbitals, shapes and reactivity.
lessons.title: The Role of Thought Experiments in Chemical Theory

lessons.notes_html:
Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that studies the relationship between the amounts of reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation. The word comes from the Greek stoicheion, “element”, and metron, “measure” — it is the quantitative measure of reactants and products.

Stoichiometry is used to calculate quantities of products, such as masses, moles, volumes and percentage yield, using a balanced chemical equation.

Balancing Rule

  • A balanced chemical equation has the same number of atoms of each type on both sides.
  • Use the correct formulae for reactants and products.
  • Never change the subscripts in a formula — changing a subscript changes the identity of the substance.
  • Balance by changing the number of molecules (coefficients) of each substance in the equation.

Key Points

  • Stoichiometry = quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced equation.
  • It is used to calculate masses, moles, volumes and percentage yields.
  • In a balanced equation, atoms of each element are equal on both sides.
  • Balance with coefficients only; never change subscripts in formulae.
lessons.title: Stoichiometry

lessons.notes_html:
A balanced chemical equation gives a complete description of a reaction. Its coefficients are used to convert between moles, representative particles, masses and volumes of gases at STP (standard temperature and pressure).

Example: Formation of Steam

2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g). At STP, 2 moles (4 g) of hydrogen react with 1 mole (32 g) of oxygen to produce 2 moles (36 g) of steam. Hydrogen occupies 44.8 litres, oxygen 22.4 litres, and the steam also occupies 44.8 litres.

Quantity2H2(g)O2(g)2H2O(g)
Moles212
Mass (g)43236
Molecules1.204 x 10^246.02 x 10^231.204 x 10^24
Volume at STP (L)44.822.444.8

Note that total mass is conserved: 4 g + 32 g = 36 g.

Key Points

  • Coefficients in a balanced equation give the mole ratio of reactants and products.
  • The same ratio converts into particles, masses and gas volumes at STP.
  • One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP, so 2 moles occupy 44.8 L.
  • Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
lessons.title: Interpreting Balanced Chemical Equations: Moles, Representative Particles, Masses, and Volumes at STP

lessons.notes_html:
We count everyday quantities in units such as a dozen (12), a pair (2), a case (24), a pack (52), a ream (500 sheets) and a gross (144). Chemists count and weigh matter with the mole.

The mole is the most convenient unit of matter for counting and weighing. It connects the macroscale world (large enough to weigh or count) with the nanoscale world (too small to weigh or count conveniently). “Mole” is a Latin word meaning a “huge mass”. Its symbol is mol and amount of substance is represented by n.

Definition

One mole is the amount of substance that has as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units) as the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.

The mass of one mole of a substance is equal to its formula mass expressed in grams: one mole of carbon atoms = 12 g; one mole of NaCl formula units = 58.5 g; one mole of CO2 molecules = 44 g; one mole of SO4^2- ions = 96 g.

Key Points

  • The mole (symbol mol) is the chemist's counting unit; amount is written as n.
  • One mole contains as many particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.
  • Mass of one mole = atomic, molecular, ionic or formula mass in grams.
  • Examples: C = 12 g, NaCl = 58.5 g, CO2 = 44 g, SO4^2- = 96 g per mole.
  • The mole links the weighable macroscale world to the nanoscale world of particles.
lessons.title: Mole

lessons.notes_html:
The number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units) present in one mole of a substance is called Avogadro's number. It is represented by NA.

One mole of any substance contains 6.022141 x 10^23 particles, usually rounded to 6.02 x 10^23. The unit of Avogadro's number is read as “per mole” or “inverse of mole” (mol-1). It is named in honour of the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro (1776–1856), who proposed his hypothesis in 1811; the number itself was experimentally determined by Jean Perrin in 1909.

Examples

  • One mole of carbon-12 contains 6.02 x 10^23 atoms of carbon-12.
  • One mole of H2O contains 6.02 x 10^23 molecules of H2O.
  • One mole of CaO contains 6.02 x 10^23 formula units of CaO.
  • One mole of CO3^2- contains 6.02 x 10^23 ions of CO3^2-.

Key Points

  • Avogadro's number NA = 6.02 x 10^23 particles per mole.
  • It applies equally to atoms, molecules, ions and formula units.
  • Every mole of every substance contains the same number of particles.
  • Avogadro proposed the hypothesis in 1811 but never measured the number himself.
lessons.title: The Avogadro's Number

lessons.notes_html:
The volume of one mole of an ideal gas at STP is called molar volume. It is denoted by Vm and its value is 22.414 dm3 at STP (0°C and 1 atm). It is the same for every ideal gas — only the molar mass differs.

GasMolar mass (g/mol)MolesVolume at STP (dm3)Number of molecules
Hydrogen2122.4146.02 x 10^23
Methane16122.4146.02 x 10^23
Ammonia17122.4146.02 x 10^23
Carbon dioxide44122.4146.02 x 10^23

The molar volume concept also helps scientists estimate the amount of oxygen your lungs can contain at sea level and compare it to high-altitude breathing conditions.

Key Points

  • Molar volume Vm = 22.414 dm3 per mole of any ideal gas at STP.
  • STP means 0°C and 1 atm pressure.
  • Equal moles of different gases occupy equal volumes at STP.
  • One molar volume of any gas contains 6.02 x 10^23 molecules.
lessons.title: Molar Volume

lessons.notes_html:
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is called its molar mass. Its unit is g/mol.

Worked Example: Benzene, C6H6

Each mole of benzene contains 6 moles of carbon atoms and 6 moles of hydrogen atoms: 6 x 12 g/mol = 72 g; 6 x 1 g/mol = 6 g. Molar mass of C6H6 = 72 + 6 = 78 g mol-1. (Similarly, molar mass of KMnO4 = 158 g/mol.)

Calculation of Gram Molecular Mass from Density

The molar mass of a gas can be calculated from its density at STP:

FormulaUse
Molar Mass = Density x Molar Volume at STPMolar mass of a gas from its density at STP (molar volume ≈ 22.4 L/mol)

Example: density 2.50 g/L at STP → Molar mass = 2.50 g/L x 22.4 L/mol ≈ 56 g/mol. The density must be in grams per litre (g/L); convert it first if it is given in another unit.

Key Points

  • Molar mass = mass of one mole, in g/mol.
  • Find it by adding the masses of all atoms in the formula: C6H6 = 78 g/mol.
  • For a gas at STP: Molar Mass = Density x Molar Volume.
  • Density for this formula must be expressed in g/L.
lessons.title: Molar Mass

lessons.notes_html:
Section 1.10 gives the basic mole conversions. If the mass of a substance is known, its number of moles is found by dividing the mass by the molar mass; the reverse conversion multiplies moles by molar mass.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Number of moles = Mass of substance / Molar massMoles from a known mass
Mass of substance = Number of moles x Molar massMass from a known number of moles

Worked Examples

  • Moles in 20 g of NaOH = 20 g / 40 g.mol-1 = 0.5 mol.
  • Moles in 12.25 g of KClO3 = 0.1 mol.
  • Mass of 0.25 moles of H2SO4 = 0.25 mol x 98 g.mol-1 = 24.5 g.
  • Mass of 1.50 moles of Ca(OH)2 = 111 g.

Key Points

  • n = m / M: divide mass by molar mass to get moles.
  • m = n x M: multiply moles by molar mass to get mass.
  • Always use the molar mass of the exact substance in the question.
  • Keep units with the data: mass in grams, molar mass in g/mol, answer in mol.
lessons.title: Mole Calculations: Number of Moles and Mass

lessons.notes_html:
Moles also convert into numbers of particles through Avogadro's number, and into gas volumes at STP through the molar volume.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Number of moles = Number of particles / Avogadro's NumberMoles from a particle count
Number of particles = Number of moles x Avogadro's Number (NA)Particles from moles
Number of particles = (Given mass m / Molar mass M) x NAParticles directly from mass
Volume of a gas = Moles of gas x Molar volumeGas volume at STP from moles
Volume of a gas = (Mass / Molar mass) x Molar volumeGas volume at STP from mass

Worked Examples

  • Sucrose: 3.76 x 10^24 molecules / 6.02 x 10^23 = 6.25 mol.
  • Atoms in 2.5 moles of sodium = 2.5 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.505 x 10^24 atoms.
  • Atoms in 50 g of gold = (50 / 197) x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.529 x 10^23 atoms.
  • Volume of 4.75 mol of ethane at STP = 4.75 x 22.414 dm3 = 106.47 dm3.
  • Volume of 3.99 g of argon at STP = (3.99 / 39.9) x 22.414 = 2.2414 dm3.

Key Points

  • Particles = moles x 6.02 x 10^23; moles = particles / 6.02 x 10^23.
  • From mass to particles: first divide by molar mass, then multiply by NA.
  • Gas volume at STP = moles x 22.414 dm3.
  • From mass to gas volume: convert mass to moles first, then multiply by molar volume.
lessons.title: Mole Calculations: Number of Particles and Volume of a Gas

lessons.notes_html:
A chemist uses stoichiometric calculations to find how much product is obtained from certain amounts of reactants, or how much reactant is used to get a certain amount of product.

Principles of Stoichiometric Calculations

  • Reactants are completely converted into products.
  • No side reaction occurs.
  • The law of conservation of mass and the law of definite proportions are obeyed.

How to Solve a Stoichiometry Problem

  • Step 1: Write all the given data with relevant units.
  • Step 2: Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
  • Step 3: Convert the given mass of all reactants to number of moles.
  • Step 4: Use the equation to determine the mole ratio of the unknown quantity to the known quantity.
  • Step 5: Convert moles back to mass by multiplying with the molar mass of the unknown substance, if necessary.

Mole-Mole Conversion (Example 1.9)

N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 1 mole of N2 needs 3 mol of H2, so 2.5 mol of N2 consumes 3 x 2.5 = 7.5 mol of H2.

Mole-Mass Conversion (Example 1.10)

2H2O(l) → 2H2(g) + O2(g). 2 moles of H2O produce 2 mol of H2, so 4.3 moles of H2O produce 4.3 mol of H2; mass = 4.3 mol x 2 g.mol-1 = 8.6 g of H2.

Key Points

  • Every stoichiometric calculation starts from a balanced equation.
  • The mole ratio from the equation links the known and unknown substances.
  • Mole-mole problems stay in moles; mole-mass problems end by multiplying by molar mass.
  • Calculations assume complete conversion, no side reactions, and conservation of mass.
lessons.title: Stoichiometric Calculations

lessons.notes_html:
Two further conversion types complete section 1.11: mass-mass and mass-volume conversions, both solved by the same five steps — data, balanced equation, moles or mass ratio, then the final quantity.

Mass-Mass Conversion (Example 1.11)

CaCO3(s) →(Δ) CaO(s) + CO2(g). 100 g of CaCO3 (1 mol) produces 56 g of CaO (1 mol). So 200 g of limestone produces (56 / 100) x 200 = 112 g of quicklime (CaO).

Mass-Volume Conversion (Example 1.12)

2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g). Moles of NO = 12 g / 30 g.mol-1 = 0.4 mol. From the equation, 2 mol of NO produce 2 mol of NO2, so 0.4 mol of NO produces 0.4 mol of NO2. Volume of NO2 = 0.4 mol x 22.414 L.mol-1 = 8.97 L.

Key Points

  • Mass-mass: use the mass ratio shown by the balanced equation (100 g CaCO3 → 56 g CaO).
  • Mass-volume: convert mass to moles, use the mole ratio, then multiply moles by 22.414 L/mol at STP.
  • The mole ratio comes only from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
  • State symbols and units should be carried through every step.
lessons.title: Stoichiometric Calculations: Mass-Mass and Mass-Volume Conversions

lessons.notes_html:
In many chemical processes the reactants are not present in the proportions indicated by the balanced equation. The reactant that is completely consumed at the completion of the reaction is called the limiting reagent (or limiting reactant). The maximum amount of product formed depends on the amount of limiting reactant; when it is consumed completely, the reaction stops and no further product forms. Reactants present in larger amounts, which remain unreacted at the end, are called excess reagents.

How to Identify the Limiting Reagent (Example 1.13)

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) →(Ignition) CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), with 30 g of CH4 and 50 g of O2: moles of CH4 = 30 / 16 = 1.875 mol; moles of O2 = 50 / 32 = 1.563 mol. From CH4, CO2 possible = 1.875 mol; from O2, CO2 possible = 1.563 / 2 = 0.7815 mol. O2 gives less product, so O2 is the limiting reactant — note the limiting reactant is not necessarily the one present in the smaller amount. Mass of CO2 = 0.7815 x 44 = 34.39 g. O2 used 0.7815 mol of CH4, leaving 1.875 − 0.7815 = 1.0935 mol = 17.5 g of excess CH4 unreacted.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Product from each reactant = moles of reactant x (coefficient ratio)The reactant giving the least product is limiting
Excess left = Starting quantity − Quantity usedUnreacted excess reagent (convert to grams with molar mass)

Key Points

  • Limiting reagent: completely consumed; it fixes the maximum product.
  • Excess reagent: present in larger amount and partly left unreacted.
  • Find the limiting reagent by calculating the product from each reactant — the smaller result wins.
  • All product and excess calculations are based on the limiting reactant.
  • Example: car engines are designed with limiting reactants in mind for efficient fuel combustion.
lessons.title: Excess and Limiting Reagents

lessons.notes_html:
The amount of product either calculated from a balanced chemical equation or actually obtained from a reaction is called yield or chemical yield.

Types of Yield

  • Theoretical yield (expected yield): the amount of product calculated from a balanced chemical equation.
  • Actual yield (practical yield): the amount of product actually obtained from a chemical reaction.
  • Percentage yield: actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100. It shows the efficiency of the reaction — the greater the percentage yield, the higher the efficiency.

Why Actual Yield Is Less Than Theoretical Yield

  • Side reactions: products may react further, giving by-products other than the main product.
  • Many reactions are reversible and do not go to completion.
  • Impurities in the reactants.
  • Reactions may be incomplete; some reactant remains unreacted.
  • Loss of product during separation, filtration, washing, drying, distillation, crystallisation, etc.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Percentage Yield = (Actual Yield / Theoretical Yield) x 100Efficiency of a reaction

Example 1.14: 6Li + N2 → 2Li3N. 42 g of Li produces 70 g of Li3N, so 30 g of Li gives a theoretical yield of 50 g. With an actual yield of 38 g, percentage yield = (38 / 50) x 100 = 76%.

Key Points

  • Theoretical yield is calculated from the equation; actual yield is obtained in practice.
  • Actual yield is almost always less than theoretical yield.
  • Percentage yield = (actual / theoretical) x 100 and measures reaction efficiency.
  • Causes of loss: side reactions, reversibility, impurities, incomplete reaction and handling losses.
lessons.title: Yield and Its Types

lessons.notes_html:
All matter is composed of very small particles called atoms. The idea that matter is made up of fundamental particles called atoms is known as the atomic theory of matter. Protons, neutrons and electrons are subatomic particles and have different properties, including their relative charges and masses.

Properties of the Three Fundamental Particles

ParticleCharge (C)Mass (amu)Mass (g)Relative ChargeMass Relative to ElectronDiscovered byYear
Electron-1.6022 x 10^-190.000549.10938 x 10^-28-11J.J. Thomson1897
Proton+1.6022 x 10^-191.007271.67262 x 10^-24+11836Rutherford1917
Neutron01.008671.67493 x 10^-2401839James Chadwick1932

The electron is by far the lightest particle; the proton and neutron each have a mass of about 1 amu. The proton and electron carry equal but opposite charges, while the neutron has no charge.

Key Points

  • Atoms are the tiny fundamental particles of which all matter is composed.
  • Electron: charge -1, mass 0.00054 amu, discovered by J.J. Thomson (1897).
  • Proton: charge +1, mass 1.00727 amu, discovered by Rutherford (1917).
  • Neutron: no charge, mass 1.00867 amu, discovered by James Chadwick (1932).
  • A proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron.
lessons.title: Relative Charges and Masses of Subatomic Particles

lessons.notes_html:
The atomic number (Z) of an atom is the number of protons in its nucleus. It is a fundamental and unique property of each element: no two elements have the same atomic number.

Proton Number

The proton number refers to the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. The terms atomic number and proton number represent the same concept.

  • In a neutral atom, the atomic number equals the number of electrons.
  • Elements are organised in the periodic table on the basis of their proton numbers (atomic numbers).
  • The number of protons identifies the element; changing the proton number changes the element itself.

Key Points

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons in the nucleus.
  • Atomic number and proton number are the same thing.
  • In a neutral atom: number of electrons = number of protons = Z.
  • Every element has its own unique atomic number.
lessons.title: Atomic and Proton Number Represent the Same Concept

lessons.notes_html:
The terms mass number and nucleon number represent the same concept in atomic and nuclear chemistry. Both indicate the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom. "Mass number" is more commonly used in general discussions, while "nucleon number" is often used in nuclear chemistry.

Key Formulae

QuantityFormula
Mass number (A)A = protons + neutrons = Z + n
Number of neutronsn = A - Z
Electrons in a neutral atom= Z
Electrons in a cation= Z - charge
Electrons in an anion= Z + charge

Worked Examples from the Book

  • Boron-11 (Z = 5, A = 11): 5 protons, 5 electrons, neutrons = 11 - 5 = 6.
  • Calcium-40 (Z = 20, A = 40): 20 protons, 20 electrons, 20 neutrons.
  • Chlorine-35 (Z = 17, A = 35): 17 protons, 17 electrons, 18 neutrons.
  • Mg2+ (Z = 12, A = 24): 12 protons, 12 neutrons, electrons = 12 - 2 = 10 (the ion has lost two electrons).
  • N3- (Z = 7, A = 14): 7 protons, 7 neutrons, electrons = 7 + 3 = 10 (the ion has gained three electrons).

Key Points

  • Mass number (A) = nucleon number = protons + neutrons.
  • Neutrons = A - Z.
  • A positive ion has fewer electrons than protons; a negative ion has more.
  • For ions, adjust the electron count by the size of the charge.
lessons.title: Mass and Nucleon Number Represent the Same Concept

lessons.notes_html:
Beams of protons, neutrons and electrons moving at the same velocity in an electric field behave differently because they have different charges.

Behaviour of Each Beam

BeamChargeBehaviour in Electric Field
ProtonsPositiveDeflected towards the negative plate; repelled by the positive plate
ElectronsNegativeDeflected towards the positive plate; repelled by the negative plate
NeutronsNeutralNot attracted or repelled; continue in a straight line without deflection

Amount of Deflection

The deflection of charged particles such as protons and electrons in an electric field depends on two key variables: the magnitude of the charge and the mass of the particle. The greater the charge and the lighter the mass, the larger the degree of deflection. Deflection is proportional to q/m, so the very light electron beam deflects much more than the proton beam.

Key Points

  • Opposite charges attract: protons bend to the negative plate, electrons to the positive plate.
  • Neutrons are electrically neutral, so they are not deflected at all.
  • Deflection increases with charge and decreases with mass (deflection ∝ q/m).
  • Electrons deflect the most because they are the lightest charged particles.
lessons.title: Behaviour of Beams of Subatomic Particles in an Electric Field

lessons.notes_html:
In chemistry, a free radical is an atomic or molecular species with one or more unpaired electrons in its orbital.

Properties and Examples

  • The presence of unpaired electrons increases the reactivity of free radicals and makes them naturally unstable.
  • Examples include the hydroxyl radical (OH), the superoxide radical (O2-) and the nitric oxide radical (NO), each carrying an unpaired electron.

Free Radicals in Life

Free radicals are not always harmful: the immune system uses them to kill bacteria. However, when out of balance they can damage DNA and cells, leading to inflammation, faster ageing and a higher risk of chronic diseases such as cancer. Antioxidants found in fruits and vegetables help neutralise free radicals and protect the body from their harmful effects.

Key Points

  • A free radical is a species with one or more unpaired electrons.
  • Unpaired electrons make free radicals highly reactive and unstable.
  • Examples: hydroxyl, superoxide and nitric oxide radicals.
  • Antioxidants in food neutralise excess free radicals in the body.
lessons.title: Free Radical

lessons.notes_html:
A mass spectrometer is a powerful analytical instrument used to measure molecular masses and analyse the composition of samples by separating gaseous ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). It is particularly useful for determining the relative atomic mass of an element from its isotopic composition.

Principle of Mass Spectrometer

Mass spectrometers do not directly determine mass; they determine the mass-to-charge ratio. They carry out three main functions: (i) ionisation of molecules, (ii) separation of these molecules according to their m/z ratio, and (iii) determination of the relative abundance of each ion produced.

  • The sample is placed in an inlet chamber and turned into vapour; the vapours enter an ionisation chamber.
  • Ion source: high-energy electrons from an electrically heated filament (usually tungsten) knock electrons out of the sample molecules, producing positively charged ions.
  • Repeller chamber: a positive electrical potential across the accelerating plates produces a beam of fast-moving positive ions.
  • Analyser: separates the fast-moving ions by their m/z ratios; lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions.
  • Ion collector: the ions are detected; the collector generates an electronic signal which is amplified and recorded.

Reading a Mass Spectrum

In the mass spectrum, the position of a peak indicates the relative atomic mass and the length of a peak shows the relative abundance of the ion. For chlorine there are two peaks: chlorine-35 with relative abundance 75.77% and chlorine-37 with 24.23%.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Average atomic mass = [(mass of isotope 1 x its % abundance) + (mass of isotope 2 x its % abundance)] / 100Relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances
For chlorine: [(35 x 75.77) + (37 x 24.23)] / 100 = 35.48 amuAverage atomic mass of chlorine

Key Points

  • A mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), not by mass alone.
  • Its three jobs are ionisation, separation and measuring relative abundance.
  • Lighter ions are deflected more in the analyser.
  • Peak position gives mass; peak height gives relative abundance.
  • Mass spectrometry is also used in forensic science to detect drugs, toxins and explosives.
lessons.title: Mass Spectrometer

lessons.notes_html:
Quantum numbers are a set of four integral values that uniquely describe the state and behaviour of an electron in an atom. They specify the energy level and position of the electron, the shape and orientation of its orbital, and its spin direction. They are: the principal quantum number, the azimuthal quantum number, the magnetic quantum number and the spin quantum number.

Principal Quantum Number (n)

This quantum number determines the energy level or shell in which an electron is located, denoted by lowercase n. Allowed values are positive integers 1, 2, 3, ... also represented by the letters K, L, M, N, O, P and Q respectively.

  • Total number of orbitals in a shell = n^2.
  • Maximum number of electrons in a shell = 2n^2.
  • Greater the value of n, greater the distance of the electron from the nucleus, greater the size of the atom, and greater the energy of the electron.

Azimuthal Quantum Number (l)

Also known as the angular momentum quantum number, it determines the number of sub-shells and the shape of the orbital, and is represented by l. Its values range from 0 to (n - 1). Subshells are denoted by the letters s, p, d and f: l = 0 gives an s orbital (spherical shape), l = 1 a p orbital (dumbbell shape) and l = 2 a d orbital (double dumbbell shape).

Value of l012345
Letter usedspdfgh
Total number of orbitals1357911
Total number of electrons2610141822

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Orbitals in a shell = n^2Total orbitals in shell n
Maximum electrons in a shell = 2n^2Capacity of shell n
Orbitals in a subshell = 2l + 1Orbitals for a given l
Maximum electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1)Capacity of a subshell

Key Points

  • Four quantum numbers completely describe an electron in an atom.
  • n gives the shell and energy; its values are 1, 2, 3, ... (K, L, M, N, ...).
  • l gives the subshell and orbital shape; its values run from 0 to (n - 1).
  • s, p, d and f correspond to l = 0, 1, 2 and 3.
  • A shell holds at most 2n^2 electrons.
lessons.title: Quantum Numbers and Orbitals

lessons.notes_html:
The last two quantum numbers describe the orientation of an orbital in space and the direction in which the electron spins.

Magnetic Quantum Number (m)

This quantum number specifies the orientation of the orbital in space, represented by m. Its values range from -l to +l through zero, giving (2l + 1) integral values in all.

  • For the s-subshell (l = 0), m = 0: only one orbital, with the same orientation along the x, y and z axes.
  • For the p-subshell (l = 1), m = -1, 0, +1: three orbitals (px, py, pz) of the same shape but different orientations. All orbitals within a given subshell possess the same energy; such orbitals are called degenerate.
  • For the d-subshell (l = 2), m = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2: five orbitals (dxy, dyz, dxz, dx2-y2, dz2), all of the same energy.

Spin Quantum Number (ms)

The spin quantum number indicates the direction of spin of an electron around its own axis; it is denoted by ms or s and has two values, +1/2 and -1/2. Spins are shown by an up arrow for +1/2 (anticlockwise spin) and a down arrow for -1/2 (clockwise spin). Two electrons in the same orbital with opposite spins are said to have paired spins, while two electrons with the same spin in different degenerate orbitals are called parallel spins.

Shells, Subshells and Orbitals at a Glance

nSubshellsTotal Orbitals in ShellTotal Electrons in Shell
11s12
22s, 2p48
33s, 3p, 3d918
44s, 4p, 4d, 4f1632

Key Points

  • m gives orbital orientation; its values run from -l to +l, (2l + 1) values in total.
  • Orbitals in the same subshell are degenerate: they have equal energy.
  • ms has only two values, +1/2 and -1/2, shown as up and down arrows.
  • Opposite spins in one orbital are paired spins; same spins in different orbitals are parallel spins.
lessons.title: Magnetic Quantum Number and Spin Quantum Number

lessons.notes_html:
The electrons of an atom are arranged in shells, which are divided into subshells, which are further divided into orbitals.

Shells

The shells are labelled by the letters K, L, M, N, O, P and Q, starting from the nucleus outward. Their principal quantum numbers (n) are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, ... respectively. The larger the value of n, the higher the energy of the shell. A shell, also known as an energy level, differs from an orbit: Bohr's model showed electrons moving in fixed two-dimensional circular paths called orbits, while the modern quantum mechanical model describes electrons as residing in three-dimensional regions called shells or energy levels.

Subshells

Each principal energy level (shell) is divided into sublevels, or subshells. The number of subshells within a given shell is equal to the value of n: the first shell (n = 1) has only 1s; the second shell (n = 2) has 2s and 2p; the third shell (n = 3) has 3s, 3p and 3d; the fourth shell (n = 4) has 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f, and so forth. The general order of subshell energies is: s lowest, then p, then d, then f highest.

Orbitals

An atomic orbital is a region surrounding the nucleus of an atom where there is a high probability of finding an electron. Each subshell has a specific number of orbitals. The number of orbitals per subshell depends on the type of subshell but not on the value of n, and is calculated by the formula 2l + 1.

Key Points

  • Shells are labelled K to Q for n = 1 to 7; energy rises with n.
  • A shell is a 3D energy level, not a fixed circular orbit.
  • The number of subshells in a shell equals n.
  • Subshell energy order: s, then p, then d, then f.
  • An orbital is a region of high probability of finding an electron; a subshell holds 2l + 1 orbitals.
lessons.title: Shells, Sub-shells and Orbitals

lessons.notes_html:
Orbitals do not have a real physical existence or precise boundaries; they are regions in space surrounding the nucleus. Their shapes help us visualise how the electron density is distributed around the nucleus.

Shape of s-Orbitals

All s orbitals (1s, 2s, 3s, 4s and so forth) are spherical in shape but differ in size. The size and energy of the s-orbital increase with an increase in the principal quantum number (n); for example, the 2s orbital is larger and higher in energy than the 1s orbital.

Shapes of p-Orbitals

The three values of the magnetic quantum number show that p-orbitals have three orientations in space, along the x, y and z axes, positioned at right angles to each other. The three p orbitals (px, py, pz) are identical in size, shape and energy, each with a dumbbell shape: two egg-shaped lobes, one on each side of the nucleus. Like s orbitals, p orbitals grow larger from 2p to 3p to 4p.

Shapes of d and f Orbitals

The d orbitals begin with the principal quantum number n = 3 (l = 2), giving five values of m and so five d orbitals: dxy, dyz, dxz, dx2-y2 and dz2. The dz2 orbital has two egg-shaped lobes and a ring-shaped doughnut in the centre, while the other four orbitals have four egg-shaped lobes each. The d-orbitals of the 4th and higher shells have shapes similar to the 3d orbitals but differ in energy and size.

Key Points

  • s orbitals are spherical; size and energy increase with n.
  • p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, in three orientations (px, py, pz) at right angles.
  • There are five d orbitals; four have four lobes, while dz2 has two lobes plus a doughnut ring.
  • Orbitals of the same subshell have the same shape family but grow with shell number.
lessons.title: Shapes of Orbitals

lessons.notes_html:
The distribution of electrons across various subshells at increasing energy levels to attain the most stable arrangement is known as the electronic configuration. Three rules govern this distribution: the Aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule.

Aufbau Principle

The Aufbau principle, from the German word "aufbauen" meaning "to build up", describes the order in which electrons occupy atomic orbitals: electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first and then progressively move to higher energy orbitals. The filling order is: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s ...

The (n + l) Rule

To determine the relative energy of atomic orbitals, the (n + l) rule is applied: the sum (n + l) gives a comparative measure of orbital energy. Orbitals with lower (n + l) values are filled first. If two orbitals have the same (n + l) value, the one with the lower value of n has lower energy and is filled first. For example, 4s has n + l = 4 + 0 = 4, while 3d has 3 + 2 = 5, so 4s is filled before 3d, even though 3d belongs to a lower principal shell.

Example: Iron (Fe, Z = 26)

Following the order of orbital filling, the configuration of iron is written as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6. Although 3d comes after 3p in principal quantum number, it is filled after 4s because 4s has the lower (n + l) value.

Key Points

  • Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons among subshells in order of increasing energy.
  • Aufbau principle: lowest energy orbitals are filled first.
  • Lower (n + l) means lower energy; for equal (n + l), lower n is filled first.
  • 4s fills before 3d; Fe = 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6.
lessons.title: Electronic Configuration

lessons.notes_html:
Two further rules control how electrons occupy orbitals within a subshell.

Pauli Exclusion Principle

In 1926, Austrian scientist Wolfgang Pauli introduced the exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all four quantum numbers. An orbital can hold at most two electrons, which have the same values of three quantum numbers (n, l and m) but must differ in the spin quantum number; that is, they must have opposite spins. Parallel spins for two electrons in the same orbital are not possible. For example, both electrons of helium in the 1s orbital have n = 1, l = 0, m = 0, but their spins are +1/2 and -1/2.

Hund's Rule

Hund's rule states that when two or more degenerate orbitals (orbitals of the same energy) are available, electrons should be placed in separate orbitals with the same spin rather than in the same orbital with opposite spins. The p subshell has three orbitals, the d subshell five and the f subshell seven. Pairing of electrons in the p orbitals begins only when the fourth electron enters; in d and f orbitals, pairing starts with the entry of the sixth and eighth electrons respectively. Hund's rule results from the fact that electrons repel one another and tend to stay as far apart as possible, so they are lower in energy when they occupy different orbitals.

Key Points

  • Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers.
  • One orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.
  • Hund's rule: degenerate orbitals are singly filled with parallel spins before pairing begins.
  • Pairing starts at the 4th electron in p, the 6th in d and the 8th in f subshells.
lessons.title: Pauli Exclusion Principle and Hund's Rule

lessons.notes_html:
There are three distinct ways to write the electronic configuration of an atom.

Three Methods

  • Subshell method: write the symbol of the occupied subshell with a superscript for the electron count, and the principal quantum number before the subshell. Nitrogen is written as N = 1s2, 2s2, 2p3.
  • Arrow in box method: each orbital of the subshell is shown as a box, with the electron represented by an arrow (up for anticlockwise spin, down for clockwise). An orbital with one electron has an upward arrow; a second electron is added as a downward arrow. Opposite spins indicate paired electrons, while a single electron without a partner is unpaired. This method is preferred because it shows all four quantum numbers.
  • Condensed method: write the noble gas symbol of the previous period in brackets to represent the inner electrons, followed by the configuration of the electrons outside that core. Silicon is written as [Ne]3s2 3p2.

Examples from the first 18 elements: Na = 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 = [Ne]3s1; Cl = 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5 = [Ne]3s2 3p5; Ar = 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 = [Ne]3s2 3p6.

Electronic Configuration of Cations

The configurations of ions are found by adding or removing electrons, following the same Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules used for neutral atoms in their ground state. For cations, electrons are removed starting from the outermost p orbital, then the s orbital, and finally the d orbitals if necessary. Neutral aluminium is 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p1; removing three electrons from the outermost 3p and 3s orbitals gives Al3+ = 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, which is isoelectronic with the noble gas neon.

Electronic Configuration of Anions

For anions, electrons are added according to Aufbau's building-up principle. Neutral sulphur is 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p4; adding two electrons fills the partially filled 3p subshell, giving S2- = 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p6, isoelectronic with argon. The stability of many ions depends on attaining a noble gas configuration: Na+, Mg2+ and Cl- all have the same electron configuration as neon (1s2 2s2 2p6).

Key Points

  • Configurations can be written by the subshell, arrow-in-box or condensed (noble gas core) method.
  • The arrow-in-box method is preferred because it displays all four quantum numbers.
  • Cations: remove electrons from the outermost subshells first; anions: add electrons by the Aufbau order.
  • Ions are especially stable when they attain a noble gas configuration.
lessons.title: Writing the Electronic Configuration of Atoms and Ions

lessons.notes_html:
The atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two similar bonded atoms and is typically used to measure the size of the atom. Atomic radii are usually measured in nanometres (nm) (1 nm = 10^-9 m), angstroms (Å) (1 Å = 10^-10 m) or picometres (pm) (1 pm = 10^-12 m).

Atomic Radius Across a Period

The atomic radius generally decreases across a period. This is due to an increase in the nuclear charge, which pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus. The number of core electrons remains the same across the period, so the shielding effect remains almost constant.

Element (Period 3)NaMgAlSiPSClAr
Atomic radius (pm)18616014311811410499188

Atomic Radius Down a Group

The atomic radius increases down a group due to the increase in the number of shells and the shielding effect. For example, the atomic radius of the alkali metals increases down the group: Li 152 pm, Na 186 pm, K 227 pm, Rb 248 pm, Cs 265 pm.

Key Points

  • Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two similar bonded atoms.
  • Across a period, atomic radius decreases as nuclear charge rises and shielding stays nearly constant.
  • Down a group, atomic radius increases because new shells are added and shielding increases.
  • Units: nm, Å and pm (1 pm = 10^-12 m).
lessons.title: Atomic Radii of Elements

lessons.notes_html:
Ionic radii are measurements of the sizes of charged particles called ions, which are formed when atoms gain or lose electrons. The size of an ion is different from that of the neutral atom because of changes in the arrangement of its electrons. Ionic radii are usually measured in nanometres, angstroms or picometres.

Cationic and Anionic Radii

  • Cationic radii: when electrons are removed, the electron cloud contracts. The loss of electrons decreases electron-electron repulsion, allowing the positive charge to draw the remaining electrons closer to the nucleus, so a cation is smaller than its parent atom.
  • Anionic radii: when electrons are added, the electron cloud expands because of increased electron-electron repulsion, so an anion is larger than its parent atom.

Trends in Ionic Radii

Cationic radii generally increase down a group due to the increase in electronic shells: Li+ 76 pm, Na+ 102 pm, K+ 138 pm, Rb+ 152 pm. Cationic radii generally decrease across a period due to increased nuclear charge while the number of shells remains constant:

ElementNaMgAlSi
Atomic radius (pm)186160143118
Ion formedNa+Mg2+Al3+Si4+
Ionic radius (pm)102725440

Anionic radii also increase down a group with the number of shells: Cl- 181 pm, Br- 196 pm, I- 220 pm (compare the atomic radii Cl 99 pm, Br 114 pm, I 133 pm). Along a period, anions remain much larger than their parent atoms, e.g. O2- 140 pm (atom 66 pm) and F- 133 pm (atom 64 pm).

Key Points

  • A cation is always smaller than its parent atom; an anion is always larger.
  • Removing electrons contracts the electron cloud; adding electrons expands it.
  • Ionic radii increase down a group as shells are added.
  • Cationic radii decrease across a period as nuclear charge increases.
lessons.title: Ionic Radii of Elements

lessons.notes_html:
Ionisation energy (IE) is the minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron of an isolated gaseous atom, positive ion or molecule. It is usually measured in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol) or electron volts (eV). For example: Na(g) → Na+(g) + e-, IE = 496 kJ/mol; Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e-, IE = 738 kJ/mol.

Factors Affecting Ionisation Energy

  • Nuclear charge: the greater the nuclear charge, the higher the ionisation energy, because a larger nuclear charge binds the electrons more tightly to the nucleus.
  • Atomic size (radius): the larger the atomic radius, the lower the ionisation energy, because the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held.
  • Electron shielding (shielding effect): inner electrons shield the outer electrons from part of the nuclear attraction, reducing the effective nuclear charge and lowering the ionisation energy.
  • Subshell and orbital: electrons in higher energy subshells are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are easier to remove; electrons in the s orbital are more difficult to remove than those in p, d or f orbitals.
  • Spin-pair repulsion: two electrons with opposite spins in the same orbital repel each other, which lowers the energy needed to remove one of them. Oxygen (2p4) has paired electrons in one 2p orbital, so oxygen is easier to ionise than nitrogen, whose half-filled 2p3 subshell is more stable and has no spin-pair repulsion.

Trends in Ionisation Energy

  • Across a period: ionisation energy generally increases, due to an increase in nuclear charge and a decrease in atomic radius.
  • Down a group: ionisation energy generally decreases, due to an increase in atomic size and the shielding effect.
  • Exception to trends: half-filled and fully-filled orbitals are more stable than partially-filled ones, so elements with half-filled or fully-filled orbitals have higher ionisation energies.

Key Points

  • Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
  • IE rises with nuclear charge and falls with atomic size and shielding.
  • IE increases across a period and decreases down a group.
  • Half-filled and fully-filled subshells give extra stability and higher IE (e.g. N higher than O).
lessons.title: Ionisation Energy

lessons.notes_html:
Successive ionisation energy is the energy required to remove the outermost electron from an atom, followed by the energy required to remove the next electron, and so on, until all electrons have been removed. The energies used to remove the first, second and third electrons are called the first (IE1), second (IE2) and third (IE3) ionisation energies. For magnesium: Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e-, IE1 = 738 kJ/mol; Mg+(g) → Mg2+(g) + e-, IE2 = 1451 kJ/mol; Mg2+(g) → Mg3+(g) + e-, IE3 = 7730 kJ/mol.

Why Successive Ionisation Energies Increase

The order is always IE3 greater than IE2 greater than IE1. As electrons are removed, the atom becomes more positively charged, making it harder to remove another electron; the ion also becomes smaller and more compact, increasing the attraction for the remaining electrons. For aluminium the successive values (kJ/mol) are 577, 1817, 2745, then a large jump to 11577 and 14842, showing that the fourth electron comes from an inner shell.

Prediction of Electronic Configuration and Position of Elements from Ionisation Energies

The electronic configuration and position of an element can be predicted by analysing its successive ionisation energies. A relatively small increase in successive ionisation energies indicates that electrons are being removed from the same outer shell, while a significant jump suggests that the next electron is being removed from an inner shell. For beryllium, IE1 = 899 kJ/mol and IE2 = 1757 kJ/mol are for the two outermost 2s electrons, but IE3 = 14849 kJ/mol jumps sharply because the third electron comes from the inner 1s orbital. This deduces the configuration 1s2 2s2, with two valence electrons in the second shell, placing beryllium in Group 2 and Period 2.

Key Points

  • Successive ionisation energies always increase: each next electron is harder to remove.
  • The ion shrinks and its positive charge grows as electrons are removed.
  • A big jump in successive IE marks the start of removal from an inner shell.
  • The position of the jump reveals the number of valence electrons, and hence the group of the element.
lessons.title: Successive Ionisation Energy

lessons.notes_html:
The forces of attraction that hold atoms or ions together in compounds are called chemical bonds. Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to complete their valence shell (2 or 8 electrons, like noble gases) and become stable. Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons (shared electrons) to itself. Fluorine attracts bonding electrons most strongly; caesium very weakly.

Factors Affecting Electronegativity

  • Nuclear charge: electronegativity generally increases as nuclear charge (number of protons) increases.
  • Atomic radius: electronegativity decreases as atomic radius increases, because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are attracted weakly.
  • Shielding effect: electrons in inner shells partly shield the outer electrons from the full effect of the nuclear charge, lowering electronegativity.

Electronegativity Trends in the Periodic Table

  • Along a period: electronegativity increases from left to right, because nuclear charge increases. Noble gases are taken as zero and do not follow the trend.
  • Down a group: electronegativity decreases from top to bottom, because atomic size and shielding effect increase.
  • Fluorine is the most electronegative atom and caesium the least. Elements at the top right have high values; those at the left have low values.

Pauling's Electronegativity Values to Predict the Formation of Ionic and Covalent Bonds

On Pauling's scale, values range from 0.70 (francium) to 3.98 (fluorine). The greater the difference in electronegativity (ΔEN) between the bonding atoms, the greater the bond polarity and the stronger the bond. ΔEN = larger value − smaller value.

ΔENBond Type
0Purely covalent (100% covalent)
0.4 or lessNonpolar covalent
Between 0.4 and 1.7Polar covalent
Equal to 1.750% covalent and 50% ionic, regarded as ionic
Exceeds 1.7Ionic

Note: in HF, ΔEN is about 1.9, near the ionic range, yet the bond remains polar covalent rather than ionic. Sharing in covalent bonds is rarely equal: in polar covalent H−Cl, one atom pulls electrons more strongly, giving partial charges.

Key Points

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electrons to itself.
  • It increases with nuclear charge and decreases with atomic radius and shielding effect.
  • It increases along a period and decreases down a group; F is highest, Cs is lowest.
  • Pauling scale: 0.70 (Fr) to 3.98 (F).
  • ΔEN up to 0.4 = nonpolar covalent; 0.4–1.7 = polar covalent; above 1.7 = ionic.
lessons.title: Electronegativity

lessons.notes_html:
In 1940, Sidgwick and Powell laid the groundwork for explaining molecular shapes from the arrangement of electron pairs in the valence shell. In 1957, Gillespie and Nyholm formalised the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory, which explains the shapes and bond angles of molecules and ions through electrostatic repulsion between electron pairs.

Main Features (Postulates) of VSEPR Theory

  • The shapes of molecules depend on the number of electron pairs (both bond pairs and lone pairs) in the outermost shell of the central atom.
  • Electron pairs in the outer shell repel each other because of their negative charges. This repulsion is minimised by placing the electron pairs at the greatest possible angular distances from each other.
  • A lone pair (lp) occupies more space (due to strong repulsions) than a bond pair (bp).
  • The order of repulsion is: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
  • A multiple bond (double or triple) is treated as a single electron pair for structure determination.
  • Molecules with only bond pairs have regular shapes, while those with lone pairs exhibit irregular shapes.

A higher electronegativity of the central atom increases repulsions between bonding pairs, while that of the attached atom reduces the effect of bond pairs. Limitation: VSEPR theory does not give a detailed explanation of electron sharing in covalent (σ and π) bonds, which is essential for understanding bond formation.

Key Points

  • VSEPR theory was formalised by Gillespie and Nyholm in 1957.
  • Molecular shape depends on the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.
  • Electron pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion.
  • Repulsion order: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp.
  • A multiple bond counts as one electron pair.
  • Only bond pairs = regular shape; lone pairs present = irregular shape.
lessons.title: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) Theory: Understanding Molecular Geometry

lessons.notes_html:
The geometry around a central atom A is described by the formula ABmEn, where B is a bonded atom, E is a lone pair, m is the number of bonded atoms and n is the number of lone pairs.

Electron PairsTypeShapeBond AngleExamples
2AB2Linear180°BeCl2, CdCl2, CO2, CS2, HgCl2
3AB3Planar triangular (trigonal planar)120°BCl3, AlCl3, CO3^2-, SO3
3AB2EDistorted triangular / bentLess than 120°SnCl2, SO2
4AB4Tetrahedral109.5°SiH4, CCl4, NH4+, SO4^2-, CH4
4AB3ETrigonal pyramidalLess than 109.5° (107.5° in NH3, H3O+)NH3, NF3, H3O+
4AB2E2Angular / bentLess than 109.5° (104.5° in H2O)H2O, H2S, SCl2, NH2-, SeCl2
5AB5Trigonal (triangular) bipyramidal120° equatorial, 90° axialPF5, PCl5, SbCl5
6AB6Octahedral90°SF6, TeF6

In PF5, the axial fluorine atoms face more repulsion from the equatorial atoms, so axial bonds are slightly longer than equatorial bonds. In an octahedral molecule the terms axial and equatorial are not used, because all six bonds are equivalent. A lone pair compresses the angles between bond pairs because of lone pair repulsion.

Key Points

  • Geometry is written as ABmEn: m = bonded atoms, n = lone pairs on the central atom.
  • 2 pairs = linear, 180°; 3 pairs = trigonal planar, 120°.
  • 4 pairs = tetrahedral, 109.5°; one lone pair gives pyramidal (107.5°), two lone pairs give bent (104.5°).
  • 5 pairs = trigonal bipyramidal, 120° and 90°.
  • 6 pairs = octahedral, 90°, with all bonds equivalent.
  • Lone pairs reduce bond angles below the regular values.
lessons.title: Shapes and Bond Angles in Molecules and Ions

lessons.notes_html:
Valence bond theory was first proposed by W. Heitler and Fritz London in 1927 and later developed by Linus Pauling and J.C. Slater in 1931. It explains bond formation (sharing of electrons), bond strength and the geometry of molecules.

Main Points

  • Covalent bonds are formed by the overlapping of half-filled atomic orbitals in the valence shell.
  • A single covalent bond is formed by the overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals.
  • A multiple bond (double or triple covalent bond) is formed by the overlap of more than two half-filled atomic orbitals. Overlapping means a common region of two orbitals with high electron density.
  • As a result of overlapping, the electrons with opposite spins pair up and become stable by releasing energy.
  • The extent of overlap determines bond strength: the greater the overlapping, the stronger the bond.
  • The direction of the bond is determined by the direction of the two overlapping orbitals, when orbitals other than s-orbitals are involved.

Bonding in Polyatomic Molecules: Methane as an Example

The ground state configuration of carbon is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz0: the 2s orbital is filled and only two p-orbitals are half-filled, so carbon should form only two bonds. Promoting one 2s electron to the empty 2p orbital gives the excited state 1s2, 2s1, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1, with four unpaired electrons. But the p-orbitals are perpendicular, so three bond angles would be 90° with different bond lengths, while experiment shows all four C−H bonds of methane are identical. VBT alone cannot explain polyatomic molecules like methane; the concept of hybridisation was introduced to explain this.

Key Points

  • VBT: Heitler and London (1927); developed by Pauling and Slater (1931).
  • A covalent bond forms by overlap of half-filled valence orbitals.
  • Paired electrons with opposite spins release energy and become stable.
  • Greater overlap means a stronger bond.
  • Bond direction follows the direction of the overlapping orbitals.
  • VBT cannot explain the four identical bonds of CH4 without hybridisation.
lessons.title: Valence Bond Theory

lessons.notes_html:
On the basis of overlapping of orbitals, covalent bonds are of two types: sigma bond and pi-bond.

Sigma Bond (σ-bond)

A covalent bond formed by head-to-head (linear) overlap of two atomic orbitals, in which electron density is maximum around the bond axis, is a sigma bond.

OverlapExampleHow It Forms
s–sH2Half-filled 1s orbitals of two H atoms overlap along the bond axis: H + H → H2
p–pF2Half-filled p-orbitals of two atoms overlap head-on: F + F → F2 (also Cl2, Br2, I2)
s–pHF1s orbital of H overlaps with the half-filled 2p orbital of F; the filled orbitals of F do not take part

Pi Bond (π-bond)

The bond formed by sidewise (parallel) overlap of two p-orbitals is a pi bond, named after the Greek letter π. Overlap in pi bonds is less effective than in sigma bonds, so pi bonds are weaker. Single bonds are sigma bonds; a double bond has one sigma and one pi bond; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds.

  • O2 molecule: each O is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz2, with two half-filled p-orbitals. Head-on overlap of 2px orbitals forms the σ-bond; side-to-side overlap of 2py orbitals forms the π-bond, with electron density maximum above and below the bond axis (O=O).
  • N2 molecule: each N is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1, with three half-filled p-orbitals. Linear overlap of 2px gives one σ-bond; parallel overlap of 2py and 2pz gives two π-bonds (N≡N).

Key Points

  • Sigma bond: head-to-head overlap; electron density maximum on the bond axis; stronger.
  • s–s overlap gives H2, p–p gives F2, s–p gives HF.
  • Pi bond: sidewise overlap of p-orbitals; density above and below the axis; weaker.
  • Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π; triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π.
  • O2 has one σ and one π bond; N2 has one σ and two π bonds.
lessons.title: Types of Overlapping and Nature of Covalent Bonds

lessons.notes_html:
In 1931, Linus Pauling introduced hybridisation to explain the characteristic geometric shapes of polyatomic molecules like CH4, NH3, BeCl2, AlCl3 and H2O, and the formation of multiple bonds in C2H2 and C2H4. According to him, the atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies combine to form a new set of equivalent atomic orbitals called hybrid orbitals; this phenomenon is known as hybridisation.

Important Features

  • The number of hybrid orbitals produced is always equal to the number of atomic orbitals combined.
  • The hybridised orbitals are always equivalent in energy and shape.
  • Hybridisation combines at least two non-equivalent atomic orbitals, such as s and p, so a hybrid orbital is not a pure atomic orbital.
  • The shape of a hybrid orbital differs from that of the original atomic orbitals.
  • The geometries match precisely those predicted by VSEPR theory.
  • Hybridisation occurs within the central atom, after excitation and before bond formation; the concept is not used for isolated atoms.
  • Hybrid orbitals form stronger, more stable bonds than pure atomic orbitals.

Key Points

  • Hybridisation was introduced by Linus Pauling in 1931.
  • Orbitals of different shapes and energies mix to give equivalent hybrid orbitals.
  • Number of hybrid orbitals formed = number of atomic orbitals mixed.
  • All hybrid orbitals are equal in energy and shape.
  • It takes place in the central atom after excitation, before bonding.
  • Hybrid orbitals form stronger bonds than pure atomic orbitals.
lessons.title: Atomic Orbital Hybridisation

lessons.notes_html:
The common types are sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation, depending on the number and type of orbitals mixed.

sp3-Hybridisation — Formation of Methane

Mixing one s and three p-orbitals gives four identical sp3 hybrid orbitals, each with 25% s and 75% p character. In CH4, excited carbon (1s2, 2s1, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1) forms four sp3 orbitals, each with a large lobe in one direction. They overlap with the 1s orbitals of four H atoms, forming four equivalent sp3–s σ bonds directed to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°.

sp2-Hybridisation — Formation of Ethene (Ethylene)

Mixing one s and two p-orbitals gives three identical sp2 hybrid orbitals, each with 33% s and 67% p character. In C2H4, each carbon bonds to three atoms with no lone pair. One 2s and two 2p orbitals form three sp2 orbitals; the 2pz orbital stays unhybridised. C−H σ bonds form by sp2 (carbon)–1s (hydrogen) overlap, the C−C σ bond by sp2–sp2 overlap, and the π bond by overlap of the unhybridised p-orbitals. All six atoms are coplanar, trigonal planar, with bond angles around 120°.

sp-Hybridisation — Formation of Ethyne (Acetylene)

Mixing one s and one p-orbital gives two identical sp hybrid orbitals, each with 50% s and 50% p character. In C2H2, one 2s and one 2p (2px) orbital of carbon hybridise. One sp orbital of each carbon overlaps with a half-filled 1s orbital of hydrogen (C−H σ bond); the other overlaps with the sp orbital of the other carbon (C≡C σ bond). The remaining 2py and 2pz orbitals form two pi bonds by sideways overlap. Ethyne is linear, 180°, with three sigma bonds and two pi bonds in total.

HybridisationAngleShapeHybrid OrbitalsSigma BondsPi BondsExample
sp3109.5°Tetrahedral440Methane
sp2120°Trigonal planar351Ethene
sp180°Linear232Ethyne

Key Points

  • sp3: 1 s + 3 p, 25% s character, tetrahedral, 109.5° — CH4.
  • sp2: 1 s + 2 p, 33% s character, trigonal planar, 120° — C2H4, one p left for the π bond.
  • sp: 1 s + 1 p, 50% s character, linear, 180° — C2H2, two p orbitals left for two π bonds.
  • Unhybridised p-orbitals always form pi bonds.
lessons.title: Types of Hybridisation

lessons.notes_html:
Valence bond theory does not explain why O2 is paramagnetic and N2 is diamagnetic. Around 1932, Friedrich Hund and Robert Mulliken introduced molecular orbital theory. Like atomic orbitals, molecular orbitals have specific energy and shapes and hold a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins. An atomic orbital belongs to one atom only, whereas a molecular orbital extends over all the atoms in the molecule.

Main Points of MOT

  • The number of molecular orbitals formed equals the number of combining atomic orbitals: two atomic orbitals give one bonding molecular orbital and one antibonding molecular orbital.
  • The overlapped atomic orbitals do not maintain their identity.
  • The molecular orbital of lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals is the bonding orbital (σ, π); the one of higher energy is the antibonding orbital (σ*, π*).
  • Electron density in a bonding orbital is maximum between the nuclei; in an antibonding orbital it is minimum between the nuclei.
  • The bonding orbital is more stable because it is lower in energy than the antibonding orbital.
  • Filling of molecular orbitals follows the same rules as filling of atomic orbitals.
  • Bond order indicates the number of bonds between two atoms: 1 = single, 2 = double, 3 = triple. Higher bond order means stronger and shorter bonds.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Bond Order = (nb − na) / 2nb = electrons in bonding MOs, na = electrons in antibonding MOs

The energy order of MOs is of two types. For molecules with atomic number Z ≤ 7 (H2, He2, Li2, Be2, B2, C2, N2), π2py and π2pz come before σ2px. For Z ≥ 8, σ2px comes before π2py and π2pz; the antibonding order also reverses.

Sigma (σ) and Pi (π) Molecular Orbitals

  • Linear head-on overlap forms a σ orbital; electron density is concentrated around the bond axis, with more attraction in the bonding MO and more repulsion in the antibonding MO (which has a node between the nuclei).
  • Parallel (sidewise) overlap forms a π orbital; electron density lies above and below the bond axis, with less attraction in the bonding MO and less repulsion in the antibonding MO.
  • Atomic orbitals of the same symmetry only combine: a 2px orbital combines with 2px, not with 2py or 2pz.

Key Points

  • MOT (Hund and Mulliken, 1932) explains the paramagnetism of O2, which VBT cannot.
  • MOs formed = atomic orbitals combined; half are bonding, half antibonding.
  • Bonding MO: lower energy, density maximum between nuclei, more stable.
  • Bond order = (nb − na)/2; higher bond order = stronger, shorter bond.
  • Energy order differs for Z ≤ 7 and Z ≥ 8 molecules.
lessons.title: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)

lessons.notes_html:
MOT gives the precise electronic configurations of homonuclear diatomic molecules, which explain their properties.

MoleculeMO PictureBond OrderResult
H2Two 1s orbitals form σ1s and σ*1s; 2 electrons fill σ1s only: σ(1s)2(2 − 0)/2 = 1Single bond; stable, exists
He2 (hypothetical)4 electrons: σ(1s)2 σ*(1s)2(2 − 2)/2 = 0No bond; unstable, helium stays monoatomic
N2σ(2s)2 σ*(2s)2 π(2py)2 = π(2pz)2 σ(2px)2(8 − 2)/2 = 3Triple bond N≡N: one σ and two π bonds
O2σ(2s)2 σ*(2s)2 σ(2px)2 π(2py)2 = π(2pz)2 π*(2py)1 = π*(2pz)1(8 − 4)/2 = 2Double bond: one σ and one π bond

Paramagnetism and Diamagnetism in Molecules

Molecules are diamagnetic when all their electrons are paired in molecular orbitals, and paramagnetic if they have one or more unpaired electrons. Paramagnetic substances are attracted to a magnetic field, while diamagnetic substances are slightly repelled. The strength of paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons. O2 has two unpaired electrons, one each in the π*2py and π*2pz orbitals, so it is paramagnetic. F2 has no unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic.

Key Points

  • H2: bond order 1, stable single bond.
  • He2: bond order 0, so it does not exist; helium is monoatomic.
  • N2: bond order 3, a triple bond, diamagnetic.
  • O2: bond order 2, a double bond, with two unpaired electrons.
  • Unpaired electrons = paramagnetic (attracted to a magnet); all paired = diamagnetic (slightly repelled).
  • O2 is paramagnetic and F2 is diamagnetic.
lessons.title: Applications of MO Theory

lessons.notes_html:
The reactivity of covalent molecules can be compared by looking at their bond energy values and bond lengths.

Bond Energy

Bond energy is the amount of energy needed to break a bond. Higher bond energy indicates stronger and more stable bonds, which make the molecule less reactive.

Bond Length

Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Shorter bond lengths are associated with stronger, higher-energy bonds, giving increased stability and lower reactivity, and vice versa.

Comparing Reactivity

In general, molecules with higher bond energy and shorter bond lengths are more stable and less reactive, while molecules with lower bond energy and longer bond lengths are less stable and more reactive. Other factors, such as functional groups, electronegativity differences and molecular geometry, also influence reactivity.

Example Comparisons of Halogen Molecules

Halogen (X2)Bond Length (pm)Bond Energy (kJ/mol)
F2142158
Cl2199243
Br2228193
I2266151

Cl2 is more stable than F2 because it has a higher bond energy, so the Cl−Cl bond is more difficult to break; F2 is more reactive despite being higher in the group. The low bond energy of fluorine comes from strong electron repulsion between its small, electronegative atoms. I2 has a longer bond length and lower bond energy, making it less stable and more likely to take part in substitution or addition reactions, though its reactivity is limited by its lower bond polarity and oxidising ability compared to Cl2 or Br2.

Key Points

  • Bond energy = energy needed to break a bond; higher = stronger, more stable, less reactive.
  • Bond length = distance between the two nuclei; shorter = stronger bond, lower reactivity.
  • Down the halogens, bond length increases: F2 142 pm to I2 266 pm.
  • Cl2 (243 kJ/mol) is more stable and less reactive than F2 (158 kJ/mol).
  • F2 is unusually reactive because of strong repulsion between its small atoms.
lessons.title: Comparing Reactivity of Covalent Molecules: Bond Energy and Bond Length

lessons.notes_html:
The attractive forces between atoms within each molecule are called intramolecular forces, while the forces of attraction between molecules of a substance are known as intermolecular forces. Intramolecular forces are the chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.

  • The physical properties of a substance, such as boiling point, vapour pressure, surface tension, viscosity, heat of vaporisation, heat of fusion and heat of sublimation, depend on intermolecular forces. The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more difficult it is to separate its molecules.
  • The chemical properties, shapes of molecules and bond energies depend on intramolecular forces, which are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.
  • In general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are stronger than intermolecular forces.

For water: H2O(l) → H2O(g) on vaporisation needs ΔH = +40.67 kJ/mol, which breaks only the intermolecular forces. Decomposing H2O(g) → 2H(g) + O(g) needs ΔH = +934 kJ/mol, which breaks the intramolecular forces. Intermolecular forces break during evaporation of water, while intramolecular forces break during its decomposition.

Key Points

  • Intramolecular forces act within a molecule: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.
  • Intermolecular forces act between molecules and decide physical properties.
  • Intramolecular forces are much stronger than intermolecular forces.
  • Vaporising water needs 40.67 kJ/mol; decomposing it needs 934 kJ/mol.
  • Evaporation breaks intermolecular forces; decomposition breaks intramolecular forces.
lessons.title: Intermolecular Forces

lessons.notes_html:
Intermolecular forces are commonly known as van der Waals forces, after the Dutch scientist Johannes van der Waals (1837–1923). There are three main types: London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding. London forces and dipole-dipole forces are collectively known as van der Waals forces.

London Dispersion Forces

Fritz London (1930) recognised these weak forces between non-polar molecules; they are also called instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces. Electron motion in an atom or molecule produces an instantaneous dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, generating a weak attraction. In neon, when atoms come close, the electron cloud of one atom is disturbed and bends toward one side, forming an instantaneous dipole; this induces a dipole in the next atom. The forces disappear when the electrons become symmetrical again. They exist in halogens, noble gases and non-polar molecules such as H2, N2, CH4, CO2, SO3, SiH4 and CCl4; without them such substances could not condense or solidify.

Strength of London Forces

  • Size: larger atoms and molecules, with more electrons and heavier mass, polarise more easily. Strength is directly proportional to polarisability (the degree to which the electron cloud is distorted). So boiling points of halogens and noble gases increase down a group.
  • Shape: C5H12 isomers boil at different temperatures: n-pentane 36°C, iso-pentane 28°C, neo-pentane 9.5°C. In n-pentane and isopentane the valence electrons are closer to the surface, so their London forces are stronger than in compact neo-pentane.

Dipole-Dipole Forces

These permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces are present only in polar molecules. In HCl, chlorine is more electronegative, so it gains a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge; the positive end of one HCl attracts the negative end of another. London forces occur in both polar and non-polar molecules, but dipole-dipole forces occur only in polar molecules. Their strength depends on the distance between molecules and the electronegativity difference: greater ΔEN means greater polarity, stronger forces and a higher boiling point. Propane and acetaldehyde both have molar mass 44 g/mol, but polar acetaldehyde boils at 20.85°C while non-polar propane boils at −42.15°C.

Key Points

  • Van der Waals forces: London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding.
  • London forces arise from instantaneous dipole–induced dipole attraction; present in all molecules.
  • London forces grow with size, electron number, polarisability and surface contact.
  • n-Pentane (36°C) > iso-pentane (28°C) > neo-pentane (9.5°C) in boiling point.
  • Dipole-dipole forces act only between polar molecules and grow with polarity.
lessons.title: Types of Intermolecular Forces

lessons.notes_html:
The attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom in one polar molecule and a lone pair of a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N) in another polar molecule is called hydrogen bonding. It is not a true chemical bond; it is a special, very strong type of dipole-dipole force, about five to ten times stronger than other dipole-dipole forces. It is limited to molecules containing N−H, O−H and H−F groups, e.g. NH3, H2O and HF, and is shown as a dotted line between molecules.

Anomalous Properties of Water

In liquid water, hydrogen bonds constantly break and reform, so molecules are connected irregularly. On cooling, the molecules arrange into a regular hexagonal pattern with stable hydrogen bonds, creating empty spaces in the structure of ice, which causes it to expand. Ice occupies about 10% more volume, so its density falls: liquid water at 4°C is about 1.00 g/cm3, while ice at 0°C is about 0.917 g/cm3. Ice therefore floats on water; the floating layer insulates the water underneath, allowing fish and other aquatic life to survive in winter.

Significance of Hydrogen Bonding

  • Thermodynamic properties: hydrogen-bonded molecules show higher heats of vaporisation, melting points and boiling points, e.g. NH3, H2O and HF.
  • Biological significance: it holds the structure of proteins and DNA; proteins adopt helical structures through hydrogen bonding between amino acids, and hydrogen bonds keep the DNA double helix together.
  • High specific heat capacity: water (4.18 J/g°C, against iron 0.45 and ethanol 2.46) warms and cools slowly, stabilising temperatures on Earth's surface.
  • Solubility: hydrogen-bonded compounds such as ethanol and acetic acid dissolve in water; methane and benzene do not.
  • Cleaning action: the polar ends of soaps and detergents form hydrogen bonds with water, while the non-polar ends attract oil and grease.
  • Materials: it gives properties to food materials (carbohydrates), adhesives in paints and dyes, and the stickiness of honey and glycerin; water also shows high heat of vaporisation, surface tension and viscosity.

Key Points

  • Hydrogen bond: H attached to F, O or N attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N of another molecule.
  • It is a very strong dipole-dipole force, 5–10 times stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole forces.
  • Ice has an open hexagonal structure, about 10% more volume and lower density (0.917 g/cm3), so it floats.
  • It raises boiling points, melting points and specific heat, and helps solubility and cleaning action.
  • It is essential for protein folding and the DNA double helix.
lessons.title: Hydrogen Bonding

lessons.notes_html:
Molecular ions or polyatomic ions can sometimes appear to have more than eight electrons around the central atom. This is called an expanded octet. It is common in elements from the third period onwards, where d-orbitals are available for bonding.

Expanded Octets in Nitrate Ions

The nitrate ion (NO3-) has three oxygen atoms attached to a central nitrogen atom. In its Lewis structure, nitrogen forms one double bond with one oxygen and two single bonds with the other two oxygens; the two single-bonded oxygens carry a negative charge each and nitrogen carries a positive charge, giving the overall 1− charge. The negative charge is delocalised, causing resonance among the three N−O bonds, so all three N−O bonds are equivalent. Nitrogen belongs to the second period and has no vacant d-orbitals, so it cannot expand its octet: it satisfies the octet rule with exactly eight electrons around it, and the π-electrons are delocalised over the three N−O bonds.

Expanded Octets in Sulphate Ions

The sulphate ion (SO4^2-) has four oxygen atoms bonded to the central sulphur atom. Sulphur forms two single bonds with two oxygen atoms and two double bonds with the other two oxygen atoms. This gives a total of 12 electrons around the sulphur atom, exceeding the octet. Sulphur is in the third period, so its available d-orbitals allow this expanded octet.

Key Points

  • An expanded octet means more than 8 electrons around the central atom.
  • It is possible only from the third period onwards, where d-orbitals are available.
  • NO3-: nitrogen keeps exactly 8 electrons; resonance makes all three N−O bonds equivalent.
  • SO4^2-: sulphur has 12 electrons around it (two single and two double bonds).
  • Second-period elements like nitrogen cannot expand their octet.
lessons.title: Expanded Octets in Molecular Ions

lessons.notes_html:
A dative bond, also known as a coordinate covalent bond, occurs when two atoms share a pair of electrons, with both electrons originating from one of the atoms involved.

Formation of Dative Bond in Carbon Monoxide

Carbon, with four valence electrons, first forms a double bond with oxygen. Carbon then has an empty orbital. Oxygen donates a lone pair into this orbital, forming a dative (coordinate covalent) bond. As a result, CO contains a triple bond made up of two covalent bonds and one dative bond: in the Lewis picture, carbon carries a lone pair and oxygen donates its lone pair toward carbon, written :C≡O:.

Formation of Dative Bond in Ozone

An ozone molecule forms when an oxygen molecule reacts with an oxygen atom. One atom in the oxygen molecule donates a lone pair of electrons to the third oxygen atom (nascent oxygen), which has six electrons, forming a dative bond to complete its octet: :O=O: + :O: → O3.

Formation of Dative Bond in Hydronium Ion

The hydronium ion is created when water reacts with a hydrogen ion. The oxygen atom in the water molecule donates a lone pair of electrons to the hydrogen ion, which has a vacant orbital, forming a dative bond: H+ + H2O → [H3O]+. In the product, oxygen is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and still carries a lone pair, inside brackets with a + charge.

Key Points

  • A dative (coordinate covalent) bond: both shared electrons come from one atom only.
  • CO has a triple bond: two covalent bonds plus one dative bond from oxygen to carbon.
  • In O3, an oxygen of O2 donates a lone pair to a third oxygen atom.
