  • In H3O+, oxygen of water donates a lone pair to H+, which has a vacant orbital.
  • The donor must have a lone pair; the acceptor must have a vacant orbital.
lessons.title: The Formation of Dative Bond in CO, O3, and H3O+

lessons.notes_html:
Dipole moment measures the polarity of a bond in a covalently bonded molecule. The greater the dipole moment, the greater the polarity; a molecule with zero dipole moment is non-polar. Polar covalent bonds form between atoms with different electronegativities: in HCl, chlorine pulls electrons toward itself, gaining a partial negative charge (δ-) while hydrogen gains a partial positive charge (δ+). Such a molecule with a net charge separation is polar and has a dipole moment.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
μ = q × dDipole moment = charge at each end of a polar bond × distance between the charges
1 D = 3.34 × 10^-30 C.mConverting Debye (D) to SI units of coulomb metres (C.m)

Dipole moment (μ) is a vector quantity directed from positive to negative. It is shown by an arrow with the arrowhead pointing toward the negative side (δ-) and a cross toward the positive side (δ+). Water has a dipole moment of 1.85 D and ammonia 1.47 D, so water is more polar. In a diatomic molecule like HF or HCl, the charge q is equal to δ+ and δ-.

  • Diatomic molecules of different atoms (HF, HCl, CO) are polar and have dipole moments; those of the same atoms (H2, O2) are non-polar.
  • In polyatomic molecules, both bond polarity and molecular geometry decide the overall dipole moment. CO2 is linear and non-polar despite having polar bonds, because the bond dipoles cancel.
  • SO3 and CCl4 have polar bonds but no dipole moment, due to their symmetrical structures. Shapes of molecules can also be determined from dipole moment.

Key Points

  • Dipole moment measures bond/molecular polarity; zero means non-polar.
  • μ = q × d, measured in Debye (D) or C.m; 1 D = 3.34 × 10^-30 C.m.
  • It is a vector, directed from positive to negative.
  • H2O (1.85 D) is more polar than NH3 (1.47 D).
  • Symmetrical molecules like CO2, SO3 and CCl4 have polar bonds but zero net dipole moment.
lessons.title: Dipole Moment

lessons.notes_html:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It is classified by its physical states: solids, liquids, gases and plasma. In liquids, the particles are closely packed compared to gases, but not as tightly as in solids.

Composition and Spaces Between Molecules

Liquids consist of atoms or molecules. The molecules are so close together that there is very little empty space between them; the gaps are larger than those in solids but smaller than those in gases.

Compression and Expansion

Liquids are almost incompressible because their molecules are tightly packed; when pressure rises, their volume reduces only slightly, unlike gases. Liquids also show no appreciable increase in volume on heating.

Intermolecular Forces and Kinetic Energy

The intermolecular forces in liquids are stronger than in gases but weaker than in solids; the greater these forces, the higher the boiling point. The kinetic energy of liquid molecules is higher than that of solids and lower than that of gases; it increases with temperature and decreases on cooling.

Motion of Molecules and Diffusion

Liquid molecules slip and slide over one another, so liquids flow and take the shape of their container; they have no definite shape but a definite volume. Liquids diffuse slowly into other liquids with which they are miscible, due to the continuous movement of their molecules.

Key Points

  • Liquid particles are closely packed, with little empty space between them.
  • Liquids are almost incompressible and expand very little on heating.
  • Intermolecular forces in liquids lie between those of gases and solids.
  • Liquid molecules slip and slide over each other, so liquids flow.
  • Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape.
  • Diffusion in liquids is slow because molecules move gradually past each other.
lessons.title: Simple Properties of Liquids Based on Kinetic Molecular Theory

lessons.notes_html:
Evaporation is the spontaneous conversion of liquid molecules into vapours from the surface of a non-boiling liquid in an open container at a given temperature. It is a type of vaporisation, the process by which a liquid or solid changes into a gas.

Why Evaporation Occurs

At a given temperature, not all liquid molecules have the same kinetic energy. A fast-moving molecule reaching the surface may overcome the attractions of its neighbours and escape into the vapour state. Evaporation is an endothermic process, because energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces; the escaping molecules carry away energy, so evaporation cools the remaining liquid. Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body in the same way.

Factors Affecting Evaporation

  • Temperature: evaporation occurs at all temperatures; its rate increases with rising temperature, because the kinetic energy of the molecules rises.
  • Surface area: evaporation is a surface phenomenon; the larger the surface area, the greater the evaporation.
  • Intermolecular forces: the stronger the intermolecular forces, the lower the rate of evaporation; petrol evaporates faster than water because its intermolecular forces are weaker.

Key Points

  • Evaporation is the escape of high-energy molecules from the surface of a liquid.
  • It takes place at all temperatures and is an endothermic, cooling process.
  • Rate of evaporation increases with temperature and surface area.
  • Rate of evaporation decreases as intermolecular forces become stronger.
lessons.title: Evaporation

lessons.notes_html:
Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by liquid vapours in equilibrium with their pure liquid at a given temperature.

Dynamic Equilibrium

In a sealed, evacuated container, vapours formed by evaporation accumulate above the liquid. Some vapour molecules striking the surface are captured again by the liquid; this return of vapours into liquid is condensation. At first evaporation is faster than condensation, but eventually the two rates become equal. This state, in which the number of molecules leaving the liquid equals the number returning, is dynamic equilibrium: Liquid ⇌ Vapours (evaporation forward, condensation back).

Factors Affecting Vapour Pressure

  • Intermolecular forces: vapour pressure is inversely related to intermolecular attractions. At 25°C, water (24 mmHg) has a lower vapour pressure than chloroform (200 mmHg), because water has strong hydrogen bonds while chloroform has only weak London forces.
  • Temperature: vapour pressure increases with temperature; for water it rises from 24 mmHg at 25°C to 760 mmHg at 100°C.

Vapour pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid or on its surface area, because at equilibrium a change of surface area affects evaporation and condensation equally.

Key Points

  • Vapour pressure is measured when evaporation and condensation rates are equal.
  • Weaker intermolecular forces give a higher vapour pressure.
  • Vapour pressure rises with temperature.
  • It does not depend on the amount of liquid or its surface area.
lessons.title: Vapour Pressure

lessons.notes_html:
The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric or external pressure. On heating, the average kinetic energy and the vapour pressure rise until bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface. The temperature remains constant during boiling, because the heat supplied is used only to break the intermolecular forces and convert the liquid into vapour.

Boiling Points of Some Liquids (at 1 atm)

LiquidBoiling Point (°C)LiquidBoiling Point (°C)
Acetic acid118.5Carbon tetrachloride76.5
Acetone56.0Ethyl alcohol78.3
Ammonia-33.3Ethylene glycol197

Factors Affecting the Boiling Point

  • Intermolecular forces: the stronger the forces, the higher the boiling point; water (100°C) boils higher than ethyl alcohol (78.26°C). Without hydrogen bonding, water would boil at about -75°C.
  • External pressure: the boiling point rises with external pressure and falls when pressure falls. Water boils at 100°C at 760 mmHg, at about 98°C at Murree (700 mmHg), at about 71°C on Mount Everest (240 mmHg), and at 110°C at 1074.6 mmHg.

Applications

In a pressure cooker, trapped steam raises the pressure, the boiling point of water rises (a commercial cooker reaches 140°C), and food cooks faster. In vacuum distillation, distillation is done at low pressure so that liquids which decompose at their boiling points can be purified; glycerin decomposes at 290°C at 760 torr but boils safely at 210°C at 50 torr.

Key Points

  • At the boiling point, vapour pressure equals external pressure.
  • Temperature stays constant while a liquid boils.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces give a higher boiling point.
  • Higher external pressure raises the boiling point; lower pressure lowers it.
  • Boiling point does not depend on the amount of liquid.
lessons.title: Boiling Point

lessons.notes_html:
The internal resistance to the flow of a liquid is called viscosity, denoted by eta (η). The greater the viscosity, the slower a liquid flows; honey and glycerin flow slowly, while gasoline and water flow quickly. A liquid flows in layers; each layer resists the flow of the others because of internal friction arising from cohesive forces between the molecules, so the flow is slowest near the walls and fastest in the centre.

Units

The unit of viscosity is the poise (1 poise = 100 centipoise). Its SI unit is newton-second per metre square, Nsm^-2; 1 poise = 10^-1 kgm^-1s^-1.

Factors Affecting Viscosity

  • Intermolecular forces: stronger forces make a liquid more viscous, because the molecules resist sliding past one another. Small, non-polar molecules like benzene have low viscosity; hydrogen-bonded liquids have high viscosity. Water is more viscous than methyl alcohol, and glycerin, with more hydrogen bonding sites, has the highest viscosity.
  • Temperature: viscosity decreases as temperature increases, because the molecules gain kinetic energy and overcome the attractive forces more easily; honey and cooking oil flow faster when warm.
  • Molecular size and shape: viscosity also depends on the size and shape of the molecules.

Key Points

  • Viscosity is the internal resistance of a liquid to flow, symbol η.
  • It is caused by internal friction between the layers of a liquid.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding increase viscosity.
  • Viscosity decreases with an increase in temperature.
  • SI unit of viscosity is Nsm^-2; the common unit is the poise.
lessons.title: Viscosity

lessons.notes_html:
Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by one unit. It is represented by the Greek letter γ (gamma). It can also be defined as the force acting along the surface of a liquid at right angles to any line of unit length drawn on the surface.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Surface tension (γ) = Force / LengthForce per unit length acting on the liquid surface

Its unit is dyne/cm in CGS or N/m in SI units (energy form: erg/cm^2).

Cause of Surface Tension

Molecules inside the liquid are pulled equally in all directions, but molecules at the surface are pulled only downwards and sideways by the inner molecules, with no upward pull. This inward pull makes the surface contract and behave like a stretched piece of rubber, so a water strider insect can walk on water and a carefully placed razor blade can float on it. The magnitude of surface tension depends on the intermolecular forces and on temperature.

Key Points

  • Surface tension is the energy needed to increase surface area by one unit.
  • γ = Force / Length; SI unit is N/m.
  • It arises from the unbalanced inward pull on surface molecules.
  • The liquid surface behaves like a stretched elastic skin.
  • It depends on intermolecular forces and temperature.
lessons.title: Surface tension

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrogen bonding between water molecules gives water its unusual properties. The key properties influenced by hydrogen bonding are:

High Boiling and Melting Points

Much energy is needed to break the strong hydrogen bonds, so water has a boiling point of 100°C and a melting point higher than expected for a molecule of its size. Without hydrogen bonding, water would boil at about -75°C and would not exist as a liquid at ordinary temperatures.

Cohesion and Surface Tension

Hydrogen bonding causes cohesion, the attraction between molecules of the same substance. This gives water a high surface tension, which lets it form droplets and allows small insects to walk on its surface.

Low Vapour Pressure of Water

The hydrogen bonds hold the molecules tightly, so few molecules escape into the gas phase; water therefore has a low vapour pressure.

High Specific Heat Capacity

Water has a high specific heat capacity (4.18 J/g°C). It absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, moderating the climate, especially in coastal areas.

High Heat of Vaporisation

Strong hydrogen bonds need much energy to be overcome during evaporation, so water has a high heat of vaporisation. This makes sweating an effective way of cooling organisms and prevents rapid temperature changes in the environment.

Key Points

  • Hydrogen bonding is responsible for the special properties of water.
  • Water has unusually high boiling and melting points for its size.
  • Cohesion from hydrogen bonding gives water high surface tension.
  • Water has a low vapour pressure and a high specific heat capacity.
  • Its high heat of vaporisation makes evaporation a strong cooling process.
lessons.title: The Role of Hydrogen Bonding in the Properties of Water

lessons.notes_html:
A phase change (state change) is the transformation of a substance from one physical state to another; it is a physical change. The energy change during a transformation at 1 atmosphere pressure is the enthalpy change, ΔH. ΔH is positive when energy is absorbed (endothermic: melting, sublimation, evaporation) and negative when heat is released (exothermic: freezing, condensation, deposition).

The Six Phase Changes

Change of StateProcessExample
Solid → LiquidMelting or fusionIce → Water
Solid → GasSublimationIodine → Iodine vapours
Liquid → SolidFreezingWater → Ice
Liquid → GasVaporisationWater → Steam
Gas → LiquidCondensationSteam → Water
Gas → SolidDepositionIodine vapours → Iodine

Molar Heat of Fusion

The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a solid into its liquid state at the melting point is the molar heat of fusion (molar enthalpy of fusion), ΔHfus. For ice it is 6.02 kJ/mol: H2O(s) → H2O(l). Freezing is the reverse process; it releases the same amount of heat, so ΔHfus for freezing is -6.02 kJ/mol.

Molar Heat of Vaporisation

The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a liquid into vapours at its boiling point is the molar heat of vaporisation, ΔHvap. For water it is 40.67 kJ/mol: H2O(l) → H2O(g). Condensation releases the same amount, with ΔHvap = -40.67 kJ/mol.

Key Formulae

ProcessΔH (kJ/mol)
H2O(s) → H2O(l) (fusion of ice)+6.02
H2O(l) → H2O(g) (vaporisation of water)+40.67
H2O(g) → H2O(l) (condensation of steam)-40.67

Key Points

  • Phase changes are physical changes with an enthalpy change ΔH.
  • Melting, sublimation and evaporation are endothermic (ΔH positive).
  • Freezing, condensation and deposition are exothermic (ΔH negative).
  • ΔHfus of ice is 6.02 kJ/mol; ΔHvap of water is 40.67 kJ/mol.
  • The reverse process has the same magnitude of ΔH with the opposite sign.
lessons.title: Energetics of Phase Changes

lessons.notes_html:
Molar heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one degree Celsius or one kelvin. It is represented by the symbol Cm and expressed in J/mol.K (or J/mol.°C). Substances with a high molar heat capacity need more energy to change their temperature. Water has a high molar heat capacity of about 75.3 J/mol.K, so it absorbs a large amount of heat with only a small temperature change; this keeps temperatures stable in coastal cities like Karachi and Gwadar.

Energy Change and Intermolecular Forces

The heats of fusion and vaporisation indicate the strengths of the intermolecular forces. These heats increase as the intermolecular forces grow stronger, because more energy is needed to change the physical state. Liquids showing hydrogen bonding, such as water, ethylene glycol and ethyl alcohol, have high heats of vaporisation. Heats of vaporisation are generally much higher than heats of fusion: fusion only loosens the particles so they can move around, with a small change in intermolecular distances, while vaporisation must completely break the intermolecular forces to separate the molecules.

Key Points

  • Molar heat capacity Cm is the heat needed to raise 1 mole by 1°C or 1 K.
  • Its unit is J/mol.K; for water Cm is about 75.3 J/mol.K.
  • High heat capacity substances resist temperature change.
  • Heats of fusion and vaporisation measure intermolecular force strength.
  • ΔHvap is much greater than ΔHfus for the same substance.
lessons.title: Molar Heat Capacity

lessons.notes_html:
The heat of fusion is crucial in studying glaciers and ice sheets, especially the polar ice caps. It is the energy needed to turn ice into water without changing its temperature, and it plays a hidden yet essential role in ice formation, movement and melting.

Ice Formation and Melting

The heat of fusion helps in the formation of glaciers from snow and tells us the energy required to convert ice back into water during melting.

Climate Change Indicators

Glaciers and ice sheets are indicators of climate change. Changes linked to the heat of fusion help in predicting temperature variations in the ice, which is crucial for understanding climate change.

Glacial Dynamics

Ice has a high heat of fusion, so a lot of energy is needed to melt it. Polar glaciers and ice sheets therefore resist small increases in temperature, stay intact and help stabilise the Earth's climate. The heat of fusion also helps in predicting glacier behaviour and modelling glacier dynamics.

Sea Level Rise

The heat of fusion determines the amount of water released when ice melts. Melted ice entering the oceans causes sea levels to rise; the heat absorbed during melting is mainly the heat of fusion.

Key Points

  • Heat of fusion is the energy that melts ice at constant temperature.
  • It governs glacier formation from snow and glacier melting.
  • Glaciers act as indicators of climate change.
  • The high heat of fusion of ice protects polar ice from small warming.
  • Melting ice, driven by the heat of fusion, raises sea levels.
lessons.title: Importance of Heat of Fusion

lessons.notes_html:
Gases differ from solids and liquids because of their particles and the large gaps between them. The kinetic molecular theory explains their compressibility, expandability and the pressure they exert.

Compressibility of Gases

Compressibility is the ability of a gas to decrease in volume when external pressure is applied. Gas molecules are widely spaced and move randomly; most of the volume of a gas is empty space (about 99.9%), so pressure pushes the molecules closer together and the volume falls greatly. For example, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is stored in compressed form in steel cylinders.

Expandability of Gases

Expandability is the property of a gas to increase in volume and fill all the space available. With high kinetic energy and no significant intermolecular forces, a gas expands to occupy its whole container; gases have no fixed shape or volume. When a perfume bottle is opened, its particles spread quickly through the room.

Pressure Exerted by Gases

Gas pressure is the force exerted by gas molecules when they collide with the walls of their container, measured as force per unit area. The total of these molecular impacts per unit area creates the pressure, for example the air pressure that keeps car and bicycle tyres in shape. Units of pressure include atmosphere (atm), pascal (Pa), mmHg or Torr, and bar.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
PV = nRTIdeal Gas Law: P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = gas constant, T = temperature in kelvin
1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101,325 PaConversion of pressure units

Key Points

  • Gases are highly compressible because of the large empty space between molecules.
  • Gases expand to fill the whole volume of their container.
  • Gas pressure is caused by molecular collisions with the container walls.
  • Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume.
  • The Ideal Gas Law, PV = nRT, relates pressure, volume, moles and temperature.
lessons.title: Physical Properties of Gases

lessons.notes_html:
Liquid crystals are the intermediate state between solids and liquids: substances have an arrangement of particles like solids but freedom of motion like liquids: Solid ⇌ Liquid Crystals ⇌ Liquid.

Discovery

Liquid crystals were discovered by the Austrian botanist and chemist Frederick Reinitzer in 1888, while studying cholesteryl benzoate. This compound melts at 145.5°C into a viscous, milky liquid and becomes a clear liquid at 178.5°C; on cooling, the changes reverse. He concluded that the liquid crystalline state lies between the crystalline solid and liquid states.

Properties

These turbid liquids possess properties of both solids, such as optical activity, and liquids, such as fluidity, viscosity and surface tension. Liquid crystals show some molecular order and are anisotropic (see the comparison in the next lesson).

Applications (Uses) of Liquid Crystals

  • As temperature sensors to detect faulty connections in microelectronic circuit boards.
  • In thermometers to measure the body temperature of infants.
  • To detect blockages in veins and arteries and infected areas like tumours, by mapping skin temperatures.
  • As a solvent in chromatographic separations.
  • In liquid crystal displays (LCDs) of digital wristwatches, clocks, flat-panel televisions, computers, laptop screens, cell phones and pH meters.
  • Some liquid crystals are used in hydraulic brakes because of their high viscosity.

Key Points

  • Liquid crystals form an intermediate state between solids and liquids.
  • They have particle order like solids and flow like liquids.
  • Cholesteryl benzoate shows two melting points: 145.5°C and 178.5°C.
  • Their most common use is in LCD screens and displays.
  • They are also used as temperature sensors and medical detectors.
lessons.title: Liquid Crystals

lessons.notes_html:
Liquid crystals, pure liquids and crystalline solids are three distinct states of matter. Pure liquids lack long-range order and flow freely to take the shape of their container. Crystalline solids have a highly ordered structure and maintain a fixed shape. Liquid crystals stand between them: they flow like liquids but show some degree of molecular alignment, which gives them unique optical properties used in LCD screens; they are anisotropic and respond to temperature changes.

Comparison Table

PropertyPure LiquidsLiquid CrystalsCrystalline Solids
FluidityYesYesNo
Definite ShapeNoNoYes
Definite Melting PointsNoNoYes
Anisotropic BehaviourNoYesYes
Optical PropertiesNoOptical AnisotropyOptical Anisotropy
Orderly Arrangement of ParticlesNoPartialYes

Key Points

  • Pure liquids are isotropic, with no orderly arrangement of particles.
  • Liquid crystals have partial particle order and show optical anisotropy.
  • Crystalline solids have a fixed, repeating arrangement and definite melting points.
  • Only crystalline solids have a definite shape; the other two flow.
lessons.title: Difference between Crystalline Solids, Liquid Crystals, and Pure Liquids

lessons.notes_html:
The kinetic molecular theory explains the behaviour of solids through the arrangement and motion of their particles.

Compression

Solids are generally less compressible than liquids and are considered incompressible. Foam, wood and cork only appear compressible because the air in their spaces is compressed; the solid matter itself remains unaffected.

Expansion

Changes of temperature or pressure have very little influence on the volume of solids.

Motion of Molecules

Solid particles are locked in place and cannot slip or slide over one another, so solids cannot flow, are rigid, and retain their shape and volume without a vessel. The particles have only vibrational motion about their fixed positions; this vibration grows stronger on heating until the lattice melts.

Interparticle Space

The particles in solids are very close to each other, tightly packed and more ordered than in liquids and gases; the spaces between them are the smallest of all three states.

Intermolecular Forces

The intermolecular forces in solids are much more effective than in liquids and gases, so solids have higher melting and boiling points.

Kinetic Energy

Solid particles have lower kinetic energy than liquids and gases. Kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature; if cooled sufficiently, all substances are converted into solids.

Key Points

  • Solids are incompressible and expand very little.
  • Solid particles only vibrate about fixed positions, so solids are rigid.
  • Interparticle spaces are smallest and forces strongest in solids.
  • Solids have the lowest kinetic energy of the three states.
  • Sufficient cooling converts every substance into a solid.
lessons.title: Simple Properties of Solids Based on Kinetic Molecular Theory

lessons.notes_html:
There are two types of solids based on the arrangement of particles: (i) crystalline solids and (ii) amorphous solids. Crystalline solids are further grouped as ionic, covalent, molecular and metallic solids.

Crystalline Solids

The solids that have a repetitive three-dimensional arrangement of particles are called crystalline solids, or true solids. Each particle occupies a fixed position, so they typically have flat faces that form specific angles with one another. Examples: diamond, quartz (SiO2), sucrose, table salt, alum, urea, KNO3 and CuSO4.

Amorphous or Non-Crystalline Solids

Solids with a non-repetitive three-dimensional arrangement of particles are called amorphous solids or pseudo solids; amorphous comes from a Greek word meaning shapeless. Their structures resemble those of liquids, but their particles lack the freedom of motion of liquids. They are intermediates between the liquid and solid states and are sometimes called supercooled liquids. Examples: glass, rubber, plastic, cement, ceramics and concrete.

Difference Between the Two Types

Crystalline SolidsAmorphous Solids
Definite geometric shapesNo definite geometric shapes
Sharp and distinct melting pointsNo sharp melting points
Anisotropic: properties differ in different directionsIsotropic: same properties in all directions
Formed by slow cooling of the liquidFormed by sudden cooling of the liquid
Examples: NaCl, CuSO4, sugar, diamondExamples: glass, plastic, rubber, coke

Key Points

  • Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating 3D arrangement of particles.
  • Amorphous solids have no regular arrangement and are called pseudo solids.
  • Amorphous solids are also known as supercooled liquids.
  • Crystalline solids are anisotropic; amorphous solids are isotropic.
  • Crystalline solids have sharp melting points; amorphous solids do not.
lessons.title: Types of Solids or Classification of Solid States

lessons.notes_html:
Crystalline solids show characteristic properties that arise from their orderly internal arrangement of particles.

Geometric Shape

Crystalline solids have definite geometrical shapes due to the orderly arrangement of their atoms, ions or molecules, held by strong attractive forces. Their interfacial angles and distances are the same regardless of the method or conditions of preparation; even the fragments of finely divided crystalline solids have definite geometric shapes.

Melting Point

The temperature at which the change from solid to liquid occurs is the melting point of a solid. At the melting point, the particles of the solid and liquid have the same average kinetic energies. Crystalline solids have sharp melting points: at this temperature the kinetic energy becomes sufficient to overcome the attractive forces and free the particles from their fixed positions, so crystalline solids can be identified by their sharp melting points.

Cleavage Plane

The process of breaking larger crystals into smaller, identical ones by applying pressure is called cleavage, and the specific planes along which a crystal fractures are its cleavage planes. A crystal breaks easily in one direction but not in others; a mica crystal consists of infinite layers of sheets with weak attractive forces, which separate easily parallel to the layers.

Habit of Crystal and Crystal Growth

The shape in which a crystal usually grows is called the habit of the crystal: NaCl has a cubic habit, white tin a tetragonal habit and graphite a hexagonal habit. Crystals are grown by slowly cooling a liquid or a saturated solution. Impurities or changed conditions can change the habit; NaCl is cubic when pure but octahedral in the presence of 10% urea, a change of habit, though the interfacial angles always remain the same.

Key Points

  • Crystalline solids have definite geometric shapes and fixed interfacial angles.
  • They melt sharply at a definite melting point.
  • They break along definite cleavage planes, as in mica.
  • The usual growth shape of a crystal is its habit, e.g. cubic for NaCl.
  • Impurities can change the habit but not the interfacial angles.
lessons.title: Properties of Crystalline Solids or Crystals

lessons.notes_html:
Thermochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with heat changes during a chemical reaction. Chemical energetics is a subfield of thermodynamics: it studies the energy stored in chemical bonds, the absorption or release of heat, and the overall energy balance of a reaction. Chemical reactions are either exothermic or endothermic.

Exothermic Reactions

Reactions that evolve heat from the system to the surroundings are exothermic (Greek: exo = outside; heat flows out). Examples: burning of gasoline, coal and wood; freezing, condensation and deposition are exothermic processes.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O + CO2(g), ΔH = -890.4 kJ
C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -393.51 kJ

Heat released is shown by a negative ΔH, because heat flows from the system to its surroundings. Most reactions at ordinary temperatures are exothermic.

Endothermic Reactions

Reactions in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings by the system are endothermic (Greek: endon = within; heat flows in). Examples: photosynthesis in plants; melting, evaporation and sublimation are endothermic processes.

C(s) + H2O(g) → CO(g) + H2(g), ΔH = +131.4 kJ
N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180.51 kJ

Heat absorbed is shown by a positive ΔH. A process that is endothermic in the forward direction is exothermic in the reverse direction, e.g. evaporation (endothermic) and condensation (exothermic).

Heat of Reaction

The amount of heat evolved or absorbed when reactants are converted into products is called the heat of reaction (also called chemical energy). An equation that shows this amount of heat is a thermochemical equation.

Key Points

  • Thermochemistry deals with heat changes during chemical reactions.
  • Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.
  • Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive.
  • Burning of fuels is exothermic; photosynthesis, melting and evaporation are endothermic.
  • A forward exothermic process is endothermic in the reverse direction, and vice versa.
  • The heat of reaction is the heat evolved or absorbed when reactants change into products.
lessons.title: Energy Change During Chemical Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum amount of energy, besides the average energy, required for a reactant to take part in a chemical reaction. It is the energy needed for molecules to form an activated complex, or to weaken the existing bonds enough that they can be broken through collision. Its unit is kJ/mol. Reactants absorb energy to form the activated complex, which then decomposes into products.

The Energy Pathway Diagrams for Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions

In an exothermic reaction, the potential energy of the reactants is higher than that of the products; the difference is shown by ΔH (negative). In an endothermic reaction, the potential energy of the reactants is lower than that of the products, and ΔH is positive. In both diagrams, Ea is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex at the peak of the barrier, and ΔH is the difference between reactants and products.

Forward and Reverse Activation Energies

FeatureExothermicEndothermic
Energy of reactants vs productsReactants higherReactants lower
Sign of ΔHNegativePositive
Ea of forward vs reverse reactionForward Ea is less than reverse EaForward Ea is greater than reverse Ea

Enthalpy Change and Bond Energies

Energy transfer occurs because bonds are broken and formed. Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases energy. If the energy required to break bonds is greater than the energy released in forming bonds, ΔH is positive and the reaction is endothermic. If more energy is released in bond formation than is needed for bond breaking, ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic.

Key Points

  • Activation energy is the minimum extra energy needed to form an activated complex; unit kJ/mol.
  • On a pathway diagram, Ea is measured from the reactants up to the peak of the barrier.
  • Exothermic: products lie lower than reactants, ΔH negative, forward Ea smaller than reverse Ea.
  • Endothermic: products lie higher than reactants, ΔH positive, forward Ea larger than reverse Ea.
  • ΔH is decided by the balance between energy used in breaking bonds and energy released in making bonds.
lessons.title: Activation Energies and Energy Pathway Diagrams in Chemical Reactions

lessons.notes_html:
The total heat content of a system at constant pressure is called enthalpy: the internal energy E plus the product of pressure (P) and volume (V), H = E + PV. The physical state of a substance at 25°C and one atmosphere, its most stable state, is its standard state. In ΔH°, ° indicates standard states. Units are kJ mol-1.

Standard Enthalpy of Reaction

The heat released or absorbed during a reaction when all reactants and products are in their standard states is the standard enthalpy of reaction, ΔH°rxn (heat of reaction). Example: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH°rxn = -393.51 kJ mol-1. ΔH is directly proportional to the quantity of reactants consumed: burning 2 mol of carbon releases twice as much heat, 2C(s) + 2O2(g) → 2CO2(g), ΔH°rxn = -787.02 kJ.

Standard Enthalpy of Atomisation (ΔH°at)

The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state: 1/2 H2(g) → H(g), ΔH°at = +218 kJ mol-1; 1/2 Cl2(g) → Cl(g), ΔH°at = +121 kJ mol-1.

Standard Enthalpy of Formation (ΔH°f)

The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. Examples: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH°f = -393.51 kJ mol-1; 1/2 N2 + 1/2 O2 → NO, ΔH°f = +90.37 kJ mol-1. A reaction exothermic in the forward direction is endothermic in reverse with the same magnitude: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, ΔH° = -46.11 kJ mol-1; 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2, ΔH° = +46.11 kJ mol-1. A highly negative ΔH°f means a very stable compound; a positive value means an unstable compound.

Key Formulae

QuantitySymbolMeaning
EnthalpyH = E + PVHeat content at constant pressure
Standard enthalpy of reactionΔH°rxnHeat change, all substances in standard states
Standard enthalpy of atomisationΔH°atElement → 1 mol gaseous atoms
Standard enthalpy of formationΔH°fElements → 1 mol of compound

Key Points

  • Enthalpy H = E + PV; standard state is 25°C, 1 atm, most stable state.
  • ΔH°rxn is proportional to the amounts in the equation.
  • Atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms from the element; always endothermic.
  • Formation forms one mole of a compound from its elements.
  • Reversing a reaction keeps |ΔH| but reverses its sign.
  • Highly negative ΔH°f = very stable compound.
lessons.title: Standard States and Standard Enthalpy Changes

lessons.notes_html:
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen at standard states is the standard enthalpy of combustion, ΔH°c, in kJ mol-1. Combustion is always exothermic, so ΔH°c values are negative. Examples: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH°c = -890 kJ mol-1; C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH°c = -393.51 kJ mol-1; C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g), ΔH°c = -283 kJ mol-1.

Standard Enthalpies of Combustion at 25°C

SubstanceFormulaΔH°c (kJ/mol)
HydrogenH2(g)-285
MethaneCH4(g)-890
ButaneC4H10(l)-2880
OctaneC8H18(l)-5474
EthyleneC2H4(g)-1412
AcetyleneC2H2(g)-1300
BenzeneC6H6(l)-3270
Carbon monoxideCO(g)-283

Standard Enthalpy of Neutralisation (ΔH°n)

The enthalpy change when one mole of hydrogen ions from an acid reacts with one mole of hydroxide ions from a base to form one mole of water at standard states is the standard enthalpy of neutralisation. In acid-base mixing the Na+ and Cl- ions remain unchanged (spectator ions); the only reaction is:

H+(aq) + OH-(aq) ⇌ H2O(l), ΔH°n = -57.4 kJ mol-1

The heat of neutralisation of any strong acid with a strong base is about -57.4 kJ/mol, because it involves only H+ and OH- ions. This heat is used in self-heating food packs for soldiers and hikers.

Key Points

  • ΔH°c: complete burning of one mole of a substance in excess oxygen; always negative.
  • Octane (-5474 kJ/mol) and butane (-2880 kJ/mol) release large amounts of heat, so they are good fuels.
  • ΔH°n: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l); -57.4 kJ/mol for every strong acid-strong base pair.
  • Spectator ions take no part in the neutralisation enthalpy change.
lessons.title: Standard Enthalpy of Combustion

lessons.notes_html:
The enthalpy change of a reaction is the sum of the energies required to break old bonds in the reactants plus the energies released when new bonds form in the products. Bond energy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of identical bonds in a substance; it is always positive. Bond formation releases the same amount, so product bond energies are entered with a negative sign:

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔH = ΣBE(reactants) + ΣBE(products)Enthalpy change from bond energies; product terms are negative (energy released on forming bonds)
ΔH = (energy to break bonds) - (energy released in making bonds)Same relation in words

Worked Example: H2(g) + F2(g) → 2HF(g)

  • Step 1: energy to break bonds: H-H = 436 kJ/mol and F-F = 159 kJ/mol; total = 436 + 159 = 595 kJ.
  • Step 2: energy released forming bonds: one H-F bond = 565 kJ/mol, so 2 mol of H-F bonds release 2 x 565 = 1130 kJ.
  • Step 3: ΔH = (+595 kJ) + (-1130 kJ) = -535 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

Key Points

  • Bond breaking is endothermic (positive); bond making is exothermic (negative).
  • ΔH = Σ bond energies of reactants - Σ bond energies of products in magnitude terms.
  • Count every bond broken and formed, multiplied by the moles in the balanced equation.
  • For H2 + F2 → 2HF, ΔH = 595 - 1130 = -535 kJ.
lessons.title: Calculation of Bond Energies for the Enthalpy Change of Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
Bond energies are categorised as exact or approximate values.

Exact Bond Energies

Exact bond energies are found in diatomic molecules such as H2 and O2, where only one bond is present. They are determined precisely through controlled experimental measurements.

Approximate Bond Energies

In complex molecules, finding an exact bond energy is challenging because the molecular environment and geometry change the strength of the same bond in different compounds. Chemists therefore use average (approximate) bond energies taken from similar compounds or theoretical calculations. Approximate values are commonly used when experimental measurement is difficult, and they give reasonable predictions of energy changes in reactions. Examples: the C-C single bond is quoted as approximately 80 kcal/mol and the C=C double bond as approximately 145 kcal/mol; these are average energies needed to break these bonds, based on theoretical models and data from numerous experiments.

Key Points

  • Exact bond energies apply to diatomic molecules like H2 and O2 and are measured precisely.
  • Approximate bond energies are average values from similar compounds.
  • The same bond has slightly different strengths in different molecular environments.
  • C-C ≈ 80 kcal/mol and C=C ≈ 145 kcal/mol are approximate (average) values.
  • Enthalpy changes calculated from average bond energies are estimates, not exact.
lessons.title: Exact and Approximate Bond Energies

lessons.notes_html:
Enthalpy changes are measured experimentally, usually in calorimetry, from the temperature change of a known mass of water or solution.

Heat Capacity

Heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a substance by one degree: c = q/ΔT, where q is heat and ΔT is the temperature change.

Specific Heat

Specific heat is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by one degree (1°C or 1 K): c = q/mΔT. Rearranged, the heat transferred is q = mcΔT.

Enthalpy Change per Mole

The enthalpy change for one mole of substance is ΔH = -q/n, i.e. ΔH = -mcΔT/n, where m is usually the mass of water or solution in the calorimeter and n is the amount of reactant. The negative sign is needed because the heat gained by the solution is the heat lost by the reaction: if the solution gains heat (ΔT positive), ΔH is negative (exothermic); if the solution loses heat (ΔT negative), ΔH is positive (endothermic).

Calculation of q and ΔH from Experimental Data

  • Given: mass of reaction mixture m = 150 g, specific heat capacity of water c = 4.18 J/g°C, ΔT = 25°C, moles reacted n = 0.75 mol.
  • q = mcΔT = 150 g x 4.18 J/g°C x 25°C = 15675 J.
  • ΔH = -mcΔT/n = -15675 J / 0.75 mol = -20900 J/mol = -20.9 kJ/mol (exothermic).

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
c = q/ΔTHeat capacity of a substance
c = q/mΔTSpecific heat (per gram)
q = mcΔTHeat absorbed or released by the solution
ΔH = -mcΔT/nEnthalpy change per mole of reactant

Key Points

  • q = mcΔT gives the heat change of the water or solution in a calorimeter.
  • Divide by the moles reacted and change the sign to get ΔH per mole.
  • Temperature rise of the solution means the reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative).
  • Temperature fall of the solution means the reaction is endothermic (ΔH positive).
  • For water, c = 4.18 J/g°C is used in these calculations.
lessons.title: Calculation of Enthalpy Changes from Experimental Results

lessons.notes_html:
Electron affinity is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to the lowest energy state of a gaseous atom, forming an anion. Examples: H(g) + 1e- → H-(g), ΔH = -73 kJ/mol; Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g), ΔH = -349 kJ/mol. Its units are kJ/mol, kcal/mol and electron volt. Electron affinity measures the attraction between the nucleus and the extra incoming electron.

When a second electron is added to a univalent negative ion, the incoming electron is repelled by the negative ion, so energy is absorbed and the second electron affinity is endothermic: O(g) + 1e- → O-(g), ΔH = -141 kJ/mol (1st E.A.); O-(g) + 1e- → O2-(g), ΔH = +844 kJ/mol (2nd E.A.).

Factors Affecting Electron Affinity

  • Atomic radius: the greater the atomic radius, the smaller the electron affinity.
  • Nuclear charge: the greater the nuclear charge, the greater the electron affinity.
  • Shielding effect: the greater the shielding effect, the smaller the electron affinity.

Trends in the Periodic Table

  • Electron affinity decreases down a group, because atomic size increases (more shells) and shielding increases.
  • Electron affinity increases across a period from left to right, because nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases.
  • Halogens have high electron affinities; chlorine's strong electron affinity lets it oxidise and kill micro-organisms in drinking water.

Key Points

  • First electron affinity is usually exothermic (energy released, negative ΔH).
  • Second electron affinity is always endothermic because the electron is repelled by the negative ion.
  • Electron affinity falls with larger atomic radius and stronger shielding.
  • Electron affinity rises with greater nuclear charge.
  • Down a group electron affinity decreases; across a period it increases.
lessons.title: Electron Affinity

lessons.notes_html:
Hess's law states that the enthalpy change during a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in a series of steps: ΔH = ΔH1 + ΔH2 + ΔH3. It was formulated in 1840 by the Swiss chemist Germain Henri Hess. It is needed when a ΔH cannot be measured directly: for example, carbon monoxide formed from carbon and oxygen reacts further with oxygen to give CO2, so the enthalpy of formation of CO is found indirectly.

Determination of Standard Enthalpy Change for Carbon Dioxide

  • Single step: C(graphite) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -393.51 kJ mol-1.
  • Multi-steps: C(graphite) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g), ΔH1 = -110.5 kJ mol-1; then CO(g) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH2 = -283.0 kJ mol-1.
  • Sum of steps: -110.5 + (-283.0) = -393.5 kJ mol-1, the same as the single step.

Applications of Hess's Law

The enthalpies of formation of methane, ethyne, CO, benzene, ethyl alcohol, etc., cannot be calculated directly; they are determined indirectly using Hess's law and the formula ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f (Products) - Σ ΔH°f (Reactants).

Determination of the Standard Enthalpy of Formation of Methane

  • Combustion: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), ΔH°rxn = -890.3 kJ/mol; ΔH°f: CO2 = -393.5, H2O(l) = -285.8, O2 = 0 (element in standard state).
  • -890.3 = [-393.5 + 2(-285.8)] - [ΔH°f(CH4) + 2(0)].
  • ΔH°f(CH4) = -965.1 + 890.3 = -74.8 kJ/mol.

Key Points

  • Total enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the route.
  • ΔH for a multi-step route is the sum of the step values.
  • Hess's law finds enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly, such as ΔH°f of methane and CO.
  • ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) - Σ ΔH°f(reactants).
  • Elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0.
lessons.title: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation

lessons.notes_html:
Lattice energy can be defined in two opposite ways. As a breaking process: the amount of heat needed to break one mole of an ionic crystal into its gaseous ions; this value is positive. Example: KCl(s) → K+(g) + Cl-(g), ΔH° = +715 kJ/mol. As a forming process: the amount of energy released when gaseous ions of opposite charges combine to form one mole of a crystalline ionic compound; this value is negative. Example: K+(g) + Cl-(g) → KCl(s), ΔH° = -715 kJ/mol. Lattice energy is expressed in kJ/mol.

The magnitude of lattice energy depends on the ionic size, the ionic charge and the arrangement of ions in the solid: smaller ions and higher charges give stronger attractions and a larger lattice energy. Lattice energy cannot be measured directly in an experiment; it is calculated indirectly with the Born-Haber cycle (an application of Hess's law).

Key Points

  • Breaking a crystal into gaseous ions needs energy: lattice energy positive (+715 kJ/mol for KCl).
  • Forming a crystal from gaseous ions releases energy: lattice energy negative (-715 kJ/mol for KCl).
  • The two definitions have equal magnitude and opposite sign.
  • Magnitude depends on ionic size, ionic charge and ion arrangement.
  • Lattice energy is found indirectly, never by direct measurement.
lessons.title: Lattice Energy

lessons.notes_html:
The Born-Haber cycle was developed by the German physicist Max Born and the German chemist Fritz Haber to calculate the lattice energies of binary ionic compounds such as NaCl. The cycle states that the sum of all the enthalpy changes in a cyclic process always equals zero; it is a special application of Hess's law. Lattice energy cannot be determined directly, so the formation of the ionic solid is split into steps.

Calculation of the Lattice Energy of NaCl

Direct route: Na(s) + 1/2 Cl2(g) → NaCl(s), ΔH°f = -411 kJ mol-1. The indirect route has five steps:

StepProcessΔH° (kJ/mol)
1Sublimation of solid sodium: Na(s) → Na(g)+107.7
2Atomisation of chlorine: 1/2 Cl2(g) → Cl(g)+121.7
3Ionisation of sodium: Na(g) → Na+(g) + 1e-+496.0
4Electron affinity of chlorine: Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g)-349.0
5Lattice formation: Na+(g) + Cl-(g) → NaCl(s)ΔH°latt = ?

Applying Hess's law: ΔH°f = ΔH°sub + ΔH°IE + ΔH°at + ΔH°EA + ΔH°latt, so -411 = 107.7 + 496.0 + 121.7 + (-349.0) + ΔH°latt = 376.4 + ΔH°latt, giving ΔH°latt = -787.4 kJ/mol. The same method gives, for example, the lattice energy of KBr as -688.2 kJ/mol.

Key Points

  • The Born-Haber cycle is Hess's law applied to the formation of an ionic solid.
  • Steps: sublimation, atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity, lattice formation.
  • Sublimation, atomisation and ionisation are endothermic; electron affinity (first) and lattice formation are exothermic.
  • ΔH°f = sum of all step enthalpy changes, so the unknown lattice energy is found by rearrangement.
  • Lattice energy of NaCl = -787.4 kJ/mol (formation definition).
lessons.title: Born-Haber Cycle

lessons.notes_html:
The heat of solution (enthalpy of solution, ΔHsoln) is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in a specified amount of solvent at constant pressure, resulting in infinite dilution. It measures the intermolecular attraction between solute and solvent molecules. The heat of solution is negative for an exothermic process and positive for an endothermic process.

Examples

When KNO3 is added to water, the temperature of the solution decreases, showing an endothermic process: KNO3(s) + H2O(l) ⇌ K+(aq) + NO3-(aq), ΔH = +35.7 kJ mol-1. When LiCl is added to water, the temperature increases, showing an exothermic process: LiCl(s) + H2O(l) ⇌ Li+(aq) + Cl-(aq), ΔH = -37 kJ mol-1.

Solubility follows the sign: the solubility of solutes with negative heats of solution (like LiCl) increases when the temperature falls and decreases when it rises. The same principle is used in instant packs: cold packs contain NH4NO3 or NH4Cl, which absorb heat on dissolving; hot packs contain CaCl2 or MgSO4, which release heat on dissolving.

Key Points

  • ΔHsoln is for one mole of solute dissolving to infinite dilution at constant pressure.
  • KNO3 dissolving is endothermic (+35.7 kJ/mol); the solution becomes colder.
  • LiCl dissolving is exothermic (-37 kJ/mol); the solution becomes warmer.
  • Temperature change of the solution reveals the sign of the heat of solution.
  • Cold packs use endothermic dissolving (NH4NO3, NH4Cl); hot packs use exothermic dissolving (CaCl2, MgSO4).
lessons.title: Heat of Solution

lessons.notes_html:
The heat of hydration (ΔHhyd) measures the energy released or absorbed when one mole of ions undergoes complete hydration. It is a specific type of dissolution energy in which water is the solvent, and it is usually measured in kJ/mol. The process is associated with salts and other compounds that can form hydrated crystals.

When an ionic compound dissolves in water, the positive and negative ions are attracted to the polar water molecules. This attraction creates ion-dipole interactions: water molecules surround the ions and release energy in the form of heat, which is the heat of hydration. Dissolving involves two energy terms: energy is needed to break the lattice apart, and energy is released when the ions are hydrated.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Heat of hydration = ΔHsoln - ΔHlatticeLinks hydration enthalpy with the heat of solution and the lattice energy
ΔHsoln = ΔHlattice (breaking) + ΔHhydHeat of solution as the balance of lattice breaking and hydration

If the heat of hydration is greater than the lattice energy, the heat of solution is negative (exothermic), and vice versa.

Key Points

  • Heat of hydration is the energy change when one mole of ions is completely hydrated.
  • It comes from ion-dipole attractions between ions and polar water molecules.
  • Hydration of ions releases energy; breaking the lattice absorbs energy.
  • The sign of ΔHsoln depends on which of hydration and lattice energy is larger.
  • Heat of hydration = ΔHsoln - ΔHlattice.
lessons.title: Heat of Hydration

lessons.notes_html:
The magnitude of the enthalpy change of hydration depends mainly on the ionic charge and the radius of the ion. Hydration enthalpy becomes more exothermic as the ionic charge increases or the ionic radius decreases. Both factors act through charge density, which determines the strength of attraction between the ion and the polar water molecules.

Effect of Ionic Radius

The smaller the ionic radius, the higher the charge density and the stronger the electrostatic attraction to water molecules, so hydration enthalpy becomes more negative. For monovalent alkali metal ions:

IonIonic Radius (pm)Hydration Enthalpy (kJ/mol)
Li+76-519
Na+102-406
K+138-322
Cs+167-263

Effect of Ionic Charge

The higher the ionic charge, the stronger the attraction to surrounding water molecules and the more negative the hydration enthalpy:

IonIonic ChargeIonic Radius (pm)Hydration Enthalpy (kJ/mol)
Na++1102-406
Mg2++272-1922
Al3++353-4665

Li+ (76 pm) and Mg2+ (72 pm) have similar radii, yet the hydration enthalpy of Mg2+ is about four times more negative, because the doubled charge increases the product of charges between the cation and the water dipoles. Hence, the enthalpy of hydration is directly proportional to the ionic charge and inversely proportional to the ionic radius.

Key Points

  • Smaller ion → higher charge density → stronger attraction to water → more negative ΔHhyd.
  • Higher ionic charge → much more negative ΔHhyd (Na+ -406, Mg2+ -1922, Al3+ -4665 kJ/mol).
  • Down the alkali metals, radius grows and hydration enthalpy becomes less negative.
  • Charge has a stronger effect than radius when the two are compared at similar size.
lessons.title: Effect of Ionic Charge and Ionic Radius on the Enthalpy Change of Hydration

lessons.notes_html:
Entropy, symbolised as S, measures the level of disorder or randomness in a system: the number of possible microscopic arrangements of particles and their energy in a given macroscopic state. When the constituents of a system become more spread out, or a gas expands at constant temperature, the number of available microscopic arrangements (microstates) increases along with entropy. Macrostates are the observable macroscopic properties, such as temperature, pressure and volume. Entropy is related to heat and temperature by S = q/T and ΔS = Δq/T.

Standard Entropy

The standard entropy change, ΔS°, is the measure of disorder of a system during a reaction under standard conditions, found from the standard molar entropies S° of reactants and products. Standard conditions here are 298.15 K (25°C), 1 atm and 1 M concentration. The SI unit of entropy is J/K.mol.

Predicting the Sign of Entropy Changes in States, Temperatures, and Gas Reactions

Three main factors affect the entropy change: change in state, temperature change, and the change in the number of gaseous molecules.

ProcessEntropy Change (ΔS°)ExplanationExample
Melting / vaporisation+Molecules move more freely and become less orderedIce melting to water
Freezing / condensation-Molecules lose freedom and become more orderedWater turning to ice
Heating+Molecules gain energy and move fasterHeating a metal rod
Cooling-Molecules lose energy and move more slowlyCooling a metal rod
More gas molecules produced+Greater freedom and movement of gas moleculesCombustion of methane
Fewer gas molecules produced-Reduced freedom and movement of gas moleculesNaOH and HCl reaction

Key Points

  • Entropy S measures disorder; more microstates means higher entropy.
  • ΔS = Δq/T; the unit of entropy is J/K.mol.
  • Positive ΔS° means more disorder; negative ΔS° means less disorder.
  • Melting, vaporisation, heating and producing more gas molecules increase entropy.
  • Freezing, condensation, cooling and producing fewer gas molecules decrease entropy.
lessons.title: Entropy

lessons.notes_html:
The standard entropy change of a reaction (ΔS°) is the change in entropy when reactants are converted to products under standard conditions (1 atm pressure and 298 K temperature). It shows the change in disorder or randomness within the system during the reaction.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔS° = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants)Standard entropy change of a reaction from standard molar entropies

Worked Example: 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g)

  • Standard entropies used: S°(H2) = 130.6 J/K.mol, S°(O2) = 205 J/K.mol, S°(H2O) = 188.7 J/K.mol.
  • ΔS° = [2(188.7)] - [2(130.6) + (205)] = 377.4 - 466.2 J/K.mol.
  • ΔS° = -88.8 J/K.mol: entropy decreases, as expected when 3 mol of gas form 2 mol of gas.

Note: exothermic reactions are not always spontaneous. Heat release alone does not decide spontaneity; both enthalpy and entropy changes are essential. Combustion of wood is exothermic, yet it still needs a spark to start it.

Key Points

  • ΔS° = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants), using standard molar entropies.
  • Multiply each S° value by the coefficient in the balanced equation.
  • A decrease in the number of gas molecules usually gives a negative ΔS°.
  • Spontaneity depends on both ΔH and ΔS, not on heat release alone.
lessons.title: Standard Entropy Change of a Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
Heat as a Form of Energy

Heat is a type of energy defined by the movement of thermal energy between objects or systems due to a temperature difference. It comes from the random movement of particles at a very small level; this movement creates kinetic energy, which is transferred between particles when they collide. Heat and temperature are different but related ideas: temperature shows the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance, while heat is the transfer of energy between substances because of a temperature difference. Heat typically moves from objects at higher temperature to those at lower temperature until they reach thermal equilibrium, where the temperatures are the same.

Relationship between Temperature and Kinetic Energy of Particles

According to the kinetic theory of matter, all particles of matter are constantly moving and have kinetic energy. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. When the temperature of a substance increases, the average kinetic energy of its particles also increases, leading to faster movement and more energetic collisions. When temperature decreases, the average kinetic energy decreases, with slower movement and less energetic collisions. There is a direct correlation between temperature and the kinetic energy of particles.

Conservation of Total Energy in Chemical Reactions

The total energy of the system, including the reactants and the products, remains constant throughout a reaction. Energy can change forms during a chemical reaction, such as chemical potential energy transforming into heat, but the overall energy stays the same before and after the reaction. This is the first law of thermodynamics: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.

Key Points

  • Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature measures average particle kinetic energy.
  • Heat flows from hotter to colder bodies until thermal equilibrium is reached.
  • Higher temperature means faster particles and more energetic collisions.
  • Total energy is conserved in chemical reactions (first law of thermodynamics).
  • Energy changes form in reactions but is never created or destroyed.
lessons.title: Principles of Energy Transfer and Conservation

lessons.notes_html:
Gibbs free energy is a thermodynamic function used to determine the spontaneity of a process. It indicates whether a reaction or physical change can proceed on its own, without requiring external energy. It is denoted by G and is also known as free enthalpy, Gibbs function, or available energy. Gibbs free energy is related to enthalpy (H), entropy (S) and temperature (T) by G = H - TS.

Free Energy Change and Reaction Spontaneity

The free energy change ΔG measures the spontaneity of a process and the useful energy available from it: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Under standard conditions: ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°, where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin. If ΔG° is negative, the process happens spontaneously; if positive, it will not happen spontaneously and needs an input of energy; if ΔG° = 0, the system is at equilibrium.

Spontaneity and the Sign of ΔG°

ΔH°ΔS°ΔG°Spontaneity
NegativePositiveNegativeSpontaneous at all temperatures
PositiveNegativePositiveNon-spontaneous at all temperatures
PositivePositiveNegative when TΔS° greater than ΔH°Spontaneous at high T (e.g. 2HgO(s) → 2Hg(l) + O2(g))
NegativeNegativeNegative when TΔS° less than ΔH°Spontaneous at low T (e.g. H2O(l) → H2O(s))

Key Points

  • Gibbs free energy G = H - TS decides whether a process is spontaneous.
  • ΔG = ΔH - TΔS combines the enthalpy and entropy effects at temperature T (in Kelvin).
  • ΔG negative = spontaneous; ΔG positive = non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0 = equilibrium.
  • Exothermic with entropy increase is always spontaneous; endothermic with entropy decrease is never spontaneous.
  • When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature decides spontaneity.
lessons.title: Gibbs Free Energy

lessons.notes_html:
The standard free energy of formation (ΔG°f) is the free energy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states; it predicts reaction spontaneity at 25°C and 1 atm. Standard states: gas = 1 atm, solid = pure solid, liquid = pure liquid, solution = 1 M, and for elements ΔG°f = 0.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔG°rxn = Σ n.ΔG°f(products) - Σ n.ΔG°f(reactants)Standard free energy change of a reaction; n is the stoichiometric coefficient
ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°Free energy change from enthalpy and entropy changes

Worked Example: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g)

  • Given ΔG°f values: NH3(g) = -16.4 kJ/mol; N2(g) = 0.0 kJ/mol and H2(g) = 0.0 kJ/mol (elements in their standard states).
  • ΔG°rxn = [2 x ΔG°f(NH3)] - [ΔG°f(N2) + 3 x ΔG°f(H2)] = [2 x (-16.4)] - [0 + 0].
  • ΔG°rxn = -32.8 kJ/mol. The negative value shows the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

Key Points

  • ΔG°rxn is calculated from standard free energies of formation of products minus reactants.
  • Each ΔG°f is multiplied by its coefficient in the balanced equation.
  • Elements in their standard states have ΔG°f = 0.
  • A negative ΔG°rxn means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
  • Gibbs free energy also predicts everyday changes, such as whether iron will rust in moist air.
lessons.title: Calculation of Gibbs Free Energy (ΔG°)

lessons.notes_html:
Reaction kinetics is the branch of chemistry that studies reaction rates, reaction mechanisms, and the factors that affect these rates. Reactions occur at very different rates: rusting of iron, setting of cement and decay of plants into coal are slow, while combustion of petrol, explosion of gunpowder and neutralisation of HCl by NaOH are fast.

The rate of reaction is defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product over a unit of time. Reactant concentrations decrease while product concentrations increase with time. The unit of rate is mol/L·s; time may be measured in seconds, minutes or hours.

Rate Expression for a General Reaction

For aA + bB → cC + dD, where a, b, c and d are the coefficients:

FormulaUse
Rate of Reaction = Change in Concentration / Change in TimeBasic definition of rate
Rate = −(1/a) Δ[A]/Δt = −(1/b) Δ[B]/Δt = (1/c) Δ[C]/Δt = (1/d) Δ[D]/ΔtOne equal rate from any reactant or product

The negative sign shows a reactant's concentration decreases (consumption); the positive sign shows a product's concentration increases (formation). Example: for 2N2O5 → 4NO2 + O2, Rate = −(1/2) Δ[N2O5]/Δt. From the book's data ([N2O5] falls from 1.4 to 0.12 mol/L in 8 h), Rate = −(1/2) x (−1.28 / 8) = 0.08 mol/L·h.

Key Points

  • Rate = change in concentration per unit time; unit mol/L·s.
  • Divide each Δ[ ]/Δt by the substance's coefficient so all give the same rate.
  • Minus sign for reactants (decreasing), plus sign for products (increasing).
  • Kinetics studies rates, mechanisms and the factors affecting them.
lessons.title: Rate of Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
The rate law (rate equation) states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to some power. For aA + bB → cC + dD, by the law of mass action:

FormulaUse
Rate of reaction = k [A]^m [B]^nRate law; k is the rate constant, m and n are the orders with respect to A and B

Here k is the proportionality constant, called the rate constant or specific rate constant. Its value depends on the nature of the reaction, reaction order and temperature. It increases with temperature and with catalysts, and remains fixed for a specific reaction at constant temperature, unaffected by reactant or product concentrations or by time.

Important Features

  • The rate law shows how the rate relates to reactant concentrations.
  • It is determined experimentally, not predicted from the balanced equation.
  • The exponents in the rate law may or may not equal the coefficients in the balanced equation.
  • The exponents indicate the order of reaction with respect to each reactant.

Key Points

  • Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where k is the rate constant.
  • k depends on the reaction, its order and temperature — not on concentrations or time.
  • k increases with temperature and in the presence of a catalyst.
  • The rate law is found by experiment; exponents need not match equation coefficients.
lessons.title: The Rate Law

lessons.notes_html:
Some reactions occur in a single step, but most proceed through a series of steps. The steps in a multi-step reaction are called the mechanism (reaction pathway) of the reaction. A single step in the mechanism is called an elementary reaction or elementary step.

Example: NO2 + CO Reaction

Overall reaction: NO2(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO2(g). If it occurred in one step, the rate law would be Rate = k[NO2][CO]. Experimentally the rate law is Rate = k[NO2]^2 — the rate depends only on NO2, not on CO, and the reaction is second-order overall. The proposed mechanism is:

  • Step 1 (slow, rate-determining step): NO2(g) + NO2(g) → NO3(g) + NO(g)
  • Step 2 (fast step): NO3(g) + CO(g) → NO2(g) + CO2(g)

Adding the two steps gives the overall reaction. The rate law is written for the rate-determining step only: Rate = k[NO2]^2. Here NO3 is a reaction intermediate — a short-lived species formed in one step and consumed in another; it does not appear in the overall equation and is unstable.

In a multi-step reaction the steps do not all happen at the same speed. The slowest step controls the overall rate and is called the rate-determining step or rate-limiting step.

Key Points

  • Mechanism = step-by-step sequence of elementary steps behind the overall reaction.
  • The experimental rate law comes from the slowest, rate-determining step.
  • An intermediate is formed in one step and used up in another; it cancels from the overall equation.
  • Example: NO2 + CO has Rate = k[NO2]^2, with NO3 as the intermediate.
lessons.title: Elementary and Overall Reactions

lessons.notes_html:
The order of reaction is the sum of all the exponents of the concentration terms in the rate equation. For Rate = k[A]^a[B]^b, order of reaction = a + b. The order is determined experimentally; it cannot be predicted from a balanced equation, because the exponents may differ from the coefficients.

OrderRate lawEffect of doubling concentrationUnit of kBook example
First orderRate = k[A]^1Rate doubless-1N2O5(g) → 2NO2(g) + 1/2 O2(g); Rate = k[N2O5]
Second orderRate = k[A][B] or k[A]^2Rate quadruples (x4)L mol-1 s-1H2 + I2 → 2HI; Rate = k[H2][I2]. Also 2O3(g) → 3O2(g); Rate = k[O3]^2
Third orderRate = k[A][B][C] or k[A]^2[B]Rate octuples (x8)L^2 mol-2 s-12NO + O2 → 2NO2; Rate = k[NO]^2[O2]. Also 2NO + 2H2 → N2 + 2H2O; Rate = k[NO]^2[H2]

Definitions

  • First order: rate directly proportional to the first power of the concentration of one reacting substance.
  • Second order: rate proportional to the square of one concentration, or to the product of two concentrations.
  • Third order: rate proportional to the product of three concentrations, or to the first power of one substance and the square of another.

Key Points

  • Order = sum of exponents in the rate law; always found experimentally.
  • Doubling concentration: first order x2, second order x4, third order x8.
  • Units of k change with order: s-1, L mol-1 s-1, L^2 mol-2 s-1.
  • Order with respect to one reactant is its own exponent in the rate law.
lessons.title: Order of Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
A reaction whose rate does not depend on the concentration of any reactant is called a zeroth order reaction: Rate of reaction = k[A]^0 = k. Enzyme-catalysed reactions and thermal decomposition reactions may be zero order. The unit of k is mol L-1 s-1. Examples given in the book: photosynthesis (photochemical reactions), and 2NH3(g) →(Tungsten) N2(g) + 3H2(g), with Rate = k[NH3]^0.

Experimental Determination of the Order of Reaction (Initial Rates)

Order is calculated from measured rates of reaction, generally by physical and chemical methods. The book's example studies A + 2B → Product with k = 1.20 mol-2 dm6 s-1:

Experiment[A] (mol/dm3)[B] (mol/dm3)Initial rate (mol/dm3·s)
10.200.020.0048
20.200.040.0192
30.400.020.0096
  • Experiments 1 and 2: [A] constant, [B] doubled → rate quadruples (0.0048 → 0.0192), so Rate ∝ [B]^2 — second order in B.
  • Experiments 1 and 3: [B] constant, [A] doubled → rate doubles (0.0048 → 0.0096), so Rate ∝ [A]^1 — first order in A.
  • Rate = k[A]^1[B]^2; overall order = 1 + 2 = 3.

Key Points

  • Zero order: rate = k, independent of concentration; unit of k is mol L-1 s-1.
  • To find an order, change one concentration at a time and compare the rates.
  • Rate x2 on doubling = first order; rate x4 on doubling = second order in that reactant.
  • Overall order = sum of the individual orders.
lessons.title: Zeroth Order Reaction and Experimental Determination of the Order of Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
The rate constant k can be determined by the initial rates method and by the half-life method. This lesson covers the initial rates method for aA + bB → Product.

Steps

  • i) Write out the rate equation: Rate of reaction = k [A]^m [B]^n.
  • ii) Rearrange the equation in terms of k.
  • iii) Substitute the values from one experiment.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
k = Rate / ([A]^m [B]^n)Rate constant from initial rate and concentrations
k = Rate / [A]First-order case (single reactant)

Worked Example

For 2A → B, the initial rates are 0.6, 1.2 and 2.4 mol/dm3·s at [A] = 0.01, 0.02 and 0.04 mol/dm3 — the reaction is first order in A, so Rate = k[A] and k = 0.6 / 0.01 = 60 s-1.

Key Points

  • First find the orders from the initial-rate data, then write the rate equation.
  • Rearrange for k and substitute any one experiment's rate and concentrations.
  • The unit of k depends on the overall order of the reaction.
  • Example result: k = 60 s-1 for a first-order reaction.
lessons.title: Calculation of Rate Constant by Initial Rates Method

lessons.notes_html:
The time required to convert half of the initial reactant concentration, [A]°, into products is called the half-life period, denoted by t1/2. For example, the decomposition of N2O5 at 45°C has a half-life of 24 minutes. The half-life depends on the nature of the reactants and the conditions of the reaction: the greater the half-life, the longer the overall time needed to complete the reaction.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life is inversely proportional to the rate constant. A fast reaction with a shorter half-life has a larger rate constant; a slow reaction with a longer half-life has a smaller rate constant.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
t1/2 = ln 2 / kHalf-life of a first-order reaction
Rate constant (k) = ln 2 / half-life = 0.693 / half-lifek from a measured half-life

Worked Example

For 2A → B with half-life 1.5 min: convert to seconds (1.5 x 60 = 90 s), then k = 0.693 / 90 = 7.7 x 10^-3 s-1.

Key Points

  • Half-life t1/2 = time for half the initial reactant to be converted to products.
  • For first order: t1/2 = ln2 / k, so k = 0.693 / t1/2.
  • Shorter half-life means larger k and a faster reaction.
  • Convert the half-life to seconds before calculating k in s-1.
lessons.title: Half-life Method

lessons.notes_html:
The minimum amount of energy required for the molecules to form an activated complex is called activation energy. It is represented by Ea, and its units are joules or kilojoules per mole (kJ mol-1).

Reactants are not directly converted into products. They first gain energy to form an activated complex, which then decomposes into products. Activation energy is therefore an energy barrier (energy hill) between reactants and products: reactant molecules must cross this barrier before they can form products. It is like carrying a ball to the top of a hill and rolling it down the other side — if the ball does not reach the top, it rolls back. Similarly, if activation energy is not provided, the reaction will not start and the reactants will not be converted into products.

Reading the Energy Diagram

  • The peak of the curve is the activated complex; Ea is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex.
  • The difference between reactants and products is the heat of reaction, ΔH.
  • For an exothermic reaction the products lie lower than the reactants and ΔH is negative.
  • For an endothermic reaction the products lie higher than the reactants and ΔH is positive.

Key Points

  • Activation energy Ea = minimum energy needed to form the activated complex.
  • Units of Ea: J/mol or kJ mol-1.
  • Ea is the height of the energy barrier from reactants to the peak of the diagram.
  • Without enough energy to cross the barrier, no reaction takes place.
  • ΔH (products minus reactants) is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
lessons.title: Activation Energy

lessons.notes_html:
Ludwig Boltzmann defined the distribution of molecular speeds (energies) in a gas at a specific temperature, shown by the Boltzmann distribution curve. The curve plots the number of particles (y-axis) against the energy level (x-axis). Its shape depends on the temperature and the type of particles in the system, and it explains the distribution of energy among particles in a gas or liquid.

What the Curve Shows

  • The curve helps determine the number of molecules with sufficient energy to initiate a reaction.
  • As temperature increases, the curve spreads out more and its peak — the most probable speed — shifts to higher speeds (to the right, and the peak becomes lower).
  • The area under the curve to the right of the activation energy line represents the fraction of molecules that have the necessary energy to react upon collision.
  • For a collision to be successful, the colliding molecules must have kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

Key Points

  • The Boltzmann curve shows how molecular energies are distributed at a given temperature.
  • Only molecules with energy ≥ Ea (area to the right of the Ea line) can react on collision.
  • Raising the temperature flattens and spreads the curve, so more molecules exceed Ea.
  • This is why heating a reaction makes it faster.
lessons.title: Boltzmann Distribution Curve

lessons.notes_html:
A substance that is not consumed during a reaction but changes the rate of a chemical reaction is called a catalyst. Usually a catalyst increases the rate, but in some cases it can decrease it. A catalyst that speeds up a reaction is a positive catalyst; one that slows a reaction down is a negative catalyst or inhibitor. The process of increasing the reaction rate by adding a catalyst is called catalysis.

How a Catalyst Works

  • Its primary function is to increase the rate by decreasing the activation energy: it alters the path or mechanism, providing a new pathway with a lower energy barrier.
  • With the lower barrier, a greater number of reactant molecules can cross it, so the rate increases — at a higher rate and a lower temperature.
  • It does not increase the amount of product; it only makes the product form in a shorter time. ΔH remains the same.
  • Example: in the Haber process, a catalyst makes ammonia production more economical; in the laboratory, MnO2 speeds up 2KClO3(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g).

Poisoning and Promoters

A catalyst can be deactivated by a very small amount of impurity — this is poisoning, and the impurity is a poison (e.g. As2O3 poisons the V2O5 catalyst in the Contact process for H2SO4). A substance that increases a catalyst's activity is a promoter (activator). Catalysts are most effective when finely divided (powder form) because of their high surface activity, e.g. Raney nickel in the hydrogenation of vegetable oil to ghee. In the body, the enzyme pepsin accelerates protein digestion in the stomach.

Key Points

  • A catalyst changes the rate without being consumed; positive catalysts speed up, negative catalysts (inhibitors) slow down.
  • It works by providing a new pathway of lower activation energy; ΔH is unchanged.
  • It does not change the amount of product, only the time taken to form it.
  • Poisons deactivate catalysts; promoters increase their activity.
  • Finely divided catalysts work best because of their large surface area.
lessons.title: Catalysis

lessons.notes_html:
Gibbs free energy change (ΔG°) measures the maximum practical work from a reaction at constant temperature and pressure. It relates to reaction feasibility — whether a reaction is spontaneous (feasible) or non-spontaneous (infeasible) under given conditions.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°Gibbs free energy change from enthalpy change, temperature and entropy change

Sign of ΔG° and Feasibility

  • ΔG° negative (less than 0): the reaction is spontaneous and proceeds in the forward direction (exergonic); it releases energy and the system moves toward a state of lower energy.
  • ΔG° positive: the reaction is non-spontaneous (endergonic) and requires energy input to proceed forward; it is unfavourable under standard conditions and occurs only at higher temperature.
  • ΔG° = 0: the system is at equilibrium — the process neither proceeds forward nor reverses at a measurable rate; this is a dynamic equilibrium between reactants and products.

Application: ΔG° is essential in designing rechargeable batteries — reactions inside the battery must be spontaneous during discharge but need energy during charging.

Key Points

  • ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, at constant temperature and pressure.
  • ΔG° less than 0: spontaneous (feasible), exergonic.
  • ΔG° greater than 0: non-spontaneous (infeasible), endergonic, needs energy input.
  • ΔG° = 0: equilibrium between reactants and products.
lessons.title: Gibbs Free Energy Change and the Feasibility of Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
