The kinetic energy of the particles in a substance is directly proportional to its temperature. By increasing the temperature, the kinetic energy of the substance increases, which in turn increases the rate constant and the rate of reaction — for both endothermic and exothermic reactions.

  • If the rate constant increases, the reaction rate also increases, assuming the reactant concentrations remain constant.
  • The rate constant generally increases as the temperature rises.
  • Usually, at room temperature, reaction rates double with every 10°C increase in temperature.

This agrees with the Boltzmann distribution: at a higher temperature more molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

Key Points

  • Particle kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature.
  • Higher temperature → larger rate constant k → faster reaction, at constant concentration.
  • The effect applies to both endothermic and exothermic reactions.
  • Rule of thumb: the rate roughly doubles for every 10°C rise near room temperature.
lessons.title: The Effect of Temperature Change on the Rate Constant and Rate of a Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
The Arrhenius equation explains how the rate constant (k) changes with temperature (T) and activation energy (Ea).

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
k = A·e^(−Ea/RT)Arrhenius equation: rate constant at temperature T
ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)·(1/T)Logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation
ln (k2/k1) = (Ea/R) x ((T2 − T1)/(T2·T1))Finds k2 at T2 when k1 at T1 is known

Symbols

  • k = rate constant for the reaction.
  • A = Arrhenius constant, or frequency factor.
  • Ea = activation energy (J/mol).
  • R = universal gas constant = 8.314 J/mol·K.
  • T = absolute temperature in Kelvin (K).

The two-temperature form is obtained by writing ln k at T1 and at T2 and subtracting one equation from the other; it is used to determine the rate constant k2 at temperature T2 when k1 is known at T1.

Key Points

  • k = A·e^(−Ea/RT): k rises quickly as temperature increases.
  • A larger Ea makes k smaller and the rate more temperature-sensitive.
  • Use Kelvin temperatures and R = 8.314 J/mol·K in the equation.
  • The ln(k2/k1) form compares the rate constant at two temperatures.
lessons.title: Arrhenius Equation

chapters.title: Unit 7: Acid, Base and Chemical Equilibrium

lessons.notes_html:
Acids, bases and salts are used daily: vinegar contains acetic acid (CH3COOH), citrus fruits contain citric acid and ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is used in soap making and ammonia (NH3) in household cleaners. Chemical equilibrium explains how such reactions balance in nature and industry.

Irreversible Reactions

An irreversible reaction takes place in only one direction and completely converts reactants into products; it is said to proceed to completion and is shown by a single arrow (→). Examples: 2H2O(g) → 2H2(g) + O2(g) (electric discharge); AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq).

Reversible Reactions

A reversible reaction can go in both forward and reverse directions at the same time: reactants form products and products convert back into reactants. Such reactions are generally incomplete and are shown by two half-arrows (⇌). Examples: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g); N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g); 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g). In the body, haemoglobin carries oxygen by a reversible reaction: Hb + O2 ⇌ HbO2.

Key Points

  • Irreversible reactions go to completion in one direction only and use a single arrow (→).
  • Reversible reactions run forward and backward together and use ⇌.
  • Reversible reactions do not go to full completion.
  • Examples of reversible reactions: formation of HI, NH3 and SO3.
lessons.title: Reversible and Irreversible Reactions

lessons.notes_html:
Chemical equilibrium is the state of balance where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant over time. It is a dynamic condition because both reactions keep occurring at the same rate, so there is no overall change at the macroscopic level.

Example: N2O4 and NO2

N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g). Colourless N2O4 placed in a flask forms dark brown NO2, so the colour deepens. As N2O4 concentration falls, the forward rate decreases; as NO2 builds up, the reverse rate increases. When the two rates become equal, equilibrium is reached and concentrations become constant. Once established, equilibrium lasts forever if conditions are not changed.

Key Points

  • At equilibrium, rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction.
  • Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, not necessarily equal.
  • Equilibrium is dynamic: reactions continue at the molecular level.
  • The N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 system shows equilibrium by a steady brown colour.
lessons.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

lessons.notes_html:
Equilibrium needs fixed conditions, clear signs by which it can be recognised, and it is of two types.

Necessary Conditions for Equilibrium

  • The reaction must take place in a sealed (closed) system so nothing escapes.
  • Temperature must remain constant.
  • Pressure should stay constant, especially for gases.
  • Both forward and reverse reactions must be possible and occur simultaneously.
  • Sufficient time must be given to reach equilibrium.

Recognition of Equilibrium

  • Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant over time.
  • Measurable properties such as pressure, colour or density become stable.
  • Rate of forward reaction exactly equals rate of reverse reaction.
  • No net macroscopic change is observed, although molecular changes continue.

Other characteristics: equilibrium is dynamic, is achieved in a closed system, can be approached from either side, and catalysts do not affect equilibrium concentrations.

Types of Chemical Equilibria

TypeMeaning and Example
HomogeneousReactants and products in the same physical state: N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g); N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)
HeterogeneousReactants and products in different physical states: CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g); 2Fe(s) + 3H2O(g) ⇌ Fe2O3(s) + 3H2(g)

Key Points

  • Equilibrium requires a closed system, constant temperature and pressure, and enough time.
  • It is recognised by constant concentrations and stable colour, pressure or density.
  • Homogeneous equilibrium: all species in the same state.
  • Heterogeneous equilibrium: species in different states.
  • A catalyst does not change equilibrium concentrations.
lessons.title: Conditions for Equilibrium and Its Recognition

lessons.notes_html:
Events in a reaction can be viewed at two levels: the invisible molecular level and the visible bulk level.

Microscopic Events

Microscopic events are processes at the atomic or molecular level that cannot be seen with the naked eye: breaking and forming of chemical bonds, rearranging of atoms, molecular collisions with energy transfer, and changes in molecular energy states. They are studied with instruments like electron microscopes and spectrometers and described in nanometres, picometres or atomic mass units.

Macroscopic Events

Macroscopic events are the visible, measurable results of many microscopic interactions: formation of gas bubbles, colour change, temperature change, mass or volume variation and pressure shifts in a closed system. They are measured with balances, thermometers and pressure gauges in grams, litres, °C and atmospheres.

Microscopic Events and Macroscopic Shifts in Equilibrium

When conditions of a system at equilibrium are disturbed, macroscopic properties such as colour, pressure or concentration change until a new equilibrium is reached. These visible changes are caused by continuous microscopic events: changes in concentration, temperature or pressure alter the frequency and energy of molecular collisions and adjust the relative rates of forward and reverse reactions. Example: heating N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 increases molecular vibrations and bond breaking in N2O4, forming more NO2 molecules (microscopic), so the gas mixture turns deeper brown (macroscopic).

Key Points

  • Microscopic events happen at atomic/molecular level and are invisible.
  • Macroscopic events are visible and measurable bulk changes.
  • Macroscopic shifts in equilibrium are caused by microscopic events.
  • Heating N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 deepens the brown colour as more NO2 forms.
lessons.title: Microscopic and Macroscopic Events in a Reaction

lessons.notes_html:
The law of mass action was given by Guldberg and Waage in 1864. It states: the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants. Active mass means molar concentration, in mol/dm3. For A + B ⇌ C + D: Rf = Kf[A][B] and Rr = Kr[C][D]. At equilibrium Rf = Rr, so Kf/Kr = [C][D]/[A][B] = Kc, the equilibrium constant: the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium. For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.

Characteristics of the Equilibrium Constant

  • It is independent of the initial concentrations at a given temperature.
  • Its value changes with temperature and is constant at fixed temperature.
  • A higher value means more products than reactants at equilibrium, and vice versa.
  • Concentrations of pure solids, pure liquids and solvents do not appear in the expression.
  • Units: if moles of reactants and products are equal, Kc has no unit (e.g. CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2). If unequal, Kc has units; for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc unit is mol^-2 dm^+6.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^bEquilibrium constant in terms of concentration
Kp = (PC)^c(PD)^d / (PA)^a(PB)^bIn terms of partial pressures (gases)
Kx = (XC)^c(XD)^d / (XA)^a(XB)^bIn terms of mole fractions
Kn = (nC)^c(nD)^d / (nA)^a(nB)^bIn terms of number of moles

Key Points

  • Law of mass action: rate ∝ product of active masses of reactants.
  • Kc = Kf/Kr = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
  • Kc depends only on temperature, not on initial concentrations.
  • Pure solids and liquids are left out of the Kc expression.
  • For gases, Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations.
lessons.title: Law of Mass Action and Expression for Equilibrium Constant

lessons.notes_html:
The same equilibrium can be expressed through concentration (Kc), partial pressure (Kp), mole fraction (Kx) or number of moles (Kn); all are interconnected at the same temperature.

Relationship between Kc and Kp

From PV = nRT, P = (n/V)RT = CRT, so each partial pressure equals concentration × RT. Substituting in the Kp expression gives Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = (sum of moles of gaseous products) − (sum of moles of gaseous reactants).

  • When Δn = 0: (RT)^0 = 1, so Kp = Kc.
  • When Δn is greater than 0: Kp is greater than Kc.
  • When Δn is less than 0: Kp is less than Kc.

Book Example 7.1: (a) N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g): Kc = [NO2]^2/[N2O4], Δn = 1, so Kp = Kc(RT). (b) N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g): Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3), Δn = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)^-2.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Kp = Kc(RT)^ΔnRelates Kp and Kc; Δn = gaseous product moles − gaseous reactant moles
P = CRTPartial pressure from concentration

Key Points

  • Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature.
  • Δn = 0 gives Kp = Kc.
  • Positive Δn gives Kp greater than Kc; negative Δn gives Kp less than Kc.
  • Only gaseous moles are counted in Δn.
lessons.title: Relationship Between Different Equilibrium Constants (Kc, Kp, Kx, and Kn)

lessons.notes_html:
By Dalton's law, the partial pressure of a gas equals its mole fraction times the total pressure: Pi = Xi × PT, and the mole fraction is Xi = ni/nT.

Relationship between Kp and Kx

Substituting PA = XA.PT etc. into the Kp expression gives Kp = Kx(PT)^Δn. For one mole of gas, PT = RT/V, so Kp = Kx(RT/V)^Δn.

Relationship between Kp and Kn

Substituting Xi = ni/nT in the partial pressures gives Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^Δn, and also Kp = Kx(RT/(V.nT))^Δn in the book's combined form. When the number of moles of reactants and products are equal (Δn = 0), all the equilibrium constants have the same value: Kc = Kp = Kx = Kn.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Pi = Xi × PTPartial pressure from mole fraction (Dalton's law)
Xi = ni/nTMole fraction of a gas
Kp = Kx(PT)^ΔnRelates Kp and Kx
Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^ΔnRelates Kp and Kn

Key Points

  • Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
  • Kp = Kx(PT)^Δn and Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^Δn.
  • When Δn = 0, Kc = Kp = Kx = Kn.
  • All four constants describe the same equilibrium at the same temperature.
lessons.title: Relationship between Kp and Kx, and Kp and Kn

lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant is far more than a number; it is used to judge and control reactions in the laboratory, industry, biology and the environment.

  • Extent of reaction: Kc indicates how far a reaction proceeds. A high Kc means products are favoured at equilibrium; a low Kc shows reactants dominate.
  • Predicting direction: comparing the reaction quotient (Q) with Kc tells whether the reaction will move forward or reverse until equilibrium is achieved.
  • Calculating equilibrium concentrations: once Kc is known, unknown equilibrium concentrations can be found using algebraic relations.
  • Industrial optimisation: in the Haber and Contact processes, Kc guides the choice of temperature, pressure and concentration to increase product output.
  • Relative stability: a higher Kc means products are more stable; a lower Kc means reactants are more stable under the given conditions.
  • Biological and environmental systems: equilibrium constants explain buffer action, solubility equilibria and how common ions affect pH and solubility.

Key Points

  • Large Kc = products favoured; small Kc = reactants favoured.
  • Comparing Q with Kc predicts the direction of reaction.
  • Kc is used to calculate unknown equilibrium concentrations.
  • Industry uses Kc to optimise yields in the Haber and Contact processes.
lessons.title: Applications of the Equilibrium Constant

lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant is calculated from the concentration or partial pressure values at equilibrium. When Kc is known, an unknown equilibrium concentration or partial pressure can be determined from it.

Book Example 7.2: Finding Kc

For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) at 500°C, equilibrium concentrations are [N2] = 0.030M, [H2] = 0.037M and [NH3] = 0.016M. Step 1: write Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3). Step 2: substitute values: Kc = (0.016)^2/((0.030)(0.037)^3) = 168.46 = 1.68 x 10^2.

Book Example 7.3: Finding an Unknown Concentration

For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), [SO2] = 0.59M, [O2] = 0.45M and Kc = 4.32. Step 1: Kc = [SO3]^2/([SO2]^2[O2]), so [SO3]^2 = Kc[SO2]^2[O2]. Step 2: [SO3]^2 = (4.32)(0.59)^2(0.45) = 0.0677. Step 3: [SO3] = √0.0677 = 0.26M.

Key Points

  • Write the Kc expression first, then substitute equilibrium values.
  • To find Kc, use the known equilibrium concentrations directly.
  • To find an unknown concentration, rearrange the Kc expression and solve.
  • Always use equilibrium, not initial, concentrations in Kc.
lessons.title: Calculation or Determination of Equilibrium Constant

lessons.notes_html:
Le Chatelier's principle (Henri Louis Le Chatelier, 1850–1936) states: if a system in equilibrium is disturbed by a change, it will shift to counteract (oppose) that effect. It applies to all dynamic equilibria, physical and chemical. Note: strength and concentration are different — a dilute HCl solution is still a strong acid, while a concentrated acetic acid solution is still weak.

The Effect of Concentration Change

For A + B ⇌ C + D: increasing a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right (more products); increasing a product shifts it to the left; decreasing a reactant shifts it to the left; decreasing a product shifts it to the right. Example: in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, adding N2 or H2 produces more NH3, while removing them decomposes NH3. Concentration changes do not change the value of Kc.

Effect of Pressure or Volume Change

Increasing pressure (decreasing volume) at constant temperature shifts the reaction towards the side with fewer moles of gas; decreasing pressure shifts it towards more moles of gas. If n(reactants) is greater than n(products), e.g. N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, increased pressure shifts right and NH3 increases, Kc unchanged. If n(reactants) is less than n(products), e.g. PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2, increased pressure shifts left. If moles are equal on both sides, e.g. N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO, pressure has no effect on position or Kc. Solids and liquids are almost incompressible, so in CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g) only the gas CO2 responds to pressure change.

Key Points

  • Le Chatelier: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts equilibrium forward.
  • Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.
  • Equal gas moles on both sides: pressure change has no effect.
  • Concentration and pressure changes do not change Kc.
lessons.title: Le Chatelier's Principle

lessons.notes_html:
Concentration, pressure and volume changes alter only the equilibrium position. The equilibrium constant itself changes only when temperature changes.

Effect of Temperature Change

Exothermic reactions are less favoured by an increase in temperature, while endothermic reactions are more favoured. Example 1 (endothermic forward): N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), ΔH = +90.25 kJ.mol^-1 — raising temperature favours NO formation (a temperature above 3000°C is used), lowering temperature favours the reverse reaction. Example 2 (exothermic forward): N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −46.11 kJ.mol^-1 — ammonia formation is favoured by a decrease in temperature; raising temperature shifts equilibrium left and decomposes NH3. A reaction exothermic in the forward direction is endothermic in the reverse direction.

The Effect of Catalyst

A catalyst is a substance that is not consumed in a reaction but changes its rate; the reaction in its presence is called catalysis. A catalyst does not affect the equilibrium position or the value of Kc. It lowers the activation energy and speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner. Example: iron mixed with aluminium oxide as catalyst in ammonia manufacture gives more NH3 in a shorter time.

Key Points

  • Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of Kc.
  • Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction.
  • Lowering temperature favours the exothermic direction, e.g. NH3 synthesis.
  • A catalyst changes neither equilibrium position nor Kc.
  • A catalyst shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium.
lessons.title: Effect of Temperature and Catalyst on Equilibrium

lessons.notes_html:
The Contact Process is the large-scale manufacture of sulphuric acid by the catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), ΔH = −196 kJ/mol. The reaction is reversible and slow at room temperature, so conditions are chosen by Le Chatelier's principle to maximise rate and yield at reasonable cost: about 400–450°C, pressure 1–2 atmospheres (typically 1.5–1.7 atm) and vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) catalyst.

  • Increasing concentration: more SO2 or O2 shifts equilibrium right, increasing SO3.
  • Temperature: the reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours yield but slows the rate; 400–450°C is the compromise.
  • Increasing pressure: 3 moles of gaseous reactants form 2 moles of product, so higher pressure shifts right; the gain is small, so pressure stays low.
  • Catalyst: V2O5 speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is achieved quickly.
  • Removing the product: SO3 is absorbed in concentrated H2SO4 to form oleum: SO3(g) + H2SO4(l) → H2S2O7(l). Removing SO3 shifts equilibrium right and increases yield.

Key Points

  • Key step: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, ΔH = −196 kJ/mol (exothermic).
  • Conditions: 400–450°C, 1–2 atm, V2O5 catalyst.
  • SO3 is removed as oleum, H2S2O7, pulling the equilibrium forward.
  • Conditions are a compromise between yield, rate and cost.
lessons.title: Contact Process (Production of Sulphuric Acid)

lessons.notes_html:
Haber's Process is the industrial synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. Conditions: 450–500°C and 200–300 atmospheres with an iron catalyst.

  • Increasing concentration: more N2 or H2 shifts equilibrium right, increasing NH3 production.
  • Temperature: the synthesis is exothermic, so low temperature favours NH3 but slows the reaction; 450–500°C balances rate and yield.
  • Increasing pressure: 4 moles of reactants form 2 moles of product, so high pressure (200–300 atm) shifts equilibrium right and raises the yield.
  • Catalyst: iron (Fe3O4) combined with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3; it loses effectiveness below 400°C.
  • Removing the product: ammonia is liquefied by cooling below its boiling point (−33°C): NH3(g) → NH3(l). Removing NH3 shifts equilibrium right and increases yield.

The Haber process revolutionised agriculture: without it, nearly half the world's population would not have enough food.

Key Points

  • Reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol (exothermic).
  • Conditions: 450–500°C, 200–300 atm, iron catalyst.
  • High pressure favours NH3 because moles decrease (4 → 2).
  • NH3 is removed by liquefaction, shifting equilibrium forward.
lessons.title: Haber's Process (Synthesis of Ammonia)

lessons.notes_html:
According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a substance that donates a proton (H+) to another substance, and a base is a substance that accepts a proton from another substance. Acid–base reactions are therefore proton-transfer reactions. Example: HCl(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq) — HCl is the acid (proton donor) and water is the base (proton acceptor). In the gas phase, HCl(g) + NH3(g) → NH4Cl(s): HCl donates a proton and NH3 accepts it, with no solvent required. Soluble bases are called alkalis; all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.

Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs

An acid and a base that differ only by a single proton form a conjugate acid–base pair. Every acid has a conjugate base, formed by loss of a proton; every base has a conjugate acid, formed by gaining a proton. General reaction: HA(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + A-(aq), where HA/A- and H3O+/H2O are the two conjugate pairs. For HCl in water: HCl is the acid, H2O the base, H3O+ the conjugate acid and Cl- the conjugate base.

Key Points

  • Brønsted–Lowry acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor.
  • Acid–base reactions are proton-transfer reactions.
  • Conjugate pairs differ by only one proton (H+).
  • Acid → conjugate base by losing H+; base → conjugate acid by gaining H+.
  • NH3 is a base even though it contains no OH- ions.
lessons.title: Brønsted-Lowry Definitions of Acids and Bases

lessons.notes_html:
The pH and pOH scales were introduced by Sørensen in 1909. pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = −log[H+]. pOH is the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration: pOH = −log[OH-]. pH values range from 0 to 14: pH less than 7 is acidic, pH = 7 is neutral and pH greater than 7 is basic. Examples: pure water pH 7, apple juice 3.1, egg 7.8, milk 6.5. The pOH scale is essentially the reverse of the pH scale. pKw is the negative logarithm of Kw: pKw = −log Kw = −log(1.0 x 10^-14) = 14, and pKw = pH + pOH = 7 + 7 = 14.

pH of Some Common Substances

SubstancepHSubstancepH
Gastric juice1.0–3.0Pure water7.0
Lemon juice1.8–2.4Human blood7.3–7.5
Vinegar2.4–3.4Sea water8.0–8.5
Orange juice3.5–4.0Rain water6.2

Book Example 7.4: carrot juice with [H+] = 5.5 x 10^-6 M has pH = −log(5.5 x 10^-6) = 5.26. Book Example 7.5: banana of pH 5.0 has [H+] = 10^-5 M; human blood of pH 7.4 has [H+] = 3.98 x 10^-8 M and, using [H+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14, [OH-] = 2.51 x 10^-7 M.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
pH = −log[H+]pH from hydrogen ion concentration
pOH = −log[OH-]pOH from hydroxide ion concentration
[H+] = 10^-pHHydrogen ion concentration from pH
pH + pOH = pKw = 14Relation at 25°C; Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14

Key Points

  • pH = −log[H+]; pOH = −log[OH-].
  • pH less than 7 acidic, equal to 7 neutral, greater than 7 basic.
  • Greater pH means smaller [H+] and a weaker acid.
  • pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.
  • Human blood pH is held near 7.4 by buffers.
lessons.title: pH, Ka, pKa, and pKw

lessons.notes_html:
For the ionisation of an acid HA in water, HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A-, the law of mass action gives Kc = [H3O+][A-]/([HA][H2O]). In dilute solution the concentration of water stays nearly constant, so Kc x [H2O] = [H3O+][A-]/[HA] = Ka, the acid ionisation constant. The greater the Ka, the stronger the acid and the higher the H+ concentration at equilibrium. Acid strength ∝ Ka: weak acids have Ka less than 10^-3, moderately weak acids have Ka from 1 to 10^-3, and strong acids have Ka greater than 1. pKa = −log Ka: the greater the Ka, the smaller the pKa and the stronger the acid. A difference of one pKa unit means one acid is 10 times stronger; two units, 100 times; three units, 1000 times.

Book Example 7.6: pH of 0.05M weak acid with Ka = 2.5 x 10^-5. With HA ⇌ H+ + A-, Ka = x^2/(0.05 − x) ≈ x^2/0.05, so x^2 = 1.25 x 10^-6, x = [H+] = 1.12 x 10^-3 M and pH = −log(1.12 x 10^-3) = 2.95. Book Example 7.7: with [HA] = 2.5 x 10^-1 M and [H3O+] = [A-] = 4.2 x 10^-2 M, Ka = (4.2 x 10^-2)(4.2 x 10^-2)/(2.5 x 10^-1) = 7.06 x 10^-3.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Ka = [H3O+][A-]/[HA]Acid ionisation constant
pKa = −log KaAcid strength on the pKa scale
[H+] ≈ √(Ka x C)H+ concentration of a weak acid of concentration C (x neglected)

Key Points

  • Ka measures acid strength: larger Ka = stronger acid.
  • pKa = −log Ka: smaller pKa = stronger acid.
  • Weak acids: Ka less than 10^-3; strong acids: Ka greater than 1.
  • For a weak acid, x is neglected in (C − x) because ionisation is very small.
  • Knowing Ka and concentration gives pH, and vice versa.
lessons.title: Acid Ionisation constant, Ka and pKa

lessons.notes_html:
The Brønsted–Lowry concept cannot explain acids and bases that contain no hydrogen ions, such as AlCl3 and FeCl3, or reactions in non-protonic solvents. In 1923 Gilbert N. Lewis proposed a broader concept based on electron pairs, not limited to any element or solvent: a Lewis acid is a substance (atom, molecule or ion) that can accept an electron pair to form a coordinate covalent bond, and a Lewis base is a substance that can donate an electron pair to form a coordinate covalent bond. Acids are electron-pair acceptors; bases are electron-pair donors.

  • All simple cations, such as H+, Sn2+ and Sn4+, act as Lewis acids; smaller cations like H+ and Be2+ are stronger Lewis acids.
  • Electron-deficient molecules with an incomplete octet, such as BeCl2, AlCl3 and BF3, act as Lewis acids.
  • All anions, such as Cl-, O2-, OH- and halide ions, act as Lewis bases because they donate electron pairs.
  • Molecules with lone pairs, such as H2O and NH3, act as Lewis bases.

Example of a Lewis acid–base reaction: Cl- (base) + AlCl3 (acid) → AlCl4-, where the base donates an electron pair and a coordinate covalent bond forms.

Key Points

  • Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor.
  • The product is formed through a coordinate covalent bond.
  • Cations and electron-deficient molecules (BF3, AlCl3) are Lewis acids.
  • Anions and lone-pair molecules (NH3, H2O) are Lewis bases.
  • The Lewis concept covers reactions with no protons and no solvent.
lessons.title: Lewis Acid-Base Concept

lessons.notes_html:
A buffer solution is a solution that resists any change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added to it. Buffer tablets, for example, stabilise stomach pH in acidity problems.

Composition of Buffer Solution

  • A weak acid and its salt with a strong base, e.g. CH3COOH and CH3COONa.
  • A weak base and its salt with a strong acid, e.g. NH4OH and NH4Cl.

Calculation of pH in a Buffer Solution

The pH is calculated with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), where [A-] is the conjugate base concentration and [HA] is the weak acid concentration. First find pKa, [A-] and [HA], then substitute. Book Example 7.8: for a buffer of 1M acetic acid and 1M acetate with pKa = 4.74, pH = 4.74 + log(1/1) = 4.74 + 0 = 4.74.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA])pH of an acidic buffer (Henderson–Hasselbalch)

Key Points

  • A buffer resists pH change on adding small amounts of acid or base.
  • Acidic buffer: weak acid + its salt with a strong base.
  • Basic buffer: weak base + its salt with a strong acid.
  • When [A-] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Buffers keep blood pH near 7.4.
lessons.title: Buffer Solution

lessons.notes_html:
The solubility product (Ksp) is the equilibrium constant that describes the dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic compound in water. It is the maximum product of the molar concentrations of the ions produced, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient, at a specific temperature. For AB(s) ⇌ A+(aq) + B-(aq), Ksp = [A+][B-]. A smaller Ksp means lower solubility; a larger Ksp means higher solubility. Ksp is temperature-dependent. For BaSO4(s) ⇌ Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq), the solid's concentration stays constant, so Ksp = [Ba2+][SO4^2-].

Applications of Solubility Product: Prediction of Precipitation

  • If Ksp is greater than the ionic product: solution is unsaturated, no precipitation; more solid dissolves.
  • If Ksp is less than the ionic product: solution is supersaturated, precipitation occurs until ionic product = Ksp.
  • If Ksp = ionic product: solution is saturated and at equilibrium; no precipitation.

Book Example 7.9: ZnS with Ksp = 3.0 x 10^-23: Ksp = s x s = s^2, so solubility s = √(3.0 x 10^-23) = 5.477 x 10^-12 M. Book Example 7.10: BaSO4 with solubility 1.03 x 10^-5 M: Ksp = (1.03 x 10^-5)(1.03 x 10^-5) = 1.06 x 10^-10 M^2.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Ksp = [A+][B-]Solubility product of a 1:1 salt AB
s = √KspSolubility of a 1:1 salt from Ksp

Key Points

  • Ksp applies to sparingly soluble salts in saturated solution.
  • The solid salt does not appear in the Ksp expression.
  • Precipitation occurs only when ionic product exceeds Ksp.
  • Ksp changes with temperature.
  • Low Ksp of BaSO4 makes it safe for medical X-ray use.
lessons.title: Solubility Product and Precipitation Reactions

lessons.notes_html:
The common ion effect is the process by which the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte decreases due to the addition of a strong electrolyte that has a common ion. It is used to reduce the solubility of slightly soluble salts by adding a more soluble electrolyte sharing a common ion, and it follows Le Chatelier's principle.

Example 1: CaCO3 and CaCl2

CaCO3(s) ⇌ Ca2+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq), with Ksp = [Ca2+][CO3^2-]. Adding CaCl2, a more soluble salt, increases the Ca2+ concentration, so the equilibrium shifts from right to left and CaCO3 precipitates out of the solution.

Example 2: KClO4 and KCl

KClO4(s) ⇌ K+(aq) + ClO4-(aq), with Ksp = [K+][ClO4-]. Adding the more soluble KCl raises the K+ (common ion) concentration, shifting the equilibrium left and causing KClO4 to precipitate. In water treatment, lime [Ca(OH)2] is added to hard water to precipitate calcium carbonate, softening the water for domestic and industrial use.

Key Points

  • Adding a common ion suppresses ionisation and solubility.
  • The equilibrium shifts towards the solid (undissolved) side.
  • The effect is an application of Le Chatelier's principle.
  • Used in water softening and in controlling salt solubility.
  • Ksp itself does not change; only the ion concentrations adjust.
lessons.title: Common Ion Effect

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis is the reaction of cations, anions, or both with water to form acidic, basic or neutral solutions. Salt hydrolysis usually affects the pH of a solution. There are four types of salts.

Salt TypeExample and Result
Weak acid + strong baseCH3COONa: CH3COO- + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH-; solution is basic, pH greater than 7
Strong acid + weak baseNH4Cl: NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH4OH + H+; solution is acidic, pH less than 7
Strong acid + strong baseNaCl: not hydrolysed; solution is neutral, pH = 7
Weak acid + weak baseDepends on relative strengths of the weak acid and weak base

For a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, compare the Ka of the cation with the Kb of the anion: if Ka is greater than Kb the solution is acidic (pH less than 7); if Ka is less than Kb the solution is basic (pH greater than 7); if Ka is almost equal to Kb the solution is neutral or nearly neutral (pH almost equal to 7). In NaCl solution, Na+ is a very weak Brønsted base and Cl- a very weak Brønsted acid, so neither affects the pH.

Key Points

  • Hydrolysis = reaction of a salt's ions with water.
  • Salt of weak acid + strong base gives a basic solution.
  • Salt of strong acid + weak base gives an acidic solution.
  • Salt of strong acid + strong base stays neutral (no hydrolysis).
  • Weak–weak salts: nature depends on Ka versus Kb.
lessons.title: Salt Hydrolysis

lessons.notes_html:
Acid–base titration is an analytical technique used to determine the concentration (molarity) of an acidic or basic solution. The moles of titrant and analyte are related by M1V1/n1 = M2V2/n2, where n1 and n2 are the stoichiometric coefficients and the mole ratio comes from the balanced equation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O has ratio 1:1, while H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O has ratio 1:2. If n1 = n2, then M2 = M1V1/V2. The strength of the analyte is found by multiplying its molarity by its molar mass: Strength (g/L) = M2 x Molar mass (g/mol).

Book Example 7.11

25.0 mL of 0.500 mol/L HCl neutralises 35.0 mL of NaOH. Step 1: moles of HCl = 0.500 x 0.0250 = 0.0125 mol. Step 2: ratio 1:1, so moles of NaOH = 0.0125 mol. Step 3: molarity of NaOH = 0.0125/0.0350 = 0.357 mol/L. Step 4: strength = 0.357 x 40.00 = 14.28 g/L.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
M1V1/n1 = M2V2/n2Titration relation between two solutions
Moles = M x VMoles from molarity and volume (in litres)
Strength (g/L) = Molarity x Molar massStrength of a solution

Key Points

  • Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, not always 1:1.
  • Convert volumes to litres before calculating moles.
  • Molarity = moles/volume; strength = molarity x molar mass.
  • Antacid action in the stomach is an everyday neutralisation example.
lessons.title: Calculation of Molarity and Strength in Acid-Base Titration

lessons.notes_html:
Indicators are special chemicals used in acid–base titrations to show when the acid has completely reacted with the base. The indicator changes colour at the endpoint, indicating completion of the reaction. The right indicator is the one whose pH range falls within the sharp pH change at the equivalence point.

Titration TypeEquivalence Point and Suitable Indicators
Strong acid + strong basepH about 7; sharp change between pH 4 and 10. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4), bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6) or phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0)
Strong acid + weak baseSolution slightly acidic; equivalence point between pH 3 and 6. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) or methyl red (4.4–6.2); methyl orange changes red to yellow as acidity decreases
Weak acid + strong baseSolution slightly basic; equivalence point between pH 8 and 10. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) is most suitable: colourless in acid, pink in base
Weak acid + weak basepH changes gradually with no sharp equivalence point; indicators are unreliable, so a pH meter is used

Farmers use simple indicator kits to test soil pH, decide suitable crops and whether lime (a base) is needed to neutralise acidic soil.

Key Points

  • An indicator signals the endpoint by a colour change.
  • Strong acid–strong base: methyl orange, bromothymol blue or phenolphthalein all work.
  • Strong acid–weak base: methyl orange or methyl red.
  • Weak acid–strong base: phenolphthalein is best.
  • Weak acid–weak base: no suitable indicator; use a pH meter.
lessons.title: Indicators for Acid-Base Titrations

lessons.notes_html:
As more elements and their compounds were discovered, chemists recognised the need to classify them. This classification enables us to understand the properties of elements systematically. Currently, there are 118 known elements arranged in a specific format for studying their properties. Elements with similar properties are grouped in columns, and these columns are organised to reveal the relationships between them. This arrangement of elements in groups and periods is known as the periodic table, and it has significantly simplified the study of elements and their compounds.

Arrangement by Atomic Number

The elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (proton number) in the periodic table. The atomic number indicates the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, so the atomic number serves as the identification number of an element. The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number, not by atomic mass: Mendeleev's early table used atomic mass, but it contained anomalies that were corrected by Moseley's discovery of atomic number in 1913.

This arrangement is not random. The properties of elements (such as size, mass, melting point, density, electronegativity and metallic character) repeat in a periodic manner as the atomic number increases. This periodicity arises from the arrangement of an element's electrons, influenced by the number of protons in its nucleus. The table is essential for predicting element properties, understanding element interactions and developing new materials; it is sometimes called the "chemist's map".

Key Points

  • There are 118 known elements arranged in the periodic table.
  • Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number (proton number), not atomic mass.
  • Atomic number is the identification number of an element.
  • Properties repeat periodically because of the repeating arrangement of electrons.
  • Moseley's work (1913) removed the anomalies of Mendeleev's atomic-mass table.
lessons.title: The Arrangement of Elements in the Periodic Table

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table can be divided into four blocks: s, p, d and f-blocks. The classification of elements into these blocks is based on the valence orbital of the element involved in bond formation, that is, the subshell into which the last electron enters.

BlockGroupsLast Electron EntersElements in Each PeriodGeneral Electronic Configuration
s-blockGroups 1 and 2, and period 1s-subshell2ns^1-2
p-blockGroups 13 to 18 (excluding helium)p-subshell6ns2 np^1-6
d-blockGroups 3 to 12d-subshell10(n-1)d^1-10 ns^1-2
f-blockLanthanides and actinidesf-subshell14(n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^1-2
  • There are two s-block elements in each period because the s-subshell can hold a maximum of two electrons; six p-block elements because the p-subshell holds at most six; ten d-block elements because the d-subshell holds ten; and fourteen f-block elements because the f-subshell holds fourteen.
  • The d-block elements are also known as transition elements.
  • For f-block elements, the f-subshell being filled is (n - 2), two less than the period number; in most periodic tables the f-block elements are placed below the main table to save space.

Key Points

  • Blocks are decided by the subshell that receives the last electron.
  • s-block: ns^1-2; p-block: ns2 np^1-6; d-block: (n-1)d^1-10 ns^1-2; f-block: (n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^1-2.
  • Block sizes per period: s = 2, p = 6, d = 10, f = 14 elements.
  • d-block elements are the transition elements; f-block elements are shown below the main table.
lessons.title: Blocks of Elements

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table is a grid of vertical columns called groups and horizontal rows called periods.

Groups of Elements

The vertical columns of elements in the periodic table are called groups. There are eighteen groups in the periodic table. There are two systems for numbering the groups: the older system and the newer IUPAC system; according to the latest IUPAC system, the modern periodic table has 18 groups. Elements in the same group of the periodic table show similar properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.

Periods of Elements

The horizontal rows of elements in the periodic table are called periods. The modern periodic table has seven periods.

PeriodNumber of ElementsDescription
1st2 (hydrogen and helium)Shortest period
2nd and 3rd8 eachShort periods
4th and 5th18 eachLong periods
6th and 7th32 eachLongest periods

Key Points

  • Groups are vertical columns; there are 18 groups (IUPAC system).
  • Same group means the same number of valence electrons and similar properties.
  • Periods are horizontal rows; there are 7 periods.
  • Period lengths: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements.
lessons.title: Periods and Groups of Elements

lessons.notes_html:
The period number (n) of an element indicates the highest energy level that contains electrons within that atom. In other words, all elements in the same period have their outermost electrons in the same energy level.

Example

Lithium is in Period 2, which means its electrons are arranged in two energy levels, with the outermost electrons in the second energy level (n = 2).

This arrangement helps us understand an element's energy levels and allows us to predict its chemical behaviour from its position in the table: read the period number and you know how many energy levels are occupied and which shell holds the valence electrons.

Key Points

  • Period number = the highest occupied energy level (shell) of the atom.
  • All elements in one period have outermost electrons in the same shell.
  • Moving down the table, the period number increases, so more energy levels are occupied.
  • Position in a period helps predict chemical behaviour.
lessons.title: Period Number and Electron Energy Levels

lessons.notes_html:
From an element's position in the periodic table we can determine both its occupied energy levels and its number of valence electrons.

Determination of Energy Levels from Period Number

The periodic table is organised to reflect the atomic structure of elements, particularly how electrons occupy various energy levels. The period number of an element indicates how many principal energy levels, or shells, contain electrons. Elements in Period 2, such as lithium and oxygen, have electrons in two energy levels: the first (1s2), followed by the second (2s and 2p). Elements in Period 3, such as sodium and chlorine, possess three energy levels, with their outermost electrons residing in the third shell.

Determination of Valence Electrons from Group Number

From the position of an element in a particular group, we can determine the number of valence electrons, the electrons in the outermost shell. This applies to the main group elements in Groups IA to VIIIA, and these valence electrons play a significant role in determining how an element reacts chemically. In Group IA, lithium has one valence electron with the electronic configuration 1s2 2s1. Oxygen, in Group VIA, has six valence electrons with the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4. In Period 3, sodium, also in Group IA, has one valence electron in the third shell, while chlorine, in Group VIIA, has seven valence electrons.

Trend Across the Periodic Table

Group I elements have one valence electron, and the count increases across the main groups. As we move down the periodic table, the period number increases, meaning that more energy levels are occupied by electrons. For example, potassium in Period 4 and Group I has four energy levels and one valence electron in the fourth shell, as shown by its electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1.

Key Points

  • Period number gives the number of occupied energy levels.
  • For main group elements (IA to VIIIA), the group number gives the number of valence electrons.
  • Valence electrons decide the chemical reactions of an element.
  • Example: K (Period 4, Group I) has 4 shells and 1 valence electron.
lessons.title: Position of an Element and Its Electron Arrangement

lessons.notes_html:
From the position of an element in the periodic table, we can identify whether it is a metal, a non-metal or a metalloid.

Position of Metals in the Periodic Table

Metals are located on the left side and in the centre of the periodic table. They include all elements in Groups IA and IIA, such as lithium, sodium, magnesium and calcium, as well as the transition metals found in the central block (Groups 3 (IIIB) to 12 (IIB)), like iron, copper and zinc. Some metals, such as aluminium and lead, are also present in the lower parts of Groups IIIA to VIA.

Position of Nonmetals in the Periodic Table

Nonmetals are located on the right side of the periodic table. They include elements in the upper parts of Groups IVA to VIIIA, such as carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine, and noble gases like neon and argon. Hydrogen, although placed in Group IA, is also a nonmetal.

Position of Metalloids in the Periodic Table

Metalloids (semi-metals) are located along the stair-step line that separates metals from non-metals. These elements, including boron, silicon, arsenic and tellurium, have intermediate properties between metals and non-metals; their position in the periodic table shows this dual behaviour.

Key Points

  • Metals: left side and centre of the table, including all transition metals.
  • Non-metals: right side of the table; hydrogen is a non-metal despite sitting in Group IA.
  • Metalloids lie on the stair-step line between metals and non-metals.
  • Metalloids such as B, Si, As and Te show properties of both metals and non-metals.
lessons.title: Position of Metals, Non-Metals, and Metalloids in the Periodic Table

lessons.notes_html:
The properties of elements are determined by their electronic configurations, specifically the arrangement of electrons in their outermost shells, known as valence electrons. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, resulting in similar chemical properties. Element properties also show periodic trends within the periods of the periodic table.

Atomic Radius

The atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together in a molecule, commonly expressed in nanometres (nm), angstroms (Å) or picometres (pm). Group trend (top to bottom): atomic radius increases within a group due to an increase in the number of electron shells and the shielding effect of inner electrons. Period trend (left to right): atomic radius decreases across a period because of an increase in nuclear charge, resulting in a stronger pull on the electrons and a smaller atomic radius.

Ionic Radius

Ionic radii refer to the average distance of the outermost shell electrons from the centre of the nucleus of an ion. When electrons are removed to form cations (positive ions), the resulting cationic radius is smaller than the parent atomic radius due to increased attraction between the nucleus and the remaining electrons; for example, the radius of Na+ (97 pm) is smaller than that of the Na atom (186 pm). Conversely, when electrons are added to form anions (negative ions), the anionic radius is larger than the parent atomic radius due to increased electron-electron repulsion; for instance, the radius of Cl- (181 pm) is larger than that of its parent atom, Cl (99 pm). Group trend: cationic and anionic radii increase from top to bottom in a group due to an increase in the number of shells. Period trend: the cationic radius decreases from left to right due to an increase in nuclear charge, while the anionic radius increases due to greater electron-electron repulsion.

Key Points

  • Valence electrons determine properties; trends repeat across periods and down groups.
  • Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period.
  • Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger.
  • Ionic radii increase down a group; cationic radii decrease across a period.
lessons.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius and Ionic Radius

lessons.notes_html:
Three more properties show clear periodic trends: ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

Ionisation Energy (Recall from Unit 2: Atomic Structure)

The energy required to remove an electron mainly depends on the distance from the nucleus and the effective nuclear charge. Electrons that are farther from the nucleus are removed more easily, whereas a stronger nuclear attraction makes removal more difficult. These principles explain why ionisation energy decreases down a group and increases across a period.

Electron Affinity (Recall from Unit 5: Chemical Energetics)

The tendency of an atom to gain an electron depends on the balance between its nuclear charge and the distance of its valence electrons from the nucleus. A strong nuclear attraction promotes electron gain, whereas increased distance and shielding reduce this tendency. These principles also explain why electron affinity decreases down a group and increases across a period. Note: when asked about the definition of electron affinity, define the first electron affinity.

Electronegativity

Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a molecule towards itself. It has no units. Elements with high electronegativity values, such as fluorine, attract bonding electrons more strongly than elements like sodium that have low electronegativity. Group trend (top to bottom): electronegativity decreases down a group due to an increase in atomic size and the shielding effect, because the inner shells block the attraction of the nucleus for the valence electrons. Period trend (left to right): electronegativity increases across a period, due to a decrease in atomic size and an increase in nuclear charge. Fluorine is so electronegative that it can even form compounds with noble gases, which were once considered completely inert.

Key Points

  • Ionisation energy decreases down a group and increases across a period.
  • Electron affinity follows the same pattern: down a group it decreases, across a period it increases.
  • Electronegativity is the pull on a shared pair of electrons and has no units.
  • Electronegativity decreases down a group and increases across a period; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
lessons.title: Ionisation Energy, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table is organised to show how electrons fill the different subshells (s, p, d and f) within an atom. The position of an element in the table (its group and period) provides significant information about its electron configuration, particularly the type of subshell filled by the outermost electrons.

The s-block: Groups 1 (IA) and 2 (IIA)

Elements in Groups IA and IIA are found in the s-block, where the outer electrons occupy the s subshell. Sodium (Group IA, Period 3) has an electron configuration that ends with 3s1, indicating one valence electron in the 3s orbital. Calcium (Group 2, Period 4) ends with 4s2, showing two valence electrons in the s subshell.

The p-block: Groups 13 (IIIA) to 18 (VIIIA)

Elements in Groups 13 (IIIA) to 18 (VIIIA) comprise the p-block, and their outermost electrons occupy the p subshell. Oxygen in Group 16 (VIA), Period 2, has an electron configuration ending with 2p4. Phosphorus in Period 3, Group 15 (VA) has a configuration ending in 3p3, which corresponds to three electrons in the p subshell.

The d-block: Transition Metals (Groups 3 to 12)

The d-block consists of transition metals, where the (n-1)d subshell is filled. Iron has an electron configuration of 3d6 4s2, indicating it contains six electrons in the 3d subshell. The group number minus two generally indicates the number of d electrons. Some elements have exceptions in their electron configurations to attain greater stability, such as chromium, which has 3d5 4s1 instead of 3d4 4s2; however, these examples are rare.

The f-block: Lanthanides and Actinides

The f-block elements are positioned separately at the bottom of the periodic table. They include the lanthanides and actinides, where electrons occupy the (n-2)f subshell. For example, cerium has a configuration ending in 4f1 5d1 6s2, with the 4f orbital starting to fill.

Key Points

  • Group and period reveal which subshell the outermost electrons occupy.
  • s-block endings: ns1 or ns2 (Na ends 3s1; Ca ends 4s2).
  • p-block endings: np1 to np6 (O ends 2p4; P ends 3p3).
  • d-block: d electrons = group number - 2 (Fe is 3d6 4s2); Cr is an exception (3d5 4s1).
  • f-block: the (n-2)f subshell fills (Ce ends 4f1 5d1 6s2).
lessons.title: Deducing Electron Configuration from Periodic Table Position

lessons.notes_html:
Sodium and magnesium are reactive metals that form oxides, chlorides and hydroxides when they react with oxygen, chlorine and water.

Key Equations

ReactionEquation
Sodium with oxygen4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s)
Magnesium with oxygen2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s)
Sodium with chlorine2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s)
Magnesium with chlorineMg(s) + Cl2(g) → MgCl2(s)
Sodium with water2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
Magnesium with waterMg(s) + 2H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s) + H2(g)

Notes on the Reactions

  • With oxygen: sodium reacts to produce sodium oxide; magnesium reacts to produce magnesium oxide.
  • With chlorine: sodium produces sodium chloride; magnesium produces magnesium chloride.
  • With water: sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide, a strong base, and hydrogen gas. Magnesium reacts with water to produce slightly soluble magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

Key Points

  • Both metals form oxides (Na2O, MgO) and chlorides (NaCl, MgCl2).
  • Sodium reacts vigorously with water, giving the strong base NaOH.
  • Magnesium gives Mg(OH)2, which is only slightly soluble.
  • Hydrogen gas is produced in both reactions with water.
lessons.title: Reactions of Sodium and Magnesium with Oxygen, Chlorine, and Water

lessons.notes_html:
The variation in the oxidation numbers of sodium and magnesium in their oxides and chlorides can be explained by their electronic configurations and positions in the periodic table, which determine the number of electrons in their outermost (valence) shells.

Oxidation States in Oxides

Sodium is a Group 1 (IA) member and has one electron in its outermost (valence) shell. To reach a stable noble gas configuration, sodium loses this electron, which gives it an oxidation state of +1 in sodium oxide (Na2O). Oxygen is more electronegative and has six valence electrons, so it gains two electrons to fill its octet, obtaining an oxidation state of -2. In magnesium oxide, magnesium is a Group 2 (IIA) member with two valence electrons; it loses both electrons to achieve a stable configuration, resulting in an oxidation state of +2, while oxygen gains two electrons to form O2-, just like in sodium oxide.

Oxidation States in Chlorides

In sodium chloride (NaCl), sodium shows an oxidation state of +1 by donating its single valence electron to chlorine, which accepts one electron to complete its outer shell, resulting in an oxidation state of -1 for chlorine. In magnesium chloride (MgCl2), magnesium donates two valence electrons, one to each of the two chlorine atoms, giving a +2 oxidation state for magnesium and a -1 oxidation state for each chloride ion.

CompoundMetal Oxidation StateNon-metal Oxidation State
Na2ONa: +1O: -2
MgOMg: +2O: -2
NaClNa: +1Cl: -1
MgCl2Mg: +2Cl: -1 (each)

Key Points

  • Oxidation number of a metal equals the number of valence electrons it loses.
  • Group 1 metals show +1; Group 2 metals show +2.
  • Oxygen gains two electrons (-2); chlorine gains one electron (-1).
  • Atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a stable noble gas configuration.
lessons.title: Variation in the Oxidation Number of Oxides and Chlorides of Sodium and Magnesium

lessons.notes_html:
Sodium and magnesium form basic oxides (sodium oxide, Na2O, and magnesium oxide, MgO) when they react with oxygen. Due to variations in solubility and reactivity, these oxides show different behaviours when reacting with water, resulting in solutions with distinct pH values.

Reaction of Sodium Oxide with Water

Sodium oxide reacts vigorously and exothermically with water, producing a strong alkaline solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH):

Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)

The resulting sodium hydroxide solution is highly basic, producing a pH range of 12 to 14, depending on the concentration.

Reaction of Magnesium Oxide with Water

Magnesium oxide, a sparingly soluble base, reacts with water to form a suspension of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, which is partly soluble in water:

MgO(s) + H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s)

The solution produced is weakly alkaline, with a pH level ranging from 8 to 10, due to the partial dissociation of magnesium hydroxide in water.

Key Points

  • Na2O and MgO are both basic oxides, but they differ in solubility and strength.
  • Na2O + water gives NaOH, a strong alkali with pH 12-14.
  • MgO + water gives Mg(OH)2, only partly soluble, a weak alkali with pH 8-10.
  • The difference in pH comes from how completely each hydroxide forms and dissociates.
lessons.title: Reactions of the Oxides of Sodium and Magnesium with Water and Their pH

lessons.notes_html:
The oxides and hydroxides of sodium and magnesium behave as bases, while aluminium hydroxide shows the special amphoteric behaviour of reacting with both acids and bases.

Basic Behaviour of Sodium Oxide and Sodium Hydroxide

Sodium oxide, a strong base, reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide (NaOH), which completely dissolves in water to create a strongly alkaline solution:

Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)

Sodium hydroxide is highly soluble in water, dissociating completely into sodium ions (Na+) and hydroxide ions (OH-), giving a very high pH, typically ranging from 12 to 14:

NaOH(s) ⇌ Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) (in H2O)

This strong base readily neutralises acids to produce a salt and water, showing typical base behaviour:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)

Basic Behaviour of Magnesium Oxide and Magnesium Hydroxide

Magnesium oxide is significantly less reactive with water. It reacts slowly and dissolves only partially, forming magnesium hydroxide:

MgO(s) + H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s)

The lower solubility and weaker basicity of magnesium hydroxide, in comparison to NaOH, result from the limited dissociation of Mg(OH)2 in water:

Mg(OH)2(s) ⇌ Mg2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) (in H2O)

Although it has limited solubility, the hydroxide ions produced can still neutralise acids, showing weak base characteristics:

Mg(OH)2(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l)

Amphoteric Behaviour of Aluminium Hydroxide

Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, which means it can react with both acids and bases. It acts as a base and reacts with strong acids to form salts:

Al(OH)3(s) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl3(aq) + 3H2O(l)

It also acts as an acid and reacts with strong bases to produce aluminate ions; with sodium hydroxide it produces sodium aluminate:

Al(OH)3(aq) + NaOH(aq) → Na[Al(OH)4](aq)

Key Points

  • NaOH is a strong base: fully soluble and completely dissociated, pH 12-14.
  • Mg(OH)2 is a weak base: sparingly soluble and only slightly dissociated.
  • Both hydroxides neutralise acids to form a salt and water.
  • Al(OH)3 is amphoteric: it reacts with acids (forming AlCl3) and with bases (forming aluminate).
lessons.title: Acid-Base Behaviour of Oxides and Hydroxides of Sodium, Magnesium, and Aluminium

lessons.notes_html:
Sodium chloride (NaCl), aluminium chloride (AlCl3) and phosphorus trichloride (PCl3) react differently with water, giving solutions of very different pH.

1. Sodium Chloride

Sodium chloride is an ionic compound that dissolves easily in water without undergoing hydrolysis. It dissociates completely into sodium and chloride ions:

NaCl(s) ⇌ Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq) (in H2O)

These ions do not react further with water, so the solution remains neutral with a pH close to 7.

2. Aluminium Chloride

Aluminium chloride is a covalent compound in its anhydrous state. It forms hydrated ions in aqueous solution and hydrolyses in water, forming hydrochloric acid (HCl) and hydrated aluminium ions, which makes the solution acidic:

AlCl3(s) + 3H2O(l) → Al(OH)3(s) + 3HCl(aq)

Al3+(aq) + 3H2O(l) → Al(OH)3(s) + 3H+(aq)

The presence of H+ ions makes aluminium chloride solution usually acidic, with a pH ranging from 3 to 4.

3. Phosphorus Trichloride

Phosphorus trichloride is a covalent compound that reacts violently with water during hydrolysis, producing phosphorus acid (H3PO3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl):

PCl3(l) + 3H2O(l) → H3PO3(aq) + 3HCl(aq)

ChlorideBondingBehaviour in WaterpH of Solution
NaClIonicDissolves; no hydrolysisAbout 7 (neutral)
AlCl3Covalent (anhydrous)Hydrolyses to give HCl3 to 4 (acidic)
PCl3CovalentViolent hydrolysis to H3PO3 and HClStrongly acidic

Key Points

  • NaCl simply dissolves and dissociates; the solution stays neutral (pH about 7).
  • AlCl3 hydrolyses, releasing H+ ions; the solution is acidic (pH 3-4).
  • PCl3 reacts violently with water, forming H3PO3 and HCl.
  • Ionic chlorides dissolve unchanged; covalent chlorides hydrolyse to give acidic solutions.
lessons.title: Reactions of the Chlorides with Water and Their pH

lessons.notes_html:
The physical and chemical properties of the oxides and chlorides of sodium and magnesium show that all four compounds have ionic bonding.

Bonding in Sodium and Magnesium Oxides

  • Sodium oxide (Na2O): a white, hygroscopic solid that reacts violently with water to produce a highly basic (alkaline) sodium hydroxide solution. It has a high melting point and forms a crystalline solid. These characteristics show that sodium oxide is an ionic compound, in which sodium atoms lose one electron each to become Na+ ions, while oxygen gains two electrons to form O2- ions. The strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions makes a stable ionic lattice.
  • Magnesium oxide (MgO): a white, powdery solid with an exceptionally high melting point; it is slightly soluble in water, forming a slightly alkaline solution of magnesium hydroxide. Magnesium donates two electrons to form Mg2+ ions, while oxygen forms O2- ions. The strong ionic bonding indicates its thermal stability and high melting point.

Bonding in Sodium and Magnesium Chlorides

  • Sodium chloride (NaCl): a white, crystalline solid that dissolves readily in water and conducts electricity when melted or in solution, showing ionic bonding. Sodium loses one electron to produce Na+, while chlorine gains one electron to form Cl- ions; the ions are held together in a giant ionic lattice, which explains the high melting point and solubility in water.
  • Magnesium chloride (MgCl2): a deliquescent white solid that dissolves easily in water, conducts electricity when in aqueous solution and has a high melting point, all typical properties of ionic compounds. Magnesium forms Mg2+ ions by losing two electrons, while each chlorine atom gains one electron to become a Cl- ion, arranged in a crystalline lattice.

Key Points

  • Na2O, MgO, NaCl and MgCl2 are all ionic compounds.
  • Signs of ionic bonding: high melting points, crystalline lattices, conductivity when molten or in solution.
  • Electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal (Na to Na+, Mg to Mg2+, O to O2-, Cl to Cl-).
  • Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions holds the lattice together.
lessons.title: Types of Chemical Bonding in the Oxides and Chlorides of Sodium and Magnesium

lessons.notes_html:
Because elements in the same group have the same valence electron arrangement, the known properties of one member can be used to predict the characteristic properties of the others. This is the power of chemical periodicity.

Group 1: Alkali Metals

Sodium is a member of the alkali metals. It readily loses its electron to form Na+ ions, resulting in the formation of ionic compounds such as sodium oxide (Na2O) and sodium chloride (NaCl). When sodium oxide reacts with water, it produces sodium hydroxide (NaOH), a strong base, which increases the pH of the solution. These properties are consistent throughout Group IA. Therefore, it can be predicted that other alkali metals like lithium and potassium will also form white, highly soluble ionic solids that produce strongly alkaline solutions upon reaction with water.

Group 2: Alkaline Earth Metals

Magnesium belongs to Group IIA (the alkaline earth metals). It loses two valence electrons to form Mg2+ ions, resulting in compounds such as magnesium oxide (MgO) and magnesium chloride (MgCl2). Magnesium oxide reacts slightly with water to produce magnesium hydroxide, which is a weakly soluble compound that results in a mildly alkaline solution. These characteristics are typical of Group 2 elements. This periodic trend suggests that calcium, strontium and barium will show similar behaviours, with increased reactivity and solubility of their hydroxides as we move down the group.

Key Points

  • Group members share properties because they share the same valence electron count.
  • Group 1 prediction: all form ionic oxides and chlorides; oxides give strong alkalis with water.
  • Group 2 prediction: all form +2 ions; hydroxides are only mildly alkaline.
  • Down Group 2, reactivity and hydroxide solubility increase.
lessons.title: Prediction of Characteristic Properties Using Chemical Periodicity

lessons.notes_html:
The nature, position and identity of an unknown element can be deduced step by step from the behaviour of its oxides and chlorides.

Nature of the Elements

The nature of an unknown element can be deduced from the behaviour of its oxides and chlorides. If an oxide reacts with water to produce a basic solution, the element is metallic in nature. For example, one element forms a strongly basic oxide, while another forms a weakly basic oxide; both indicate metallic characteristics.

Oxidation State and Group Position

The oxidation state further indicates the group placement of the elements. An element that forms a +1 ion is characteristic of Group IA, while one that forms a +2 ion is typical of Group IIA.

Bonding Characteristics

The bonding in their oxides and chlorides is ionic because both elements combine with highly electronegative atoms like oxygen and chlorine. The low electronegativities of these metals, compared to oxygen and chlorine, promote electron transfer and confirm their placement in the s-block of the periodic table.

Periodic Table Placement

The unknown elements can be identified from their physical and chemical properties: the element with a +1 oxidation state and a strongly basic oxide is identified as sodium (Na), Group IA, while the element with a +2 oxidation state and a weakly basic oxide is magnesium (Mg), Group IIA.

Key Points

  • A basic oxide points to a metallic element.
  • Oxidation state +1 means Group IA; +2 means Group IIA.
  • Ionic oxides and chlorides with O and Cl confirm a low-electronegativity s-block metal.
  • Worked deduction: +1 with a strongly basic oxide = sodium; +2 with a weakly basic oxide = magnesium.
lessons.title: Deducing the Nature, Position in the Periodic Table, and Identity of Unknown Elements

lessons.notes_html:
The first ionisation energies and electron affinities of the Group IA (alkali metal) and Group VIIA (halogen) elements show regular trends down each group.

Trends in First Ionisation Energy of the Group 1 Elements

Alkali metals have one electron in the valence shell (ns1). This ns1 electron is loosely bound to the nucleus and can be easily detached. Therefore, they possess the lowest first ionisation energies of all the elements in the periodic table, making them powerful reducing agents. The ionisation energy of alkali metals decreases down the group due to an increase in atomic size.

ElementLiNaKRbCs
Ionisation energy (kJ/mol)520.3495.8418.9403.0375.7
Electron affinity (kJ/mol)-59.6-52.9-48.4-47.9-45.5

Trends in Electron Affinity of the Group 1 Elements

The electron affinity of alkali metals decreases down the group because of an increase in atomic radius and the shielding effect: the added electron is more shielded from the nucleus and farther from it, so less energy is released when an electron is added to form a negative ion.

Trends in Ionisation Energy of the Group VIIA Elements

Down the group, the size of the atom increases due to the addition of new energy levels. This leads to a decrease in ionisation energy, as the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and less strongly attracted to it.

ElementFClBrI
Ionisation energy (kJ/mol)1680125611421008
Electron affinity (kJ/mol)-328-349-325-295

Trends in Electron Affinity of Group VIIA Elements

Electron affinity values decrease from chlorine to iodine. However, the electron affinity of fluorine is less than that of chlorine. This is due to the smaller size of the fluorine atom: when an extra electron is added, high electron density is produced around the fluoride ion, and the repulsion between the electrons already present in the relatively compact 2p orbitals of fluorine and the electron being added reduces its tendency to attract an electron. Hence chlorine, not fluorine, has the greatest electron affinity; the order of electron affinity values of the halogens is: Cl greatest, then F, then Br, then I.

Key Points

  • Group 1 first IE decreases down the group (Li 520.3 to Cs 375.7 kJ/mol); alkali metals are strong reducing agents.
  • Group 1 electron affinity also decreases down the group as radius and shielding increase.
  • Halogen IE decreases down the group (F 1680 to I 1008 kJ/mol) as atomic size increases.
  • Halogen electron affinity decreases from Cl to I, but F is anomalously lower than Cl because of electron repulsion in its compact 2p orbitals.
lessons.title: Trends in the Ionisation Energies and Electron Affinities of the Group IA and Group VIIA Elements

chapters.title: Unit 9: p-Block Elements: Nitrogen, Sulphur, and Halogens

lessons.notes_html:
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the Earth's atmosphere and belongs to Group VA (15). Pure nitrogen is colourless, odourless and relatively unreactive, yet it is essential for life and is used for fertilisers, explosives and ammonia.

Reasons for Low Reactivity

  • Strong triple bond: the two nitrogen atoms in N2 are joined by a strong triple bond with a high bond dissociation energy of 941 kJ/mol. Breaking this bond needs a great deal of energy, so nitrogen hardly reacts at room temperature.
  • Lack of polarity: nitrogen is a non-polar molecule with electrons evenly distributed between the two atoms. This reduces its attraction to other molecules and hinders chemical reactions.

Only under extreme conditions, or with the help of catalysts and enzymes, can nitrogen overcome these barriers and take part in reactions, as in nitrogen fixation and ammonia production. Only lightning strikes or specialised industrial processes such as the Haber process can break the N≡N bond.

Key Points

  • N2 has a very strong triple bond, bond dissociation energy 941 kJ/mol.
  • N2 is non-polar, so it attracts other molecules only weakly.
  • Nitrogen is therefore unreactive at room temperature despite its abundance.
  • High energy, catalysts or enzymes are needed to make nitrogen react.
lessons.title: The Low Reactivity of Nitrogen

lessons.notes_html:
Ammonia (NH3) is a Bronsted-Lowry base because it has a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. In the Bronsted-Lowry theory, a base is a proton (H+) acceptor and an acid is a proton donor.

Formation of the Ammonium Ion

When ammonia meets a proton, it readily accepts the proton with its lone pair, forming the ammonium ion (NH4+). With water, the proton transfer is: NH3(g) + H2O(l) → NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq). Here NH3 accepts a proton from water, so ammonia acts as the base and water as the acid; the OH- ions produced make the solution alkaline. Ammonia is only a weak (low) base because this reaction is partial. Ammonia also reacts directly with acids, e.g. NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl.

Key Equations

EquationPoint shown
NH3 + H+ → NH4+Ammonia accepts a proton (base)
NH3(g) + H2O(l) → NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)Ammonia solution is alkaline

Key Points

  • A Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton; ammonia does this through its lone pair.
  • Proton acceptance converts NH3 into the ammonium ion, NH4+.
  • In water, ammonia produces OH- ions and an alkaline solution.
  • NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3.
lessons.title: The Low Basicity of Ammonia

lessons.notes_html:
Ammonia can be displaced (released) from its ammonium salts in two ways: by a strong base, and by heat.

Reaction with Strong Bases

When a strong base such as sodium hydroxide is added to an ammonium salt, the hydroxide ion readily removes a proton from the ammonium ion (deprotonates it), forming water and leaving behind free ammonia gas: NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq) → NH3(g) + H2O(l). Warming an ammonium salt with an alkali is therefore a test for ammonium salts, and the ammonia released turns damp red litmus paper blue.

Thermal Decomposition

Some ammonium salts, such as ammonium chloride, decompose on heating without any additional base: NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g) (on heating, Δ). On cooling, the two gases recombine to form ammonium chloride again, so the change is reversible.

Key Equations

EquationProcess
NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq) → NH3(g) + H2O(l)Displacement by a strong base
NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g)Thermal decomposition (reversible on cooling)

Key Points

  • Strong bases displace ammonia from ammonium salts as a gas.
  • The OH- ion takes the proton from NH4+, forming water.
  • Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating into NH3 and HCl.
  • The gases recombine on cooling, so the decomposition is reversible.
lessons.title: Displacement of Ammonia from Ammonium Salts through Acid-Base Reactions

lessons.notes_html:
Oxides of nitrogen (NOx) occur both naturally and as a result of human activities. They are harmful gases that damage air quality.

Natural Occurrences of Oxides of Nitrogen

Natural sources of NOx include lightning, soil bacteria, forest fires and volcanic eruptions. Lightning contributes about 80% of natural NOx emissions, while soil bacteria produce NOx as a byproduct during processes like nitrification and denitrification, as part of natural nitrogen cycling in the soil. In this way soil bacteria quietly manage soil fertility and affect crop yields.

Man-Made Occurrences of Oxides of Nitrogen

Man-made sources of NOx include fuel combustion from burning fossil fuels in vehicles, power stations and industries, together with industrial processes and agricultural activities.

Key Points

  • NOx comes from both natural and man-made sources.
  • Lightning gives about 80% of natural NOx emissions.
  • Soil bacteria release NOx during nitrification and denitrification.
  • Burning fossil fuels in vehicles and industries is the main man-made source.
lessons.title: Natural and Man-made Occurrences of Oxides of Nitrogen (NOx)

lessons.notes_html:
Catalytic removal of NOx from exhaust gases uses three main methods, which convert harmful gases into harmless nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water.

Three-Way Catalysts

Three-way catalysts use precious metals such as rhodium, platinum and palladium to reduce NOx, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons simultaneously in a catalytic converter.

Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR)

In SCR, ammonia or urea is injected into the exhaust stream to react with NOx over a catalyst, forming nitrogen and water. It is widely used in diesel vehicles and power plants.

Lean NOx Traps (LNT)

LNT traps capture NOx under lean (oxygen-rich) conditions and subsequently release and reduce it under rich conditions using stored hydrocarbons.

Key Equations

ReactionEquation
Reduction of NO2NO(g) → N2(g) + O2(g)
Reduction of NO with CO2NO(g) + 2CO(g) → N2(g) + 2CO2(g)
Oxidation of CO2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g)
Oxidation of unburnt hydrocarbonsCxHy + O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(g)

These catalytic processes are essential for reducing emissions from engines and other fuel-burning sources, improving air quality and protecting the environment.

Key Points

  • Three-way catalysts use Rh, Pt and Pd and treat NOx, CO and hydrocarbons together.
  • SCR uses ammonia or urea to reduce NOx to N2 and water.
  • Lean NOx traps store NOx when lean and reduce it when rich.
  • The end products are harmless N2, CO2 and H2O.
lessons.title: Catalytic Removal from Exhaust Gases

lessons.notes_html:
Nitrification is the biological process of converting ammonia (NH3) or ammonium (NH4+) to nitrite (NO2-) and then to nitrate (NO3-). Denitrification is the opposite process: the biological reduction of nitrate or nitrite back to nitrogen gas or nitrous oxide.

Nitrification

Nitrification takes place under aerobic conditions and is performed by two groups of specialised autotrophic bacteria. Ammonia-oxidising bacteria (AOB), such as Nitrosomonas, convert ammonia or ammonium into nitrite: NH4+ + 1.5O2 → NO2- + 2H+ + H2O. Nitrite-oxidising bacteria (NOB), such as Nitrobacter, further oxidise nitrite into nitrate: NO2- + 0.5O2 → NO3-. Overall: NH4+ + 2O2 → NO3- + 2H+ + H2O. Farmers apply ammonium fertilisers, and nitrifying bacteria convert them into nitrates that plants can use.

Denitrification

Denitrification is performed by bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Paracoccus under anaerobic conditions, using organic matter as an energy source and nitrate as an electron acceptor: 2NO3- + 10e- + 12H+ → N2 + 6H2O.

Comparison

FeatureNitrificationDenitrification
ProcessOxidation of ammonia/ammoniumReduction of nitrate/nitrite
Starting compoundAmmoniaNitrate or nitrite
Ending compoundNitrateNitrogen gas or nitrous oxide
MicroorganismsNitrosomonas, NitrobacterPseudomonas, Paracoccus
Oxygen requirementAerobicAnaerobic
ResultProduces usable nitrate for plantsRemoves nitrate from the soil

Key Points

  • Nitrification is an aerobic oxidation: NH3/NH4+ → NO2- → NO3-.
  • Denitrification is an anaerobic reduction: NO3- → N2.
  • Nitrification makes nitrogen available to plants; denitrification removes it.
  • Both processes are essential parts of the nitrogen cycle.
lessons.title: Difference between Nitrification and Denitrification

lessons.notes_html:
Sulphur is the tenth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and belongs to Group VIA (16). It is a bright yellow element, once called brimstone, found in volcanic regions. Its lack of reactivity can be explained by a combination of factors.

Strong S-S Bonds in S8 Molecules

Sulphur occurs in nature as S8, in which eight atoms form a stable ring connected by covalent bonds. The S-S bonds in these rings are relatively strong and require a significant amount of energy to break, which makes sulphur less reactive.

Multiple Oxidation States

Sulphur can show various oxidation states, ranging from -2 to +6. Because it can exist in many oxidation states, it does not have a strong tendency to gain or lose electrons, which limits its reactivity.

Formation of Stable Compounds

Sulphur readily forms stable compounds with many elements, often with strong covalent bonds, such as hydrogen sulphide (H2S) and sulphur dioxide (SO2), which do not readily undergo further reactions under normal conditions. Sulphur is not entirely inert, however, and reacts under specific conditions, for example on heating.

Key Points

  • Sulphur exists as stable S8 rings with strong S-S bonds.
  • Breaking the S-S bonds needs considerable energy.
  • Sulphur shows oxidation states from -2 to +6.
  • It forms very stable compounds such as H2S and SO2.
  • Heat or specific conditions are needed to make sulphur react.
lessons.title: The Low Reactivity of Sulphur

lessons.notes_html:
