Sulphur takes part in reactions such as combustion and oxidation, especially on heating.

Combustion

Sulphur reacts with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide. Under specific conditions, sulphur dioxide can further react with oxygen to yield sulphur trioxide.

Oxidation

Sulphur reacts with halogens such as chlorine and fluorine to form sulphur chlorides and fluorides, oxidising sulphur to higher states.

Key Equations

ReactionEquation
Combustion of sulphurS(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g), ΔH = -297 kJ/mol
Further oxidation2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g) (V2O5 catalyst), ΔH = -199 kJ/mol
With chlorineS8(s) + 4Cl2(g) → 4S2Cl2(l)
With fluorineS(s) + 3F2(g) → SF6(g)

Sulphur is also present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine, which help stabilise protein structures in hair, nails and enzymes.

Key Points

  • Sulphur burns in oxygen to give SO2.
  • SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over a V2O5 catalyst.
  • With halogens, sulphur forms compounds such as S2Cl2 and SF6.
  • These reactions oxidise sulphur from 0 to higher oxidation states.
lessons.title: Reactions of Sulphur

lessons.notes_html:
Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) was first prepared by the Muslim chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan in the eighth century. Once called 'oil of vitriol', it is now known as the 'king of chemicals' because it is used to manufacture many industrial products, including fertilisers, detergents, paints and dyes.

Production: The Contact Process

Sulphuric acid is primarily prepared by the Contact process, in four steps:

  • Formation of SO2: sulphur is burnt in air (oxygen): S + O2 → SO2.
  • Formation of SO3: dry, pure SO2 is oxidised to sulphur trioxide over a catalyst: 2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3 (V2O5).
  • Formation of oleum: SO3 is absorbed in 98% sulphuric acid to form oleum, or fuming sulphuric acid (H2S2O7): SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7.
  • Dilution: the oleum is mixed with water to obtain pure sulphuric acid of any desired concentration: H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4.

Physical Properties

Sulphuric acid is a colourless, oily liquid. It is a powerful dehydrating agent with a strong affinity for water and absorbs moisture from the atmosphere. It is a strong acid that dissociates in water, releasing heat. Pure sulphuric acid is a non-conductor of electricity, but adding water makes it a good conductor. It is highly corrosive to skin and burns animal tissues. Its freezing point is 10.5°C and its boiling point is around 338°C.

Key Points

  • H2SO4 is made by the Contact process: SO2 → SO3 → oleum → acid.
  • SO3 is absorbed in 98% acid, not directly in water.
  • It is a colourless, oily, highly corrosive liquid.
  • Freezing point 10.5°C; boiling point about 338°C.
  • It has a strong affinity for water and is a powerful dehydrating agent.
lessons.title: Sulphuric Acid

lessons.notes_html:
The chemical behaviour of sulphuric acid depends on whether it is dilute or concentrated.

Properties of Dilute Sulphuric Acid

ReactionEquation
With active metalsZn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)
Neutralisation with basesH2SO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)
With carbonatesNa2CO3(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)
With bicarbonatesNaHCO3(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → NaHSO4(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)
With metal sulphidesFeS(s) + H2SO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + H2S(g)
With metal sulphitesNa2SO3(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + SO2(g) + H2O(l)

Dilute acid reacts with metals above hydrogen in the activity series, giving hydrogen and a metallic sulphate; metals below hydrogen, like copper, do not react.

Properties of Concentrated Sulphuric Acid

  • Non-volatile nature: it displaces volatile acids from their salts, e.g. NaCl(s) + H2SO4(conc.) → NaHSO4(s) + HCl(g) and NaNO3(s) + H2SO4(conc.) → NaHSO4(s) + HNO3(g) (on heating).
  • Oxidising properties: when heated, it decomposes to release nascent oxygen, H2SO4(conc.) → H2O(l) + SO2(g) + [O], which oxidises metals and non-metals: C(s) + 2H2SO4(conc.) → CO2(g) + 2SO2(g) + 2H2O(l); S(s) + 2H2SO4(conc.) → 3SO2(g) + 2H2O(l); 2P(s) + 6H2SO4(conc.) → 2H3PO4(aq) + 3SO2(g).
  • As a dehydrating agent: it removes water from organic and inorganic compounds: C6H12O6(s) → 6C(s) + 6H2O(l) (charring of sugar/glucose to black carbon); C2H5OH(l) → C2H4(g) + H2O(l); CuSO4.5H2O(s) → CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l).

Applications

  • Manufacture of fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate and calcium superphosphate.
  • In lead storage batteries; refining of petroleum; production of explosives such as nitroglycerin.
  • Manufacture of dyes, paints, plastics, detergents and pharmaceuticals.
  • In the paper, iron, steel, leather and textile industries, and in the electrolytic purification of metals.

Key Points

  • Dilute H2SO4 behaves as a typical acid: H2 with active metals, CO2 with carbonates, H2S with sulphides, SO2 with sulphites.
  • Concentrated H2SO4 is non-volatile and displaces volatile acids from their salts.
  • Hot concentrated acid is an oxidising agent, releasing nascent oxygen.
  • It is a strong dehydrating agent and chars sugar to black carbon.
  • A country's industrial progress is judged by its annual H2SO4 consumption.
lessons.title: Chemical Properties

lessons.notes_html:
The halogens (Group VIIA, 17) are called 'salt formers' because they react directly with metals to form salts. Their properties change in regular trends down the group.

Trends in Colours

The colours of the halogens become darker down the group from fluorine to iodine. As atomic size increases, the electron clouds become more diffuse and electrons are excited and de-excited more easily, so the colours deepen.

ElementF2Cl2Br2I2
Physical stateGasGasLiquidSolid
ColourPale-yellowGreenish-yellowReddish-brownLustrous violet black

Trends in Volatility

Halogens form simple diatomic molecules that are non-polar; the only intermolecular forces between them are weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces). Down the group, atomic size and the number of electrons increase, the larger electron clouds are distorted more easily, and the London forces become stronger. More energy is then needed to separate the molecules, so volatility decreases: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Bromine is the only non-metallic element that is a liquid under normal conditions.

Trends in Bond Strength

Bond strength generally decreases down the group because the larger atoms overlap their orbitals less effectively. However, the F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond, because the small fluorine atoms bring their dense lone pair electron clouds close together and the repulsion destabilises the bond. Bond dissociation energies (kJ/mol): Cl2 ~243 (strongest), Br2 ~193, F2 ~158, I2 ~151 (weakest). Order of bond strength: Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2.

Key Points

  • Halogen colours deepen down the group: pale-yellow to violet-black.
  • Volatility decreases down the group as London forces strengthen.
  • States change down the group: gas, gas, liquid, solid.
  • Bond strength order is Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2.
  • The F-F bond is weakened by lone pair repulsion between the small atoms.
lessons.title: Trends of Group VIIA Elements

lessons.notes_html:
Halogens are strong oxidising agents because they can easily accept an electron to complete their octet. Their oxidising power decreases down the group, because atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Fluorine, the smallest and most electronegative halogen, is the strongest oxidising agent.

Displacement Reactions

A stronger oxidising halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of the halogens below it:

ReactionResult
F2(g) + 2Cl-(aq) → 2F-(aq) + Cl2(g)Fluorine oxidises chloride ions
F2(g) + 2Br-(aq) → 2F-(aq) + Br2(l)Fluorine oxidises bromide ions
F2(g) + 2I-(aq) → 2F-(aq) + I2(s)Fluorine oxidises iodide ions
Cl2(g) + 2F-(aq) → no actionChlorine cannot oxidise fluoride ions
Cl2(g) + 2Br-(aq) → 2Cl-(aq) + Br2(l)Chlorine oxidises bromide ions
Cl2(g) + 2I-(aq) → 2Cl-(aq) + I2(s)Chlorine oxidises iodide ions

In the same way, bromine oxidises iodide ions but not chloride or fluoride ions, and iodine oxidises none of the other halide ions.

Key Points

  • Halogens gain one electron to complete their octet, so they oxidise other species.
  • Oxidising power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • A halogen displaces the halide ions of halogens below it in the group.
  • No halogen can oxidise the halide ions of a halogen above it.
lessons.title: Relative Reactivity of Halogens as Oxidising Agents

lessons.notes_html:
The halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides. These are redox reactions, with the general equation: X2 + H2 → 2HX. Reactivity decreases down the group, so the reaction conditions become more drastic (more severe).

Trend in Reactivity

HalogenEquationConditions
Fluorine (F2)F2 + H2 → 2HFExplosive, even in the dark and at very low temperature
Chlorine (Cl2)Cl2 + H2 → 2HClHeat or light (diffused sunlight)
Bromine (Br2)Br2 + H2 → 2HBrHigher temperature (Δ)
Iodine (I2)I2 + H2 ⇌ 2HIHigh temperature (450°C) and a Pt catalyst; slow and reversible

Fluorine is the most reactive halogen and iodine the least reactive. Astatine (At2) is a highly radioactive element whose reactions are studied in nuclear chemistry.

Key Points

  • All halogens form hydrogen halides, HX, with hydrogen.
  • Reactivity with hydrogen falls down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • F2 reacts explosively in the dark; I2 needs 450°C and a platinum catalyst.
  • The iodine reaction is slow and reversible.
lessons.title: Reactions of Halogens with Hydrogen: Trends and Redox Reactions

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrogen halides are binary compounds of halogens and hydrogen: HF, HCl, HBr and HI. The thermal stability of a hydrogen halide depends on the difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms; a larger difference results in a stronger bond.

Trend in Thermal Stability

The order of decreasing thermal stability is: HF > HCl > HBr > HI. HF has the highest thermal stability because of the small size of the fluorine atom and its large electronegativity difference with hydrogen. HI has the lowest stability because of the large iodine atom and the smallest electronegativity difference.

Hydrogen HalideElectronegativity Difference (ΔEN)Bond Length (pm)Bond Energy (kJ/mol)
HF1.7892562
HCl0.96121431
HBr0.76141266
HI0.46161299

Down the group the halogen atom becomes larger, the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, and the hydrogen halide decomposes more easily on heating. Although HF has the strongest bond, it is one of the most hazardous acids: it penetrates skin deeply and can even dissolve calcium in bones.

Key Points

  • Thermal stability decreases down the group: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
  • Stability follows the H-X bond strength and electronegativity difference.
  • Bond length increases down the group, so the bond weakens.
  • HF is the most stable hydrogen halide; HI is the least stable.
lessons.title: Thermal Stabilities of Hydrogen Halides

lessons.notes_html:
A reducing agent reduces other substances and is oxidised itself. The halide ions reduce oxidising agents and are themselves oxidised to X2 molecules, for example: 4HX + O2 → 2H2O + 2X2.

Trend in Reducing Power

The trend in the reducing ability of halide ions is opposite to the trend in the oxidising power of the halogens. The relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents is: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-. Down the group the ions become larger, hold their outer electrons less tightly, and lose electrons (are oxidised) more easily, so iodide ions are the strongest reducing agents and fluoride ions the weakest. A halide ion can only reduce halogen molecules that are above it in Group 17 (VIIA). For example, iodide ions reduce chlorine and bromine, while fluoride ions, at the bottom of this reducing-power order, reduce none of the halogens.

Key Points

  • Halide ions act as reducing agents and are oxidised to X2.
  • Reducing power increases down the group: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
  • This trend is opposite to the oxidising power of the halogens.
  • I- is the strongest reducing agent; F- is the weakest.
lessons.title: Relative Reactivity of Halide ions as Reducing Agents

lessons.notes_html:
When halide ions react with aqueous silver ions, they produce insoluble silver halide precipitates. The colour of the precipitate identifies the halide ion, so these reactions are used to test for halide ions in a solution. The general reaction is: X-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgX(s).

Precipitate Colours

Halide IonEquationPrecipitate
Chloride, Cl-Cl-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgCl(s)White precipitate
Bromide, Br-Br-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgBr(s)Cream-coloured precipitate
Iodide, I-I-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgI(s)Yellow precipitate

No precipitate forms with fluoride ions, because silver fluoride (AgF) is soluble in water. Forensic scientists use silver nitrate sprays to detect fingerprints, because the salts in sweat, including halides, react to form visible patterns.

Key Points

  • Silver ions give insoluble precipitates with Cl-, Br- and I-.
  • AgCl is white, AgBr is cream and AgI is yellow.
  • AgF is soluble, so fluoride ions give no precipitate.
  • These reactions identify halide ions in qualitative analysis.
lessons.title: Reactions of Halide Ions with Aqueous Silver Ions

lessons.notes_html:
When halide ions react with concentrated sulphuric acid, different reactions occur depending on the halide, because the stronger reducing halides are oxidised by the acid.

Fluoride Ions

Concentrated sulphuric acid has no significant effect on fluoride ions, the weakest reducing agents.

Chloride Ions

Concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with chloride ions to produce steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride gas; the chloride is not oxidised: H2SO4 + Cl-(aq) → HCl(g) + HSO4-(aq).

Bromide Ions

With bromide ions, hydrogen bromide forms first: H2SO4 + Br-(aq) → HBr(g) + HSO4-(aq). Some of the HBr is then oxidised by the concentrated acid, giving orange-brown bromine fumes: 2HBr + H2SO4 → Br2(g) + 2H2O(l) + SO2(g).

Iodide Ions

With iodide ions, hydrogen iodide forms: H2SO4 + I-(aq) → HI(g) + HSO4-(aq). The HI is oxidised by the acid to purple vapours of iodine: 8HI + H2SO4 → 4I2(g) + 4H2O(l) + H2S(g).

Key Points

  • F- is not affected by concentrated H2SO4.
  • Cl- gives steamy HCl fumes only; no oxidation occurs.
  • Br- gives HBr, partly oxidised to orange-brown Br2, with SO2 formed.
  • I- gives HI, oxidised to purple I2 vapour, with H2S formed.
  • The reactions confirm the increasing reducing power F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
lessons.title: Reaction with Concentrated Sulphuric Acid

lessons.notes_html:
The silver nitrate test followed by aqueous ammonia is the standard qualitative method to detect and identify halide ions (Cl-, Br-, I-) in a solution.

Silver Nitrate Test (Ag+ with Halides)

The sample is first dissolved in dilute nitric acid, to remove other reactive ions such as carbonates or hydroxides. When silver nitrate is added, a precipitate of silver halide (AgX) forms: Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) → AgX(s). Chloride ions give a white precipitate (AgCl), bromide ions a cream-coloured precipitate (AgBr), and iodide ions a bright-yellow precipitate (AgI).

Ammonia Test (Addition of Aqueous Ammonia)

Aqueous ammonia is then added to the precipitate. Silver chloride dissolves easily in dilute ammonia, forming a colourless [Ag(NH3)2]+ complex: AgCl(s) + 2NH3(aq) → [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + Cl-(aq). Silver bromide is only sparingly soluble in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia. Silver iodide does not dissolve in either dilute or concentrated ammonia. This stepwise solubility reliably distinguishes the three halide ions.

Summary Table

HalidePrecipitate with Ag+Effect of Aqueous Ammonia
Cl-White (AgCl)Dissolves in dilute ammonia
Br-Cream (AgBr)Dissolves only in concentrated ammonia
I-Yellow (AgI)Insoluble in dilute and concentrated ammonia

Key Points

  • Acidify with dilute HNO3 before adding silver nitrate.
  • Precipitate colours: white AgCl, cream AgBr, yellow AgI.
  • AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia; AgBr only in concentrated ammonia; AgI not at all.
  • The ammonia step confirms which halide is present.
lessons.title: Silver Nitrate and Ammonia Method for Halide Identification

lessons.notes_html:
A reaction in which an atom, ion or molecule is both oxidised and reduced simultaneously is called a disproportionation reaction. The reaction of chlorine with sodium hydroxide is an example; which reaction occurs depends on the temperature.

Reaction of Chlorine with Cold Dilute NaOH

When chlorine is bubbled through cold dilute NaOH solution (at 15°C), sodium hypochlorite and sodium chloride are produced: 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) → NaClO(aq) + NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). This is disproportionation because chlorine (oxidation state 0) is reduced to -1 in NaCl and oxidised to +1 in sodium hypochlorite.

Reaction of Chlorine with Hot Dilute NaOH

When chlorine is bubbled through a hot dilute NaOH solution (at 70°C), sodium chlorate and sodium chloride are produced: 6NaOH(aq) + 3Cl2(g) → NaClO3(aq) + 5NaCl(aq) + 3H2O(l). This is also disproportionation: chlorine goes from 0 to -1 in NaCl and to +5 in sodium chlorate.

Key Equations

ConditionsEquationChlorine oxidation states
Cold dilute NaOH, 15°C2NaOH + Cl2 → NaClO + NaCl + H2O0 → +1 and -1
Hot dilute NaOH, 70°C6NaOH + 3Cl2 → NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O0 → +5 and -1

Key Points

  • In disproportionation, the same element is oxidised and reduced together.
  • Cold dilute NaOH gives sodium hypochlorite (NaClO) and NaCl.
  • Hot dilute NaOH gives sodium chlorate (NaClO3) and NaCl.
  • Temperature decides which disproportionation products form.
lessons.title: Disproportionation Reactions of Chlorine with NaOH

lessons.notes_html:
Chlorine is used to purify water because the products of its reaction with water kill germs.

Reactions Involved

When chlorine reacts with water, hypochlorous acid and hydrogen chloride are produced: Cl2 + H2O → HOCl + HCl. When HOCl loses a proton (H+), the hypochlorite ion is formed: HOCl → OCl- + H+.

How Chlorination Protects Water

Both hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hypochlorite ions (OCl-) are powerful oxidising agents and effective germ-killers. In water treatment, HOCl eliminates harmful microorganisms, while OCl- remains in the water to provide ongoing protection by maintaining a residual disinfectant level. Municipal water treatment plants therefore add chlorine to ensure safe drinking water and prevent waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In small, controlled doses the health benefits of chlorination greatly outweigh its risks, although excessive amounts must be avoided.

Key Points

  • Cl2 + H2O → HOCl + HCl; HOCl also gives OCl- ions.
  • HOCl and OCl- are strong oxidising agents that kill bacteria and germs.
  • OCl- stays in the water as a residual disinfectant.
  • Chlorination prevents diseases like cholera and typhoid.
  • Only small, controlled doses of chlorine are used.
lessons.title: Chlorine in Water Purification

chapters.title: Unit 10: Environmental Chemistry: Atmosphere and Water

lessons.title: Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
Environmental chemistry is the study of chemical phenomena in natural environments — air, water and soil: the sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of chemical substances, and their impacts on human health and nature. The environment has four segments: lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere.

The atmosphere is the protective layer of gases surrounding the Earth, about 500 km thick. It sustains life and shields the Earth from harmful cosmic rays. Its major components are nitrogen (78.08%) and oxygen (20.94%); minor components are argon (0.93%), carbon dioxide (0.03%) and trace gases. Nearly 75% of its total mass lies within the first 11 km (the troposphere), where most of the air is concentrated.

The Four Layers

LayerExtentTemperature ChangeKey Feature
TroposphereSurface to 8–15 kmDecreases with altitude, +15°C at surface to −55°C at topAll weather phenomena occur here
Stratosphere15 to 50 kmIncreases with altitude, −55°C at base to 0°C at topContains the ozone (O3) layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays
Mesosphere50 to 85 kmDrops from 0°C at base to −90°C at topThe coldest layer; ozone concentration decreases
Thermosphere85 to 500 kmRises sharply from −90°C to 1,200–2,000°CExtremely low density, so it would not feel hot; auroras (Northern and Southern Lights) occur here

Beyond these layers lies the exosphere, the outermost region where the atmosphere transitions into space. Overall composition stays fairly consistent across the layers, though trace gas concentrations vary with location and weather.

Key Points

  • Environmental chemistry studies sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of chemicals in air, water and soil.
  • Atmosphere composition: N2 78.08%, O2 20.94%, Ar 0.93%, CO2 0.03%.
  • Four layers in order: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere.
  • Temperature falls with altitude in the troposphere and mesosphere, but rises in the stratosphere and thermosphere.
  • The stratospheric ozone layer protects Earth from ultraviolet radiation.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Air Quality
lessons.notes_html:
Air quality is affected by pollutants released from human activities and natural sources, and by environmental and geographical factors that control how pollutants disperse.

Sources of Pollutants

  • Human-related sources: vehicles, industries, power plants, agriculture, construction and waste management emit nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon oxides (COx), sulphur oxides (SOx), particulate matter (PM) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
  • Natural sources: wildfires and dust storms release large amounts of particulate matter; biological sources such as pollen add further; natural processes release greenhouse gases like methane.

Dispersion Factors

  • Wind, temperature and humidity control dispersion; calm conditions trap pollutants near the ground and cause smog.
  • Sunlight promotes ozone formation and the breakdown of pollutants.
  • Mountains can trap emissions in valleys; coastal breezes help disperse them.
  • Vegetation improves air quality by absorbing pollutants and releasing oxygen, while urban heat islands intensify pollution in cities.

Indoor Air Quality

Indoor air quality is a major concern: cooking, smoking, cleaning products and handling building materials, combined with poor ventilation, significantly increase indoor pollution. In big cities poor indoor air can be more harmful than outdoor pollution; keeping windows open, using exhaust fans and planting indoor plants help improve it.

Key Points

  • Human sources emit NOx, COx, SOx, particulate matter and VOCs.
  • Wildfires, dust storms and pollen are natural pollutant sources.
  • Calm weather traps pollutants and causes smog; wind and coastal breezes disperse them.
  • Sunlight drives ozone formation; vegetation cleans the air.
  • Indoor pollution rises with cooking, smoking and poor ventilation.

lessons.title: Sources and Effects of Common Air Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Air pollution occurs when harmful substances, called pollutants, are released into the atmosphere. Common pollutants, their sources and effects are:

PollutantSourceEffects
Ozone (O3)Not emitted directly; forms when sunlight reacts with gases from vehicles and factories (ground-level ozone)Chest pain, coughing, difficulty breathing; damages plants; major component of smog
Lead (Pb)Once in gasoline; now mainly old paint, dust and soilHarmful even in small amounts, especially to children: damages brain, slows learning, heart and blood issues
Mercury (Hg)Burning coal, mining and industrial processesAccumulates in lakes, rivers and fish; harms brain and nervous system, especially in pregnant women and small children
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs)Combustion of wood, coal, oil or wasteRespiratory issues, weakened immune system, increased cancer risk
Persistent organic pollutants (POPs)Outdated pesticides, industrial waste, specific productsRemain in the environment for long periods; accumulate in bodies; disrupt hormones, cause cancer, affect child development
Greenhouse gasesCO2, CH4 and N2O released from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and farmsTrap heat and cause climate change: rising temperatures, extreme weather, melting ice, rising sea levels
Ozone-depleting substances (CFCs)Old air conditioners, refrigerators and aerosol spraysDestroy the protective ozone layer; more UV reaches Earth, raising skin cancer and eye problems
Volatile organic compounds (VOCs)Paint, cleaning products, burning wood, vehicle exhaustIrritate eyes, nose and throat; make breathing difficult; help form smog and ground-level ozone
Heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd)Power plants, smelters and vehiclesDamage brain, kidneys, heart and other organs; especially harmful to children and infants

Primary and Secondary Pollutants

Primary pollutants are emitted directly from a source, e.g. total suspended particulates (smoke, dust, fumes) and oxides of carbon, nitrogen and sulphur from industrial chimneys and automobile exhaust. Secondary pollutants are created in the atmosphere by reactions (oxidation, photochemical reactions) involving primary pollutants, e.g. hydrogen peroxide, ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), sulphuric and nitric acids and their salts.

Key Points

  • Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant and a main part of smog; stratospheric ozone is protective.
  • Lead and mercury attack the brain and nervous system, worst in children.
  • POPs persist for long periods and accumulate in living bodies.
  • Greenhouse gases trap heat; CFCs deplete the ozone layer — two different problems.
  • Primary pollutants are emitted directly; secondary pollutants form by reactions in the air.

lessons.title: Impact of Human Activities on the Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities have greatly changed the Earth's atmosphere, primarily due to the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.

Burning of Fossil Fuels

When fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas are burned, they emit a large amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) into the atmosphere. This gas traps heat, leading to global warming and climate change. The excess CO2 warms the Earth's surface, resulting in melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather patterns.

Deforestation

Deforestation is cutting down trees for agriculture, construction or other human activities. Trees absorb CO2 and produce oxygen, helping to maintain a balanced atmosphere. When forests are destroyed, this natural purification process is lost, leading to higher levels of CO2 in the air. This enhances the greenhouse effect and worsens climate change.

Key Points

  • Burning coal, oil and natural gas is the main human source of extra CO2.
  • Excess CO2 traps heat and causes global warming and climate change.
  • Effects include melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather.
  • Trees absorb CO2 and release oxygen; cutting them removes this natural purification.
  • Deforestation therefore raises atmospheric CO2 and strengthens the greenhouse effect.

lessons.title: Ozone Depletion
lessons.notes_html:
In the stratosphere, ozone (O3) is formed naturally from oxygen, but it is broken down by chlorine atoms released from chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), causing ozone layer depletion.

Formation of Ozone

Diatomic oxygen absorbs an ultraviolet photon and splits into two oxygen free radicals. Each radical reacts with another O2 molecule to form triatomic oxygen (ozone). M is a third body (N2 or O2) that absorbs the excess energy released, stabilising the ozone.

Destruction of Ozone by CFCs

Ultraviolet radiation breaks down CFCs, releasing chlorine atoms. A chlorine atom reacts with ozone to form chlorine monoxide and O2; the chlorine monoxide then reacts with an oxygen atom, regenerating the chlorine atom. The cycle repeats, so one chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules.

Key Equations

StepEquation
O2 photolysisO2(g) —hv→ O•(g) + O•(g)
Ozone formationO•(g) + O2(g) + M(N2 or O2) → O3(g) + M
CFC breakdownCCl2F2 —UV→ CClF2 + Cl•
Ozone attackCl• + O3 → ClO• + O2
Chlorine regeneratedClO• + O• → Cl• + O2
Net reactionO3 + O• → 2O2

Ozone depletion lets more harmful UV radiation reach the Earth, causing skin cancer, eye damage, weakening of the immune system and reduced crop yields.

Key Points

  • Ozone forms when O2 splits under UV and O atoms combine with O2 in the presence of a third body M.
  • CFCs release chlorine atoms under UV radiation in the stratosphere.
  • Chlorine acts as a catalyst: it is regenerated and destroys thousands of O3 molecules.
  • Net reaction of the depletion cycle: O3 + O• → 2O2.
  • Effects of depletion: skin cancer, eye damage, weak immunity and lower crop yields.

lessons.title: Industrial Smog
lessons.notes_html:
Smog is a combination of smoke and fog. Industrial smog (also called London smog or grey smog) creates a yellow-brown colour near ground level. It is a mixture of fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs, and is common in cities with heavy industry and power plants, especially cold, damp urban areas. The Great Smog of London (1952) killed about 4,000 people in a few days. Smog harms humans, plants and animals, causing asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung infections and even cancer.

Reactions Forming Industrial Smog

Combustion of coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which is further oxidised to sulphur trioxide. The trioxide reacts with water in fog to form sulphuric acid. These acidic droplets, combined with particulates such as soot and ash, create the thick, grey smog characteristic of industrial pollution.

Key Equations

StepEquation
Sulphur burns in oxygenS(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g)
Oxidation of SO22SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g)
Acid formation in fogSO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq)

Key Points

  • Industrial (London/grey) smog = fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and VOCs near ground level.
  • It forms mainly where coal and oil are burned in heavy industry and power plants.
  • The key acid formed is H2SO4, from SO2 → SO3 → H2SO4 in fog water.
  • It is worst in cold, damp conditions.
  • Health effects: asthma, bronchitis, emphysema, lung infections and cancer.

lessons.title: Photochemical Smog
lessons.notes_html:
Photochemical smog (sometimes called Los Angeles smog or brown smog) is created when oxides of nitrogen react with volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight. It produces a mixture of hundreds of hazardous secondary pollutants, including ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), aldehydes and peroxybenzoyl nitrate (PBzN), and appears as a yellow-brown haze. It is common in cities with many automobiles and a sunny, warm, dry climate, developing on hot, sunny days in heavy traffic.

Reactions Forming Photochemical Smog

StepReaction
1. N2 and O2 combine at high temperature in vehicle enginesN2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g)
2. Nitric oxide oxidises in air2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g)
3. NO2 undergoes photolysis in sunlight (UV)NO2(g) —hv (sunlight)→ NO(g) + O•(g)
4. Oxygen radical forms ozoneO•(g) + O2(g) → O3(g)
5. Ozone reacts with VOCs and NO2 to give secondary pollutants such as PANVOCs(g) + O3(g) + NO2(g) → CH3CO3NO2(g) (peroxyacetyl nitrate, PAN)

Similar reactions generate aldehydes, peroxybenzoyl nitrate (PBzN) and other oxidants, which give the brownish haze and toxic effects. Health hazards include headaches, eye irritation, asthma, lung tissue damage, bronchial infections, pulmonary oedema (fluid in the lungs) and lung cancer.

Key Points

  • Photochemical (Los Angeles/brown) smog needs NOx + VOCs + sunlight.
  • Its harmful products are secondary pollutants: O3, PAN, aldehydes and PBzN.
  • NO2 photolysis is the step that starts ozone formation.
  • It forms in sunny, warm, dry cities with heavy automobile traffic.
  • Unlike industrial smog, it is not based on sulphur compounds and coal smoke.

lessons.title: Acid Rain
lessons.notes_html:
Acid rain (more accurately, acid precipitation) is created when SO2, NO2 and CO2 combine with water molecules in the atmosphere, resulting in mild solutions of sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3) and carbonic acid (H2CO3). It can also fall as snow, sleet, fog, dew, hail, or as dry material that settles to Earth. Normal rainwater is slightly acidic, with pH 5.3 to 6.0, because CO2 and H2O combine to produce weak carbonic acid; when the pH of rainwater drops below this range, it becomes acid rain.

Reactions of Acid Rain Formation

Acid FormedEquations
Carbonic acid (normal rain)CO2(g) + H2O(l) → H2CO3(aq)
Sulphuric acid (acid rain)2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g); SO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq)
Nitric acid (acid rain)2NO2(g) + H2O(l) → HNO2(aq) + HNO3(aq); 4NO2(g) + 2H2O(l) + O2(g) → 4HNO3(aq)

SO2 comes mainly from burning fossil fuels such as coal and oil; oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2) are produced by vehicle engines and power plants.

Harmful Effects of Acid Rain

Acid rain damages forests, buildings and monuments. Its low pH dissolves metals such as iron (Fe) and aluminium (Al) from the soil, contaminating water sources and potentially causing kidney damage and nervous disorders in humans.

Key Points

  • Acid rain contains H2SO4 and HNO3 formed from SO2 and NO2 in the atmosphere.
  • Normal rain is already slightly acidic (pH 5.3–6.0) due to carbonic acid.
  • Rain below this pH range is classified as acid rain.
  • Main sources: fossil fuel burning (SO2) and vehicle engines and power plants (NOx).
  • It damages forests, buildings and monuments, and leaches toxic metals from soil into water.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
The greenhouse effect is the process by which thermal infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface is absorbed and trapped by certain gases in the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone, preventing heat from escaping into space. Some solar radiation is reflected by the Earth and atmosphere, most is absorbed by the surface, and the infrared radiation re-emitted by the surface is absorbed and re-emitted in all directions by greenhouse gas molecules.

Global Warming

Global warming (also known as climate change) is the gradual increase in the overall temperature of the Earth's atmosphere, caused by gases accumulating in the air and preventing heat from escaping into space. The natural greenhouse effect maintains average global temperatures at about 15°C; without it, average temperatures might have been around −17°C, at which life would not have been able to exist. Greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, thus play a crucial role in keeping the Earth warm and sustaining life.

Share of Global Greenhouse Gas Emissions

GasShare
Carbon dioxide (fossil fuel and industrial processes)65%
Carbon dioxide (forestry and other land use)11%
Methane16%
Nitrous oxide6%
Fluorinated gases2%

Key Points

  • Greenhouse gases absorb and trap infrared radiation from the Earth's surface.
  • Main greenhouse gases: CO2, water vapour, CH4, N2O and O3.
  • The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth at about 15°C instead of about −17°C.
  • Global warming is the gradual rise in temperature from extra accumulated greenhouse gases.
  • CO2 is the largest contributor to emissions (65% from fossil fuels and industry, 11% from land use).

lessons.title: Causes of Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
The main cause of global warming is the build-up of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere from human activities, especially the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.

Greenhouse Gases

  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapour and ozone trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere, thereby enhancing the greenhouse effect.
  • CO2 contributes 76% to total global warming (65% from fossil fuel and industrial processes plus 11% from forestry and other land use).
  • CH4 contributes 16% and N2O 6%.
  • Fluorinated gases (2%) play a significant role despite their small share, because of their high heat absorption potential.

Anything that adds greenhouse gases — burning coal, oil and gas, cutting forests that would absorb CO2, and farm emissions — strengthens the heat-trapping blanket and raises global temperatures.

Key Points

  • Global warming is caused by enhanced greenhouse gas concentrations.
  • CO2 is the biggest contributor at 76% of total global warming.
  • CH4 (16%) and N2O (6%) are the next largest contributors.
  • Fluorinated gases are only 2% but absorb heat very strongly.
  • Fossil fuel burning and deforestation are the human activities behind the increase.

lessons.title: Consequences of Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
Global warming is the slow rise in Earth's average temperature. If it remains unchecked, temperatures might increase by up to 5°C by the end of the century, leading to serious environmental and societal issues.

Drowning of Coastal Cities

Melting glaciers and polar ice caps are causing rising sea levels, which threaten to submerge low-lying coastal areas and cities. As temperatures continue to rise, sea levels will rise further, leading to increased flooding and the displacement of populations.

Seasonal Shifting

Global warming disrupts natural climate cycles, resulting in changes to seasonal timing, such as earlier springs or delayed winters.

Change in Rainfall Pattern

Changes in global temperatures greatly influence precipitation patterns, causing some regions to experience severe droughts while others face increased rainfall and flooding.

Winds and Storms

Higher global temperatures result in more frequent and intense extreme weather events, including hurricanes, cyclones, strong winds and storms.

Key Points

  • Unchecked warming could raise temperatures by up to 5°C by 2100.
  • Melting ice raises sea levels, flooding and drowning low-lying coastal cities.
  • Seasons shift: earlier springs and delayed winters.
  • Rainfall patterns change — droughts in some regions, floods in others.
  • Extreme weather (hurricanes, cyclones, storms) becomes more frequent and intense.

lessons.title: Technologies and Strategies for Air Quality Improvement
lessons.notes_html:
Air pollution can be reduced by controlling emissions at source, switching to renewable energy, using energy efficiently and choosing greener transport.

Emissions Control Technologies

TechnologyFunction
Catalytic convertersDevices in vehicles that convert harmful pollutants in the exhaust system into less toxic substances
Smokestack filtersUsed in industrial facilities to trap particulate matter and prevent its release into the atmosphere
ScrubbersDevices that employ a chemical process to remove pollutants from industrial exhaust gases

Renewable Energy Sources

  • Solar power: sunlight captured by solar panels and converted to electricity; clean and renewable, it decreases dependence on fossil fuels and reduces greenhouse gas emissions (e.g. Quaid-e-Azam Solar Park, Bahawalpur).
  • Wind power: turbines capture the kinetic energy of air and produce electricity without carbon emissions.
  • Hydropower: electricity from flowing water (rivers or dams) turning turbines; dependable and renewable, with no direct air pollution or greenhouse gases.

Energy Efficiency and Green Transportation

  • Improving fuel efficiency: vehicles with higher fuel efficiency, and hybrid and electric options, reduce transportation emissions.
  • Energy-efficient appliances: efficient appliances and lighting minimise overall energy consumption and emissions.
  • Public transit: expanding public transport reduces the number of individual vehicles on the road.
  • Cycling infrastructure: bicycle-friendly infrastructure promotes cycling as an alternative mode of transportation.

Key Points

  • Catalytic converters clean vehicle exhaust; filters trap particulates; scrubbers chemically remove pollutants.
  • Solar, wind and hydropower produce energy without burning fossil fuels.
  • Fuel-efficient, hybrid and electric vehicles cut transport emissions.
  • Energy-efficient appliances and lighting reduce total energy demand.
  • Public transit and cycling reduce the number of polluting vehicles.

lessons.title: Types of Water Pollution
lessons.notes_html:
Water pollution is any physical, chemical or biological change in the quality of water, resulting from the addition of harmful substances, that affects living organisms. Water pollution is classified by the source of contamination into two primary categories: point source and nonpoint source pollution.

Point Source Pollution

Point source pollution originates from a specific, single source, making monitoring and regulation easier. Examples include industrial discharges from factories, municipal wastewater from sewage treatment plants, and oil spills from tankers or pipelines; also wastewater from manufacturers, oil refineries or treatment facilities, leaks from septic systems, chemical spills and illegal dumping. The EPA regulates point source pollution by setting discharge limits for facilities. Despite its localised origin, it can affect extended stretches of waterways and oceans — the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill released approximately 4.9 million barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico.

Nonpoint Source Pollution

Nonpoint source pollution originates from diffuse sources, making it more challenging to trace back to a specific origin. Examples include agricultural runoff (fertilisers, pesticides and animal waste), urban runoff (oil, grease, heavy metals and debris), atmospheric deposition (heavy metals and acidic compounds), residential runoff (pollutants from lawns, gardens and residential areas) and transportation runoff (oil, heavy metals, tyre particles and exhaust-related pollutants). Rain can carry tiny rubber particles from vehicle tyres into rivers; tyre wear releases more microplastics into oceans than plastic bags and bottles combined.

Key Points

  • Point source = one identifiable source, e.g. a factory discharge pipe or an oil spill from a tanker.
  • Point sources are easier to monitor and regulate through discharge limits.
  • Nonpoint source = diffuse sources spread over an area, e.g. farm and urban runoff.
  • Nonpoint pollution is harder to trace and control.
  • Both types can damage long stretches of waterways and oceans.

lessons.title: Common Water Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Water pollution occurs when harmful substances are introduced into water bodies, adversely affecting living organisms and disrupting ecological balance. The most common types of water pollutants are:

Pollutant TypeExamples and Effects
Suspended solids and sedimentsSilt, clay, coal dust, plankton and industrial wastes; cause turbidity, reduce sunlight penetration and harm aquatic vegetation and animals
Dissolved solidsOrganic and inorganic compounds dissolved in water — calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chlorides, sulphates, carbonates; excess dissolved solids (salts, metals, fertilisers, pesticides) disturb growth of aquatic life and make water unsafe for drinking
Toxic elements and heavy metalsMercury, cadmium, lead, arsenic, chromium, nickel and zinc from industrial effluents, mining and waste disposal; toxic even in small amounts to humans and aquatic life
Pesticides and agricultural runoffDDT, endosulfan, atrazine and chlorpyrifos enter water via agricultural runoff; these persistent organic pollutants accumulate in the food chain
Volatile organic compounds (VOCs)Benzene, toluene and xylene from industrial discharges, solvents and fuels; toxic and carcinogenic
Oil and greaseOil spills and industrial runoff cover the water surface, lowering oxygen availability for aquatic life
Thermal pollutionHot water discharged from thermal or nuclear power plants (often 10–15°C warmer) raises water temperature, reduces dissolved oxygen and harms aquatic life

Key Points

  • Suspended solids make water turbid and block sunlight for aquatic plants.
  • Heavy metals are toxic even in very small amounts and enter through industry and mining.
  • Pesticides such as DDT are persistent and accumulate in the food chain.
  • Oil films on the surface cut off oxygen for aquatic organisms.
  • Thermal pollution lowers dissolved oxygen by warming the water.

lessons.title: Water Treatment
lessons.notes_html:
Water treatment is the process of making raw water suitable for drinking and other domestic uses by removing foreign materials. Its purpose is to eliminate contaminants and organisms through a combination of biological, chemical and physical methods, ensuring the water is safe for consumption. Contaminated water is a primary source of infectious diseases such as amoebiasis, dysentery, cholera, typhoid, jaundice, malaria and paratyphoid fever.

Steps of Water Treatment

StepPurpose
1. PretreatmentWater passes through screens to eliminate large debris and floating materials such as leaves and sticks
2. CoagulationChemicals induce clumping of small suspended particles, aiding removal of colloidal clay precipitates
3. SedimentationWater rests in sedimentation tanks so large or heavy particles settle, reducing the overall load of impurities
4. FiltrationWater is filtered through layers of sand and gravel to remove fine particles and organic matter
5. Carbon adsorptionWater passes over beds of activated charcoal, which eliminate unpleasant tastes, odours and certain organic contaminants
6. ChlorinationChlorine or chlorine compounds are added to kill harmful microorganisms — the final, critical disinfection step
7. UV disinfectionUltraviolet light disrupts the DNA of microorganisms, preventing reproduction and rendering them harmless

The treated water is then stored and distributed for home consumption (Fig. 10.7 sequence: intake → coagulation → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection → treated water storage → distribution).

Key Points

  • Water treatment combines physical, chemical and biological methods to make water safe.
  • Order of steps: pretreatment → coagulation → sedimentation → filtration → carbon adsorption → disinfection.
  • Coagulation clumps fine suspended particles so they can settle out.
  • Activated charcoal removes tastes, odours and organic contaminants.
  • Chlorination and UV light disinfect by killing or inactivating microorganisms.

lessons.title: Human Impact on Water Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities, particularly in agriculture and industrial processes, significantly and complexly impact water resources. These impacts affect both the quantity of water available and its quality, which in turn has consequences for ecosystems and human communities.

Agriculture's Impact on Water Resources

Farming uses a large amount of the world's freshwater supply for irrigation, which can lead to water scarcity and further deplete water sources like rivers and aquifers; inefficient irrigation practices worsen the problem by putting additional strain on water sources. Chemicals from fertilisers and pesticides used in farming can contaminate rivers and streams, harming ecosystems and posing risks to wildlife and human health. Deforestation and unsustainable farming practices lead to soil erosion, which pollutes waterways with sediment and reduces water quality.

Industrial Processes and Water Resources

Industries use significant amounts of water for cooling, manufacturing and other processes, which can strain water resources, especially in areas already facing water scarcity. Industrial activities release pollutants like heavy metals and toxic chemicals into waterways, making them unsuitable for various purposes. Excess heat generated by industrial processes can disrupt aquatic ecosystems and create uninhabitable zones for many species. Additionally, both agriculture and industry contribute to climate change, further worsening water scarcity and altering hydrological cycles.

Key Points

  • Agriculture is the largest user of freshwater, mainly for irrigation.
  • Inefficient irrigation depletes rivers and aquifers and causes scarcity.
  • Fertilisers and pesticides from farms contaminate rivers and streams.
  • Industry uses water for cooling and manufacturing and discharges heavy metals and toxic chemicals.
  • Industrial waste heat creates uninhabitable zones for aquatic species.

lessons.title: Strategies for Conservation and Preservation of Water Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Water conservation involves promoting responsible water use in homes, businesses and agriculture, encouraging water-efficient technologies and appliances, and implementing methods like rainwater harvesting and efficient irrigation to conserve water.

Strategies for Conservation and Preservation (Table 10.1)

StrategyFocusKey ExamplesBenefits
Water conservationReduce demandLow-flow appliances, smart irrigation, rainwater harvesting, research in advanced water-saving technologiesLess pressure on water sources; reduces stress during droughts and floods
Watershed managementProtect sourcesRiparian buffers, wetland restoration, erosion control, runoff managementSustained water supplies, improved water quality, remote sensing for informed management
Pollution controlSafeguard purityRegulations on discharges, advanced wastewater treatment, responsible chemical use, septic tank filters, storm water managementMinimises water pollution, protects ecosystems and human health, stronger legislation holds polluters accountable
Infrastructure investmentModernise and optimiseLeak detection, smart systems, efficient storage and desalination, replacing aging pipesReduced water losses, increased efficiency and resilience, equitable access to water
Education and awarenessEmpower individuals and communitiesWater conservation campaigns, educational workshops, media outreach, integrating water education into schoolsFosters individual responsibility; builds a sustainable, water-conscious society

Key Points

  • Conservation reduces demand through efficient appliances, smart irrigation and rainwater harvesting.
  • Watershed management protects the sources of water themselves.
  • Pollution control safeguards purity through discharge regulations and wastewater treatment.
  • Modern infrastructure cuts losses from leaks and aging pipes.
  • Education builds a water-conscious society that sustains all other strategies.

lessons.title: The Influence of Chemical Properties on Water Quality and Pollution
lessons.notes_html:
The physical, biological and chemical properties of drinking water — including its molecular structure, polarity, ability to form hydrogen bonds and role as a solvent — play a critical role in determining water quality and potential pollution. Even minor variations in these parameters can have significant implications for human health.

Chemical Properties of Water

  • Molecular structure and polarity: H2O is a polar molecule due to the electronegativity difference between oxygen and hydrogen. This polarity makes water an excellent solvent, attracting polar molecules and dissolving substances — essential for transporting nutrients and minerals in living organisms.
  • Hydrogen bonding: water molecules form (weak) hydrogen bonds due to their polarity, giving properties like high surface tension, cohesion, adhesion, capillary action and water transport in plants.
  • Solvent properties: water is a universal solvent that transports nutrients and minerals, but it is also susceptible to pollution from acid rain, industrial discharges and runoff, as it can dissolve and carry harmful chemicals.

Relation to Water Quality

  • pH level: drinking water should be near neutral (pH 7); deviations can harm aquatic life and human health.
  • Dissolved oxygen (DO): aquatic organisms rely on dissolved oxygen for respiration; pollution such as organic matter from sewage or agricultural runoff can deplete oxygen levels.
  • Ion concentrations: elevated nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers cause nutrient pollution, leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion; vital minerals like calcium and magnesium are beneficial in moderation.

Relation to Water Pollution

  • Solubility: water's ability to dissolve substances makes it vulnerable to pollution from agricultural runoff, industrial waste and urban wastewater.
  • Bioaccumulation: pollutants like pesticides or heavy metals accumulate in the tissues of organisms over time, especially when absorption exceeds breakdown or excretion.
  • Chemical reactions: pollutants can react in water, forming toxic by-products; industrial discharges may produce harmful compounds.

Key Points

  • Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, making it a universal solvent.
  • The same solvent power that carries nutrients also carries pollutants.
  • Water quality is judged by pH, dissolved oxygen and ion concentrations.
  • Excess nitrates and phosphates cause algal blooms and oxygen depletion.
  • Bioaccumulation builds up pesticides and heavy metals in organism tissues over time.

lessons.title: Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons and their derivatives are organic compounds. Compounds of only carbon and hydrogen are hydrocarbons; those also containing O, N, S, P or halogens are derivatives of hydrocarbons. Their study is organic chemistry.

Functional Group

A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that mainly determines the chemical behaviour of the molecule. Double and triple bonds are also functional groups. Compounds with the same functional group show similar properties: methanol CH3OH, ethanol CH3CH2OH and propanol CH3CH2CH2OH are alike because of the —OH group. The functional group is the reactive part; the hydrocarbon part is inert. A compound with two or more functional groups is a polyfunctional compound.

Key Formulae

ClassFunctional groupExampleSuffix/Prefix
Alkanes— (R—H)CH3—CH3, ethane-ane
AlkenesC=CH2C=CH2, ethene-ene
AlkynesC≡CCH≡CH, ethyne-yne
Alkyl halides—XCH3CH2Cl, chloroethanehalo-
Alcohols—OHCH3CH2OH, ethanol-ol
Ethers—O—CH3—O—CH3, methoxymethane—
Aldehydes—CHOCH3CHO, ethanal-al
KetonesC=O (carbonyl)propan-2-one-one
Carboxylic acids—COOHCH3COOH, ethanoic acid-oic acid
Esters—COORmethyl ethanoate-oate
Amides—CONH2ethanamide-amide
Amines—NH2methanamine-amine
Nitriles—CNCH3—C≡N, ethanenitrile-nitrile

Key Points

  • Functional group decides chemical behaviour, nomenclature and classification.
  • Same functional group = similar chemical properties.
  • Ethanol (—OH) is in alcoholic beverages; acetic acid (—COOH) gives vinegar its sour flavour; formaldehyde (—CHO) preserves specimens.
  • Phenols have —OH on an aromatic ring; acyl halides —COX take suffix -oyl halide; acid anhydrides take -oic anhydride.

lessons.title: Homologous Series
lessons.notes_html:
A homologous series is a group of organic compounds in which each member differs from the next by a methylene group (—CH2—). Its members are called homologs.

Alkane Series

NameC atomsMolecular formulaCondensed formula
Methane1CH4CH4
Ethane2C2H6CH3CH3
Propane3C3H8CH3CH2CH3
Butane4C4H10CH3(CH2)2CH3
Pentane5C5H12CH3(CH2)3CH3
Hexane6C6H14CH3(CH2)4CH3
Heptane7C7H16CH3(CH2)5CH3
Octane8C8H18CH3(CH2)6CH3
Nonane9C9H20CH3(CH2)7CH3
Decane10C10H22CH3(CH2)8CH3

General Characteristics

  • Same functional group, same general formula, same types of elements.
  • Similar chemical properties; different physical properties because molecular masses differ.
  • Successive members differ by CH2; molecular mass differs by 14 units (CH2 = 12 + 2 = 14).
  • All members are prepared by the same general methods.

Key Formulae

ClassGeneral formula
AlkaneCnH2n+2
AlkeneCnH2n
AlkyneCnH2n-2
AlcoholCnH2n+1OH
Alkyl halideCnH2n+1X (X = F, Cl, Br, I)

Here n is the number of carbon atoms.

Key Points

  • Homologs differ by —CH2— and 14 mass units.
  • Chemical properties stay similar down the series.
  • Physical properties change gradually with molecular mass.
  • One general formula represents the whole series.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
The system for naming compounds is called nomenclature. Two primary systems name organic compounds: the Common System and the IUPAC System. Common names are often shorter and useful when the IUPAC name is lengthy, e.g. tartaric acid for 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid.

IUPAC System

To avoid memorising millions of names, a commission of 34 chemists from nine countries met in Geneva (Switzerland) in 1892 and developed the Geneva system. The group became the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), pronounced eye-you-pack. Its rules are continually revised. The fundamental principle: each different compound should have a distinct and unambiguous name.

Parts of an IUPAC Name

  • Root: number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain.
  • Suffix: the family of the compound.
  • Prefix: identity, position and number of substituents on the chain.

Key Points

  • Nomenclature = the naming system for compounds.
  • IUPAC began with the Geneva meeting of 1892.
  • One compound, one distinct unambiguous IUPAC name.
  • Every IUPAC name has root + suffix, with prefixes for substituents.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Straight Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
The first four alkanes keep common names: methane, ethane, propane and butane. Names of larger alkanes use a Latin or Greek prefix for the number of carbon atoms, followed by -ane.

Common-System Prefixes for Isomers

In the common system all isomeric alkanes share one parent name, e.g. pentane for the three C5H12 isomers. Prefixes n-, iso- and neo- distinguish them.

  • n- (normal): all carbons in one continuous unbranched chain, e.g. n-pentane CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, n-hexane.
  • iso-: one methyl group on the second carbon of the chain, e.g. isopentane, isohexane.
  • neo-: two methyl groups on the second carbon, e.g. neohexane, neoheptane.

Key Formulae

C atomsRootParent nameC atomsRootParent name
1MethMethane11UndecUndecane
2EthEthane12DodecDodecane
3PropPropane13TridecTridecane
4ButButane14TetradecTetradecane
5PentPentane15PentadecPentadecane
6HexHexane16HexadecHexadecane
7HeptHeptane17HeptadecHeptadecane
8OctOctane18OctadecOctadecane
9NonNonane19NonadecNonadecane
10DecDecane20EicosEicosane

Skeletal formula: a zigzag line; each end and corner is a carbon, e.g. ethane is one line segment, propane two segments.

Key Points

  • Root + -ane names a straight-chain alkane.
  • n- = unbranched; iso- = one methyl at C-2; neo- = two methyls at C-2.
  • First four names (methane to butane) are retained common names.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Branched Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Branched-chain alkanes are named by the IUPAC rules below.

Rules

  • (i) Select the longest continuous chain as parent (stem) name. It may turn a corner; e.g. the worked example gives an 8-carbon parent, octane.
  • (ii) Number from the end closer to the substituents: 3-methylhexane, not 4-methylhexane.
  • (iii) Show the substituent position by its carbon number: 4-methyloctane.
  • (iv) Identical substituents take di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-: 2,4-dimethylpentane.
  • (v) If the first substituent is equidistant from both ends, give the lower number to the second substituent (first point of difference): 2,4,7-trimethyloctane, not 2,5,7-trimethyloctane.
  • (vi) Different substituents are listed alphabetically: 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane. Ignore di-, tri-, sec-, tert- in alphabetising; iso- and cyclo- are not ignored. If numbering ties both ways, the first-listed substituent alphabetically gets the lower number.
  • (vii) Between equal-length chains, choose the one with more substituents: 3-ethyl-2-methylheptane, not 3-isopropylheptane.

Branch name and parent name are written as one word; numbers are separated by commas, and a hyphen separates number from word.

Key Points

  • Longest chain first, then lowest locants.
  • Alphabetical order for different substituents.
  • di-/tri- show repeated identical substituents.
  • More substituents wins when chains are equal in length.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Cycloalkanes are named by IUPAC rules for rings.

Rules

  • (i) Add prefix cyclo- to the alkane with the same number of carbons as the ring: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane. They are drawn as geometric figures — triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon; each corner is one carbon with two hydrogens.
  • (ii) A single substituent needs no position number, as all positions are equivalent: methylcyclopropane, ethylcyclobutane.
  • (iii) With two or more substituents, number the ring for the lowest possible numbers and name substituents alphabetically: 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane; 1-ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane; 1-ethyl-2,5-dimethylcyclohexane.
  • (iv) If the substituent chain has more carbons than the ring, the chain is the parent and the ring is a substituent: 1-cyclopropylbutane, 2-cyclobutylpentane.

Key Points

  • cyclo- + alkane name = cycloalkane.
  • Mono-substituted rings need no locant.
  • Lowest locants, then alphabetical order, for several substituents.
  • Larger chain beats the ring as parent.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alkenes and Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes

  • Select the longest continuous chain containing the C=C bond; position of the double bond follows the root, then suffix -ene: CH2=CH—CH2—CH3 is butene (parent).
  • Number from the end closest to the double bond; give its position by the lower-numbered carbon. Two- and three-carbon alkenes need no number. Example: pent-2-ene.
  • Name substituents as in alkanes: 4-methylpent-2-ene.
  • Two or more double bonds: -diene, -triene, -tetraene replace -ene, e.g. buta-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH2.

Alkynes

  • Select the longest chain containing C≡C; suffix -yne: CH3—C≡C—CH3 is butyne (parent).
  • Number from the end nearest the triple bond; position by the lower carbon: pent-2-yne. Two-/three-carbon alkynes need no numbering.
  • Substituents as usual, triple bond lowest: 4-methylhex-2-yne.
  • Several triple bonds: -diyne, -triyne, -tetrayne, e.g. buta-1,3-diyne.
  • Both double and triple bonds: root ends in -en, suffix -yne for the whole molecule. Number from the end closest to either bond; if equidistant, the double bond gets the lower number: pent-1-en-4-yne, pent-1-en-3-yne, pent-3-en-1-yne.

Key Points

  • Parent chain must contain the multiple bond.
  • Multiple bond gets the lowest possible locant.
  • -diene/-diyne etc. show several multiple bonds.
  • In enynes, a tie is broken in favour of the double bond.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Haloalkanes (Alkyl Halides)

Select the longest chain including the halogen as parent. Number from the end closest to the halogen for its lowest number. Name the halogen as a prefix — fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo — with its position number. Several identical halogens take di-, tri-, tetra-; different halogens are written alphabetically.

Examples: bromoethane CH3—CH2—Br; 2-chloropropane; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane.

Alcohols

The longest chain containing —OH is the parent; suffix -ol replaces the final -e of the alkane. Number from the end closer to —OH so it gets the lowest number, and show its position. Other substituents follow standard rules, with priority to —OH in numbering. Several —OH groups take -diol, -triol and the final -e is retained.

Examples: ethanol CH3—CH2—OH; propan-2-ol; 3-methylbutan-1-ol; pentane-2,4-diol; 4-bromo-3-chloro-2-methylbutan-1-ol.

Key Points

  • Halogens are always prefixes, never the suffix.
  • Alcohol suffix is -ol; —OH controls numbering.
  • Multiple —OH groups: -diol, -triol, keeping the -e.
  • Different halogens are listed alphabetically.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes

The longest chain containing the —CHO group is the parent. Suffix -al replaces the final -e of the alkane. The —CHO carbon is always carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single aldehyde group. Other substituents follow standard rules.

Examples: methanal HCHO; ethanal CH3CHO; propanal; 3-methylbutanal; 4-bromo-3-chloro-2-methylbutanal.

Ketones

The longest chain containing the carbonyl group (C=O) is the parent. Suffix -one replaces the final -e. Number from the end nearer the carbonyl group and place its locant before the name. Substituents follow standard rules.

Examples: propan-2-one CH3—CO—CH3; butan-2-one; 2-methylpentan-3-one; 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one.

Note the contrast: an aldehyde group is terminal (at the chain end, —CHO with a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon), while a ketone carbonyl is bonded to two carbons inside the chain. That is why aldehydes never need a locant for one group, but ketones from butan-2-one onwards do; propan-2-one needs none because the carbonyl can only sit on the middle carbon.

Key Points

  • Aldehyde carbon is always C-1; suffix -al.
  • Ketone suffix is -one with a locant for C=O.
  • Carbonyl carbon in a ketone lies inside the chain.
  • Substituents are numbered from the functional-group end.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Ethers and Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers

Ethers are alkoxy derivatives of hydrocarbons. The larger alkyl chain is the parent alkane; the smaller alkyl group on oxygen is an alkoxy substituent. Number from the end closer to oxygen and show the alkoxy position by its locant.

Examples: methoxymethane CH3—O—CH3; methoxyethane CH3—O—CH2—CH3; 2-methoxypropane; 2-ethoxybutane.

Amines

Amines are alkyl derivatives of ammonia. The longest chain containing —NH2 is the parent; suffix -amine replaces the final -e. Number from the end closest to —NH2 for its lowest number; the locant is not needed when —NH2 is at carbon-1 in a primary amine. Several —NH2 groups take -diamine, -triamine, retaining the final -e.

Examples: methanamine CH3—NH2; ethanamine; propan-2-amine; butane-2,3-diamine. In secondary and tertiary amines, extra alkyl groups on nitrogen are N-substituents: N-methylethanamine; N,N-dimethylmethanamine; N-ethyl-N-methylpropan-2-amine.

Key Points

  • Ether: larger group = parent, smaller = alkoxy prefix.
  • Amine suffix is -amine; —NH2 controls numbering.
  • Groups on nitrogen are named with the locant N-.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Nitriles and Carboxylic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Nitriles

Select the longest chain that includes the —C≡N group and add suffix -nitrile to the parent name. The nitrile carbon is always carbon-1, so no separate locant is needed for a simple nitrile. Substituents follow standard rules; several —C≡N groups take dinitrile, trinitrile.

Examples: ethanenitrile CH3—C≡N; propanenitrile; 2-methylpropanenitrile; 2-ethylpropane-1,3-dinitrile.

Carboxylic Acids

The longest chain containing —COOH is the parent; suffix -oic acid replaces the final -e. The —COOH carbon is always carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single carboxyl group. Substituents follow the lowest-locant rule.

Examples: ethanoic acid CH3COOH (common name acetic acid, vinegar); propanoic acid; 2-methylpropanoic acid.

Counting the functional carbon in the chain length is the common trap in both classes: CH3—C≡N has two carbons in total, so it is ethanenitrile, not methanenitrile; likewise CH3COOH is ethanoic acid. The book's household example makes the point — CH3COOH is commonly called acetic acid (vinegar), while its systematic IUPAC name is ethanoic acid, and systematic naming avoids such confusion in science and industry.

Key Points

  • Nitrile and carboxyl carbons are both counted as C-1.
  • Suffixes: -nitrile and -oic acid.
  • No locant is needed for one —CN or one —COOH group.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Acyl Halides, Amides and Esters
lessons.notes_html:
Acyl Halides

Replace the suffix -ic acid in the parent carboxylic acid name with -yl halide. Examples: methanoyl chloride H—CO—Cl; propanoyl bromide; butanoyl bromide.

Amides

Replace the suffix -oic acid of the parent acid with -amide. Examples: methanamide H—CO—NH2; ethanamide CH3—CO—NH2; propanamide; 4-chloropentanamide.

Esters

An ester name has two words. The first word is the alkyl group bonded to the oxygen atom; the second is obtained by replacing -ic acid in the parent acid name with -ate. Examples: methyl methanoate H—CO—OCH3; ethyl ethanoate CH3—CO—OCH2CH3; methyl propanoate.

Key Formulae

ClassGroupSuffix change
Acyl halide—COX-ic acid → -yl halide
Amide—CONH2-oic acid → -amide
Ester—COOR-ic acid → -ate, alkyl group first

Key Points

  • All three classes are named from the parent carboxylic acid.
  • Ester names are two words: alkyl + alkanoate.
  • Acyl halide: -oyl chloride / bromide etc.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Acid Anhydrides and Compounds with Multiple Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Acid Anhydrides

Symmetrical anhydrides: replace acid in the parent acid name with anhydride — methanoic anhydride, ethanoic anhydride. Unsymmetrical (mixed) anhydrides, from two different acids, are named by alphabetising both acid names and replacing acid with anhydride: ethanoic methanoic anhydride; ethanoic propanoic anhydride.

Multiple Functional Groups

Prioritise functional groups by a set hierarchy; the highest-priority group gives the suffix, the others are named as prefixes, in alphabetical order.

Priority order (book): Carboxylic acids (—COOH) > Esters (—COOR) > Amides (—CONH2) > Nitriles (—CN) > Aldehydes (—CHO) > Ketones (>C=O) > Alcohols (—OH) > Amines (—NH2) > Alkenes (C=C) > Alkynes (C≡C) > Alkanes (C—C) > Halides (—X).

Examples: 2-chloropropanal (—CHO wins over Cl); 3-bromo-2-hydroxybutanoic acid; 3-hydroxybutanal; 4-hydroxy-2-methylhexan-3-one (ketone suffix, —OH as hydroxy- prefix).

Key Points

  • Only the top-priority group becomes the suffix.
  • Lower groups appear as prefixes: hydroxy-, halo-, etc.
  • Mixed anhydrides list both acids alphabetically.
  • Carboxylic acid has the highest priority in the book list.

lessons.title: Empirical and Molecular Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
The symbolic representation of a compound is its formula (chemical formula): empirical, molecular, structural, displayed and skeletal.

Empirical Formula

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Examples: glucose CH2O, benzene CH, hydrogen peroxide HO, ammonia NH3, water H2O.

Molecular Formula

The molecular formula shows the total number of atoms in a molecule: glucose C6H12O6, benzene C6H6, hydrogen peroxide H2O2, ammonia NH3, water H2O.

Key Formulae

QuantityFormula
Moles of an elementMole = Percentage of an Element / Atomic Mass
Value of nn = Molecular Formula Mass / Empirical Formula Mass
Molecular formulaMolecular formula = n × Empirical Formula

Determination

  • Empirical: (i) divide each percentage by its atomic mass to get moles (assume 100 g); (ii) divide all moles by the smallest to get the simple ratio; (iii) multiply fractions to whole numbers; (iv) write ratios as subscripts.
  • Example 11.1: 92.3% C, 7.69% H → moles C = 92.3/12 ≈ 7.69, H = 7.69/1 = 7.69; ratio 1:1; empirical formula CH.
  • Molecular: find n, then multiply. Example 11.2: acetylene, empirical CH (mass 13), molecular mass 26 → n = 26/13 = 2 → C2H2.

Key Points

  • Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual atom counts.
  • Molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of empirical.
  • Percentages are treated as grams in a 100 g sample.

lessons.title: Condensed, Structural, Displayed and Skeletal Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
Condensed Formula

The condensed formula is a structural formula that indicates the number and type of atoms but gives no indication of the bonds between them. Example: propanol is CH3CH2CH2OH.

Structural Formula

The structural formula is the most detailed representation of a molecule, showing the arrangement of atoms and the bonds between them. For propanol (C3H7OH) it shows each C bonded in a chain, hydrogens on each carbon, and —O—H at the end, all joined by single bonds. Its two types are displayed formula and skeletal formula.

Displayed Formula

The displayed formula is a simplified structural formula that explicitly draws each atom and bond, giving a clear visual picture of the spatial arrangement, e.g. propanol drawn with every H, C and O and every bond shown.

Skeletal Formula

The skeletal formula emphasises the carbon skeleton and functional groups, using lines for carbon—carbon bonds while omitting carbon and hydrogen atoms. Hydrogens on carbon are excluded; only heteroatoms (atoms other than C and H) and the skeleton are shown, e.g. propanol as a two-segment zigzag ending in —OH.

Key Points

  • Condensed: atoms counted, bonds not shown.
  • Structural/displayed: every atom and bond shown.
  • Skeletal: lines only; C and its H atoms are understood.
  • Heteroatoms are always written in a skeletal formula.

lessons.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Compounds, Fission and Free Radicals
lessons.notes_html:
Saturated and Unsaturated

Saturated compounds contain only single bonds between carbon atoms and the maximum possible hydrogens, e.g. butane. Unsaturated compounds contain at least one multiple bond (double or triple) and fewer hydrogens, e.g. butene and butyne.

Homolytic and Heterolytic Fission

Homolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks with each atom keeping one electron, forming two free radicals: Cl2 → 2Cl•. Heterolytic fission: one atom takes both electrons, forming ions: H—Cl → H+ + Cl-.

Free Radical

A free radical is a highly reactive species with an unpaired electron; it initiates chain reactions. Examples: methyl radical •CH3 and chlorine radical •Cl.

Initiation, Propagation and Termination

  • Initiation: first step, generates free radicals: Cl2 → 2Cl•.
  • Propagation: radicals react with molecules, making new radicals and continuing the chain: Cl• + CH4 → HCl + •CH3.
  • Termination: radicals combine to form a stable molecule, ending the chain: •CH3 + •Cl → CH3Cl.

Key Points

  • Homolytic = one electron each, radicals; heterolytic = both to one atom, ions.
  • Radicals carry an unpaired electron and are very reactive.
  • Chain sequence: initiation → propagation → termination.

lessons.title: Nucleophiles, Electrophiles and Types of Reaction
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleophile and Electrophile

A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates a pair of electrons and is attracted to electron-deficient sites, e.g. OH- attacking carbon in haloalkanes. An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts a pair of electrons and is attracted to electron-rich sites, e.g. the carbocation CH3+.

Addition, Substitution and Elimination

  • Addition: atoms are added with nothing removed, e.g. hydrogenation of ethene: CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3 (Ni catalyst, 150-200°C as printed in this section).
  • Substitution: atoms or groups are replaced, e.g. CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (hv).
  • Elimination: atoms or groups are removed, e.g. dehydrohalogenation: CH3CH2Br + NaOH → CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O (heat).

Hydrolysis and Condensation

Hydrolysis: a compound reacts with water and its bonds break: C12H22O11 + H2O → 2C6H12O6 (maltose → glucose, H+). Enzymes hydrolyse starch and proteins in digestion. Condensation: two or more molecules join into a larger molecule, often losing a small molecule such as water — esterification: CH3COOH + C2H5OH → CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (H+). Condensation makes polyester and nylon.

Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state, e.g. combustion: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O. Reduction is gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation state, e.g. CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3 (Pt, 45-100°C). LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols: R—CHO → R—CH2—OH.

Key Points

  • Nucleophile donates an electron pair; electrophile accepts one.
  • Addition adds, substitution swaps, elimination removes.
  • Hydrolysis splits with water; condensation joins with loss of water.
  • Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains them.

lessons.title: Importance of Catenation in Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Catenation (from Latin catena, chain) is the ability of atoms of the same element to bond with each other to form chains or rings. It is especially significant for carbon.

Why Carbon Catenates Best

  • Carbon has four valence electrons and a small size, so it forms strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.
  • Its C—C bonds are stable, giving long chains, branched structures and rings.
  • This diversity is the basis of organic and biomolecules — proteins, nucleic acids and carbohydrates.
  • Silicon, boron and sulphur also catenate, but to a lesser extent because their bonds are weaker; they form only smaller chains or rings.

Forms shown in the book: straight chain, branched chain and cyclic chain of carbon atoms.

The book illustrates catenation with three arrangements of linked carbon atoms: a straight chain of four carbons in a row, a branched chain with one carbon attached below the chain, and a cyclic chain forming a ring. One mole of carbon atoms joined end-to-end would make a chain long enough to wrap around the Earth's equator millions of times, showing the scale of diversity catenation allows.

Key Points

  • Catenation = self-linking into chains and rings.
  • Strong, stable C—C bonds make carbon unique.
  • Catenation explains the huge number of organic compounds.
  • Other elements catenate only weakly by comparison.

lessons.title: Nucleophilic Substitution and Electrophilic Addition
lessons.notes_html:
Curly arrows show the movement of a pair of electrons in a reaction.

Nucleophilic Substitution (SN)

A nucleophile (Nu-) attacks and replaces a leaving group (X) on the substrate. Two types: SN2, one-step bimolecular, and SN1, two-step unimolecular. In SN2 the nucleophile attacks carbon from the back side, displacing the functional group; one group is substituted by another. The curly arrow starts at the nucleophile and goes to the electrophilic centre (the electron-deficient carbon, δ+ next to X δ-); a second arrow shows the C—X bond electrons moving onto X, which leaves as X-.

Electrophilic Addition (Alkene Hydrogenation)

A double bond reacts with an electrophile (which accepts an electron pair) to form a new functional group. Curly arrows show pi electrons moving from the double bond to the electrophilic centre, usually a positively charged atom such as H+. A carbocation forms, then a nucleophile such as X- attacks it, giving new sigma bonds at both carbons. Hydrogenation of vegetable oils to margarine is given as an everyday electrophilic addition.

Key Points

  • Curly arrow = movement of an electron pair, from electron-rich to electron-poor.
  • SN2 is one step with back-side attack; SN1 is two steps.
  • Electrophilic addition passes through a carbocation.
  • The pi bond supplies the electrons in electrophilic addition.

lessons.title: Elimination, Free-radical Substitution and Nucleophilic Addition
lessons.notes_html:
Elimination Reaction

Atoms or groups are removed from neighbouring carbon atoms of a saturated substrate, forming a double bond. A base abstracts a proton (H+) from the β-carbon while a leaving group such as halide departs from the adjacent α-carbon; simultaneous removal creates C=C, e.g. a primary alkyl halide + OH- → ethene + H2O + X-.

Free-radical Substitution

A covalent bond breaks to give highly reactive free radicals, which then replace atoms or groups in a molecule — a substitution reaction. Example: chlorination of methane, CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. The same radical chemistry lets CFCs release chlorine radicals that damage the ozone layer.

Nucleophilic Addition

A nucleophile (Nu-) adds to a multiple bond in the substrate, such as a double bond. The main examples are additions to carbonyl groups, e.g. HCN adding to ethanal: CH3—CHO + H—CN → CH3—CH(OH)—CN. Curly arrows show the nucleophile (CN-) attacking the carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen.

Key Points

  • Elimination removes H from β-C and X from α-C to form C=C.
