  • Free-radical substitution works through radical intermediates.
  • Nucleophilic addition is typical of carbonyl compounds.
  • Mechanism arrows always follow the electron pairs.

lessons.title: Planarity in Organic Molecules: Impact on Structure and Reactivity
lessons.notes_html:
A molecule is planar when its atoms lie in a single plane, bonded so they occupy the same flat plane without significant deviation. Planarity is important for structure and reactivity.

Planar Example: Benzene

Benzene's carbon atoms form a hexagonal ring and all its atoms lie in one plane. This planar arrangement enhances its stability and aromatic properties. Planar molecules may contain single, double or triple bonds.

Non-planar Molecules

Not all organic molecules are planar. Steric hindrance, bulky substituents and ring strain make some non-planar. Cyclohexane adopts a non-planar, puckered conformation — shown in the book as the boat conformation and the chair conformation.

The book draws benzene in two ways: a full structural form with alternating double bonds in a six-carbon ring, and the skeletal hexagon with a circle/double-bond representation. In both, every carbon and hydrogen lies flat. Planarity therefore links directly to how a molecule packs, how stable it is, and how it reacts — flat aromatic systems behave very differently from puckered saturated rings such as cyclohexane.

Key Points

  • Planar = all atoms in one flat plane.
  • Benzene is planar, which aids its stability and aromatic character.
  • Bulky groups and ring strain can force non-planar shapes.
  • Cyclohexane is puckered (chair and boat forms).

lessons.title: Structural Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different properties are isomers; the phenomenon is isomerism, e.g. n-butane and isobutane, both C4H10. Two main types: stereoisomerism and structural isomerism. Octane C8H18 has 18 structural isomers.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas — a different arrangement of atoms. They divide into five types:

Key Formulae

TypeDifferenceBook example
Chain (skeleton)Different carbon chainn-pentane, isopentane, neopentane (C5H12)
PositionDifferent position of same functional group1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane (C4H9Cl); but-1-ene and but-2-ene (C4H8)
Functional groupDifferent functional groupEthanol CH3CH2OH and dimethyl ether CH3OCH3 (C2H6O); methyl acetate and propanoic acid (C3H6O2)
MetamersDifferent distribution of carbons on either side of the functional groupDiethyl ether and methyl-n-propyl ether; trimethylamine and ethylmethylamine
TautomersDifferent positions of protons and electrons; keto and enol forms in dynamic equilibriumPropan-2-one (keto) ⇌ propen-2-ol (enol), as drawn in the book

Metamers belong to the same homologous series. Tautomerism matters in biology: keto—enol tautomerism affects DNA base pairing, and errors can cause mutations.

Key Points

  • Structural isomers differ in atom arrangement, not just in space.
  • Five types: chain, position, functional group, metamers, tautomers.
  • Tautomers interconvert rapidly and exist in dynamic equilibrium.
  • Metamers keep the same functional group and series.

lessons.title: Stereoisomers (Configurational Isomers)
lessons.notes_html:
Stereoisomers have the same molecular and structural formulas but differ in the arrangement of atoms or groups in space; the phenomenon is stereoisomerism. Two types: geometric isomers and optical isomers; this unit discusses only geometric isomers.

Geometric Isomers (cis-trans Isomers)

Geometric isomers have restricted rotation, caused by a C=C double bond or by single bonds in cyclic compounds. The cis isomer (Latin cisoid, same side) has similar groups on the same side of the double bond; the trans isomer (transoid, opposite side) has them on opposite sides.

Example: cis-but-2-ene has both H atoms on the same side; trans-but-2-ene has them opposite. Cis and trans are distinct compounds with different physical properties. Trans is more stable: in cis, bulky groups on the same side repel each other, lowering stability.

Cyclic example: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane has both methyl groups on the same side of the ring; trans has them on opposite sides.

Key Points

  • Stereoisomers differ only in spatial arrangement.
  • Geometric isomerism needs restricted rotation.
  • cis = same side; trans = opposite sides.
  • Trans isomers are generally more stable than cis.

lessons.title: Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds, composed solely of carbon and hydrogen, joined by covalent bonds: methane CH4, ethylene C2H4, acetylene C2H2 and benzene C6H6. They are classified as aliphatic or aromatic, depending on the presence of a benzene ring.

Aliphatic Hydrocarbons

Straight-chained, branched or cyclic but non-aromatic hydrocarbons are aliphatic. Most are volatile and flammable. Saturated: only single bonds — alkanes and cycloalkanes, e.g. ethane CH3—CH3, cyclopropane (triangle). Unsaturated: at least one double or triple bond — alkenes, e.g. ethene CH2=CH2, and alkynes, e.g. ethyne HC≡CH.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons containing at least one benzene ring are aromatic: benzene, toluene, m-xylene and naphthalene.

In a straight chain, a carbon is never bonded to more than two carbons; in a branched compound a carbon may bond to three or four carbons at a time.

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons contain C and H only.
  • Aliphatic = non-aromatic chains, branches or rings.
  • Aromatic = contains a benzene ring.
  • Aliphatic splits into saturated and unsaturated.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes

Alkanes contain only single bonds between carbon atoms. They are also called paraffins, from Latin parum (little) + affin (affinity) — little affinity, the least reactive. Petroleum and natural gas are usually composed of alkanes.

Cycloalkanes

Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which carbons are linked by single covalent bonds to form a ring; they are also called cycloparaffins. Their formula has two hydrogens fewer than the corresponding alkane because of the ring, e.g. cyclopropane (triangle) and cyclobutane (square).

Key Formulae

ClassGeneral formula
AlkanesCnH2n+2
CycloalkanesCnH2n

Petroleum and natural gas, the main fossil sources studied later in this unit, consist largely of alkanes, which is why alkane chemistry underlies fuels and petrochemicals. Cycloalkanes occur alongside them in crude oil. Despite sharing single bonds, a cycloalkane is not an alkane isomer series member: its ring closes the chain, so it follows CnH2n, the same general formula as alkenes.

Key Points

  • Alkanes: single bonds only, general formula CnH2n+2.
  • Paraffin means little affinity — alkanes are least reactive.
  • Cycloalkanes are ring alkanes with formula CnH2n.
  • Ring formation costs two hydrogen atoms.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of Alkanes — Ethane

Ethane (C2H6), the second alkane, has two carbons joined by a single covalent bond, each carbon bonded to three hydrogens. The atoms arrange so the bonds are as far apart as possible: each carbon is tetrahedral, with bond angles of approximately 109.5°. The molecule can rotate freely about the C—C single bond — a characteristic feature of alkanes.

Structure of Cycloalkanes — Cyclopropane

Cyclopropane is the simplest cycloalkane. Cycloalkanes are written with a line-angle formula: a regular polygon with as many sides as ring carbons — triangle for cyclopropane, square for cyclobutane, pentagon for cyclopentane, hexagon for cyclohexane. Cyclopropane has significant bond angle strain (60° instead of 109.5°), which makes it highly reactive; it was once used as an anaesthetic.

Key Points

  • Ethane carbons are tetrahedral, angle about 109.5°.
  • Free rotation occurs about C—C single bonds.
  • Cycloalkanes are drawn as polygons (line-angle formula).
  • Cyclopropane is strained and unusually reactive.

lessons.title: The Unreactive Nature of Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes are generally unreactive to polar reagents. Carbon electronegativity is 2.5 and hydrogen 2.1 — a difference of only about 0.4 — so the C—H bond is nearly non-polar, and the C—C bond, with no electronegativity difference, is completely non-polar. Alkane molecules therefore lack partial positive or negative charges that could attract polar reagents.

In methane, ethane and propane, bonding involves only strong sigma bonds formed by head-on orbital overlap. These bonds are stable and difficult to break under normal conditions. With non-polar character and strong bonding, alkanes show little or no electrophilic or nucleophilic behaviour and stay largely unreactive to polar reagents.

Reactions of alkanes usually need extreme conditions: high temperature, strong oxidising agents or catalysts. They do react in specific cases, e.g. halogenation when exposed to light.

Key Points

  • C—H is nearly non-polar; C—C is non-polar.
  • No partial charges, so polar reagents are not attracted.
  • Strong sigma bonds are hard to break.
  • Alkane reactions need heat, light, strong oxidisers or catalysts.

lessons.title: Radical Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
A radical (free radical) is a highly reactive species with an unpaired electron, formed by homolysis of a covalent bond. Heterolysis: both bonding electrons stay with one atom, A—B → A+ + :B-. Homolysis: each atom keeps one electron, A—B → A• + B• (shown with single-headed curly arrows).

Reaction Mechanism — Chlorination of Methane

  • Initiation: Cl2 undergoes homolytic fission in heat or light: Cl—Cl → Cl• + Cl• (UV).
  • Propagation: Cl• + CH4 → •CH3 + HCl; then •CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•. Further substitution gives CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4 step by step, each step regenerating Cl•.
  • Termination: two radicals combine: •CH3 + •CH3 → CH3—CH3; •Cl + •Cl → Cl2; •CH3 + •Cl → CH3Cl. This reduces the radicals available and ends the chain.

Chlorination of Ethane

Same mechanism: initiation Cl2 → 2Cl• (hv); propagation Cl• + CH3CH3 → •CH2CH3 + HCl, then •CH2CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + Cl•; termination gives CH3CH2CH2CH3, Cl2 or CH3CH2Cl. Propagation differs slightly because ethane has secondary-type hydrogens in the book's wording.

Key Points

  • Free-radical chain: initiation, propagation, termination.
  • UV light or heat starts homolysis of Cl2.
  • Methane chlorination can continue to CCl4.
  • Termination removes radicals by combining them.

lessons.title: Identification of Organic Redox Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Organic redox reactions involve changes in oxidation states, identified by the gain or loss of oxygen and/or hydrogen.

Oxidation

Oxidation increases oxygen content or decreases hydrogen content, e.g. converting alcohols to aldehydes or ketones, and alkanes to alcohols.

  • Alkane to alcohol: CH3CH3 + 1/2 O2(g) → CH3CH2OH (PdCl2/CuCl2, 150-250°C).
  • Alcohol to aldehyde: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4); ethyl alcohol → acetaldehyde.
  • Secondary alcohol to ketone: CH3—CH(OH)—CH3 + [O] → CH3—CO—CH3 + H2O; sec-propyl alcohol → acetone.

Reduction

Reduction decreases oxygen content and/or increases hydrogen content, e.g. aldehydes/ketones are reduced to alcohols and alkenes to alkanes. The book shows acetone with NaBH4/H2O giving isopropyl alcohol under this heading.

In the body, glucose is oxidised in cells to release energy (ATP), just as hydrocarbons burn in engines.

Key Points

  • Oxidation: gain O or lose H.
  • Reduction: lose O or gain H.
  • Alcohol → aldehyde/ketone is oxidation; carbonyl → alcohol is reduction.
  • K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 is the oxidising system used in the examples.

lessons.title: Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more carbon—carbon double bonds (C=C). They are also known as olefins, from the French word olefiant, oil-forming, because lower alkenes give oily products with chlorine or bromine.

Alkenes occur in natural gas, coal gas and gasoline in small amounts, and are produced in large quantities by the cracking of petroleum. Ethene was first identified in the 18th century as olefiant gas because it formed oily liquids with chlorine. Ethylene (ethene) is the first member of the series.

Key Formulae

ClassGeneral formula
Alkenes (monoenes)CnH2n

Ethene itself is the starting material for polythene and many other products studied later in this unit, and propene is the second member of the series. Alkenes are also called monoenes when they contain one double bond. Their occurrence is small in nature compared with alkanes, so industry makes them deliberately by cracking long-chain petroleum fractions into shorter, more useful molecules.

Key Points

  • Alkenes contain C=C and are unsaturated.
  • General formula CnH2n; first member is ethene.
  • Main source: cracking of petroleum.
  • Olefins = oil-forming, from their oily halogen products.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Ethene contains a carbon—carbon double bond made of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The double-bonded carbons are sp2 hybridised: each has three sp2 hybrid orbitals and one pure p-orbital.

  • Each sp2 orbital overlaps with another atom's orbital to form sigma bonds (head-to-head overlap).
  • The remaining p-orbital on one sp2 carbon overlaps side-to-side with the p-orbital of the other to form the pi bond.
  • All six atoms of ethene lie in the same plane: ethene is trigonal planar.
  • HCH and HCC bond angles are approximately 120°.
  • C=C bond length is 134 pm; C—H bond length is 109 pm.

Because the pi bond is made by sideways overlap above and below the C—C line, rotation about C=C is restricted — the two carbons cannot twist without breaking the pi overlap. This is the structural reason behind the geometric (cis-trans) isomerism described in section 11.11, and behind ethene's flat shape: all six atoms must stay in one plane for the p-orbitals to overlap.

Key Points

  • C=C = one sigma + one pi bond.
  • Double-bond carbons are sp2, trigonal planar, about 120°.
  • Sigma forms head-on; pi forms side-on from p-orbitals.
  • Ethene is a flat (planar) molecule.

lessons.title: Preparation of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are typically produced by β-elimination reactions: two atoms or groups on adjacent carbon atoms are eliminated and a double bond forms.

Dehydration of Alcohols

Removal of H2O from adjacent carbons of an alcohol by heating with a dehydrating agent is dehydration. The best dehydrating reagents are (i) conc. H2SO4, (ii) Al2O3, (iii) P2O5 (printed P2O2 in the book); all work at high temperatures. Ethyl alcohol needs conc. H2SO4 at 170-180°C: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O (OH leaves the α-carbon, H leaves the β-carbon).

Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halides

Removal of HX from adjacent carbons of an alkyl halide by heating with alcoholic KOH is dehydrohalogenation. X is removed from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon: CH2(X)—CH2(H) skeleton + KOH → CH2=CH2 + HX (alcohol, heat), as drawn in the book.

In both methods the carbon skeleton keeps the same number of carbons; only H2O or HX is lost and a single bond becomes a double bond.

Key Points

  • Both methods are β-eliminations forming C=C.
  • Dehydration: conc. H2SO4, 170-180°C for ethanol.
  • Dehydrohalogenation: alcoholic KOH with heat.
  • Leaving atoms come from adjacent (α and β) carbons.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the pi bond. The pi bond is formed by parallel (side-to-side) overlapping of p-orbitals.

The pi electrons of the double bond lie much farther from the carbon nuclei and are therefore less firmly bound to them. This makes the pi bond a weak bond compared with the sigma bond, so it breaks much more easily under attack by an electrophilic reagent.

Contrast with Alkanes

FeatureAlkanesAlkenes
BondsOnly strong sigma bondsOne sigma + one weak pi bond at C=C
ReactivityUnreactive to polar reagentsReadily attacked by electrophiles
Typical reactionFree-radical substitution under UVElectrophilic addition

The pi electrons form an exposed electron cloud above and below the double bond. An electrophile is attracted to this electron-rich region, donates nothing and accepts the pi electron pair, so addition begins. Once the pi bond breaks, two new sigma bonds can form, giving a saturated product — the pattern followed by every reaction in section 11.22.

Key Points

  • The exposed pi electrons make alkenes reactive.
  • Pi bond is weaker than sigma bond.
  • Electrophiles attack the pi bond first.
  • Most alkene reactions break the pi bond, keeping sigma intact.

lessons.title: Hydrogenation and Hydrohalogenation of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The most important reactions of alkenes are addition reactions: two molecules combine into one product and the double bond becomes a single bond.

Catalytic Hydrogenation

H2 adds to an alkene with a catalyst (Pt, Ni or Pd) at moderate pressure 1-5 atm to give an alkane: CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3—CH3; CH3—CH=CH2 + H2 → CH3—CH2—CH3 (Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C). The heat evolved per mole is the heat of hydrogenation, about 120 kJ/mol for each double bond. Hydrogenation of vegetable oils gives margarine and vegetable ghee.

Hydrohalogenation (Electrophilic Addition)

Addition of HX to an alkene gives an alkyl halide, in acetic acid or by passing dry HX gas over the alkene: CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3—CH2—Br (ethyl bromide); propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane. Reactivity order: HI > HBr > HCl > HF.

Mechanism (HBr + ethene): Step 1 — pi electrons attack H of HBr, forming a carbocation + Br-. Step 2 — Br- (nucleophile) attacks the carbocation to give ethyl bromide.

Markovnikov's rule: when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the halide attaches to the carbon with fewer hydrogens and the proton to the carbon with more hydrogens, because the more stable carbocation forms. Propene gives mainly 2-bromopropane via the secondary carbocation, which is more stable than the primary one; 1-bromopropane is the minor product.

Key Points

  • Addition converts C=C into C—C.
  • Hydrogenation needs Ni/Pt/Pd and gives alkanes.
  • Markovnikov: X goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
  • Carbocation stability decides the major product.

lessons.title: Hydration, Halogenation and Halohydration of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Inductive Effect and Carbocation Stability

The inductive effect is the electron-donating tendency of alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl) that stabilises carbocations: electron density shifts towards the electron-deficient carbon and reduces its charge. Stability order: tertiary (3 alkyl groups) > secondary (2) > primary (1). This explains Markovnikov addition.

Hydration

Addition of water is hydration. Alkenes react with H2O in the presence of H2SO4 at 100°C to form alcohols, via ethyl hydrogensulphate from ethene, which then hydrolyses to ethyl alcohol (ethanol).

Halogenation

Addition of Cl2 or Br2 is halogenation. Alkenes react in an inert solvent such as CCl4 in the dark to form vicinal dihalides, e.g. propene + Cl2 → 1,2-dichloropropane. Mechanism: Step 1 — pi electrons attack X—X, forming a halonium ion + X-. Step 2 — X- attacks to give the vicinal dihalide. Bromine water test: reddish-brown bromine water turns colourless with an alkene, detecting a C=C bond.

Halohydration

Addition of hypohalous acid is halohydration. Aqueous Cl2 or Br2 gives halohydrins with adjacent halo and hydroxyl groups: alkene + X2 + H2O → halohydrin + HX; propene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloropropan-2-ol + HCl.

Key Points

  • Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary.
  • Hydration (H2SO4, 100°C) gives alcohols.
  • Halogenation gives vicinal dihalides; bromine water is decolourised.
  • Halohydration gives a halohydrin (X and OH on adjacent carbons).

lessons.title: Epoxidation, Ozonolysis and Polymerization of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Epoxidation

Addition of oxygen to an alkene is epoxidation. With O2 over a silver catalyst at high pressure and temperature it gives epoxides: 2CH2=CH2 + O2 → 2 ethylene oxide (Ag, 300°C); propene similarly gives propylene oxide.

Ozonolysis

Ozonolysis is the reaction of ozone (O3) with alkenes to break the C=C bond. In an inert solvent such as ether, ozone forms an unstable molozonide, which rearranges to an ozonide. Ozonides are explosive and are not isolated; decomposition with zinc and water gives aldehydes and/or ketones: ethylene ozonide + Zn → 2HCHO + ZnO (H2O, 100°C). If a double-bonded carbon is fully substituted, a ketone forms instead. Ozonolysis locates the position of a double bond, since molecules cleave at the double bond.

Polymerization

Small molecules (monomers) combine into large molecules (polymers) in polymerisation. Ethene polymerises with a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to polythene (polyethylene): nCH2=CH2 → —[CH2—CH2]n— (400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2/peroxide).

Key Points

  • Epoxidation adds one O atom across C=C (Ag catalyst).
  • Ozonolysis cleaves C=C to aldehydes/ketones.
  • Ozonolysis finds the double-bond position.
  • Polymerisation: ethene → polythene.

lessons.title: Conjugation in Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Conjugation (Latin: to link together) describes pi systems, such as double bonds, linked together.

Conjugated Dienes

Dienes in which the double bonds are separated by a single bond are conjugated dienes, e.g. pent-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH—CH3. The simplest conjugated diene is but-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH2.

Conjugation

Conjugation occurs whenever p-orbitals overlap on three or more adjacent atoms. In 1,3-butadiene all four carbons are sp2 hybridised, each with a pure p-orbital; the four p-orbitals on adjacent atoms form the conjugated system. With three or more pure p-orbitals on adjacent atoms, electrons delocalise throughout the molecule: pi electron density is spread over all four atoms, lowering the molecule's energy and enhancing its stability. Penta-1,4-diene is not conjugated because its double bonds are not separated by just one single bond, so its p-orbitals cannot overlap continuously.

Key Points

  • Conjugated diene: C=C—C=C pattern.
  • Needs overlapping p-orbitals on adjacent atoms.
  • Delocalisation lowers energy and increases stability.
  • Simplest example: but-1,3-diene.

lessons.title: Energy and Petrochemicals
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is the foundation of civilisation: it powers homes, fuels industries, drives transport and supports economic growth. Fossil fuels — crude oil, natural gas and coal — are major energy sources and the backbone of the petrochemical industry.

Petrochemicals are vital for modern life: they produce plastics, fibres, fertilisers, medicines, fuels and construction materials. Without them, modern technology, healthcare and infrastructure would not exist. Energy sustains the world, while petrochemicals shape the materials and products of modern life. Nearly 8% of the world's crude oil is not used as fuel but is diverted to produce plastics, fibres, medicines and detergents.

Fossil fuels such as crude oil, natural gas and coal are therefore studied twice in this unit: once as fuels that release energy on burning, and once as raw materials. The petrochemical route is covered in the sections that follow — what petrochemicals are, how they differ from the chemicals derived from them, the raw materials used, fractional distillation of petroleum, the major petrochemicals and their importance, and finally the formation, properties and uses of fossil fuels themselves.

Key Points

  • Fossil fuels supply both energy and petrochemical feedstocks.
  • Petrochemicals underpin plastics, medicines, fertilisers and fibres.
  • About 8% of crude oil goes to non-fuel products.
  • Energy and petrochemicals together sustain modern life.

lessons.title: Difference between Petrochemical and Derived Chemicals
lessons.notes_html:
Petrochemicals are chemicals derived from petroleum or natural gas through cracking and refining, e.g. ethylene, propylene, benzene, toluene and xylene. They are not used directly by consumers but are essential across industries. Chemicals derived from petrochemicals are secondary products made by processing primary petrochemicals: plastics, synthetic rubber, solvents, detergents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals for pharmaceuticals and textiles.

Key Formulae

FeaturePetrochemicalsChemicals derived from them
SourcePrimary products directly from petroleum or natural gasSecondary products made using petrochemicals as raw materials
NatureBasic building blocks, often simple organic compoundsComplex and varied, for specific purposes
ApplicationsLimited direct consumer applicationsWide range: plastics, pharmaceuticals, textiles, etc.
ProcessingInitial processes like cracking and refiningFurther refined and combined for specific uses
ExamplesEthylene, propylene, benzene, toluene, xylenePlastics, synthetic rubber, solvents, detergents, pharmaceuticals

Key Points

  • Petrochemicals are primary building blocks.
  • Derived chemicals are the finished, consumer-facing products.
  • Ethylene and propylene are petrochemicals; plastics are derived.

lessons.title: Raw Materials for the Petrochemical Industry
lessons.notes_html:
Main Raw Materials

  • Crude oil: a complex mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons; the primary source, refined into naphtha, gasoline, diesel and fuel oil.
  • Natural gas: mainly methane, with ethane, propane and butane; feedstock especially for ethylene and propylene.
  • Coal: converted into syngas (hydrogen + carbon monoxide), then used to make methanol and ammonia.
  • Naphtha: a volatile hydrocarbon fraction from distillation of crude oil, used to produce ethylene and propylene.
  • Refinery off-gases: methane, ethane, propane and butane from refining, used as plant feedstocks.
  • Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG): propane + butane from natural gas processing or refining; fuel for cooking, heating and power, and feedstock for propylene and butadiene.
  • Aromatics: benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX) from catalytic reforming of naphtha or extraction; used for styrene, phenol and other aromatics.
  • Hydrogen: from natural gas by steam reforming; essential for hydrogenation and hydrocracking.

Key Points

  • Crude oil and natural gas are the main feedstocks.
  • Naphtha and refinery gases feed olefin production.
  • BTX aromatics come from reforming naphtha.
  • Coal works through syngas to methanol and ammonia.

lessons.title: Fractional Distillation of Petroleum
lessons.notes_html:
Fractional distillation separates petroleum by boiling points. Crude oil is heated to about 400°C to vaporise it; vapours rise through a tall column with trays or packing and cool, so hydrocarbons condense at different heights. Each fraction has similar boiling points: lighter fractions condense higher up, middle fractions in the middle, heavier fractions lower down.

Key Formulae

FractionCarbons / boiling rangeUse
Refinery gasC1-C4, below 20°CFuel for heating, cooking, power
Petroleum etherC5-C6, 30-60°CNonpolar solvent
Ligroin / light naphthaC6-C7, 60-100°CNonpolar solvent
PetrolC5-C10, 40-200°CMotor fuel
Kerosene oilC12-C18, 150-275°CJet fuel, lamps, domestic heating
Diesel oilC12-C20, 250-400°C (text)Diesel engines, buses, trucks, machinery
Lubricating oilC20-C30 and higherReduces friction in machines
Paraffin waxC23-C35 and higher, m.p. 50-60°CPolishes, candles, cosmetics
Asphalt (pitch/bitumen)Non-volatile solids, above C40Roads and roofs

The figure also shows fuel oil between diesel and lubricating oil. Lubricating oil is obtained by vacuum distillation of the residue.

Key Points

  • Separation is by boiling point in a fractionating column.
  • Light fractions rise highest; heavy residue stays lowest.
  • Petrol, kerosene and diesel are the main fuel fractions.
  • Asphalt is the final non-volatile residue.

lessons.title: Role and Significance of Petrochemicals in the Modern World
lessons.notes_html:
Petrochemicals are chemical products derived primarily from petroleum and natural gas; they are the building blocks for countless everyday products.

Major Petrochemicals

  • Ethylene: polyethylene (plastics, packaging), ethylene glycol (antifreeze, polyester).
  • Propylene: polypropylene, acrylonitrile (synthetic fibres), propylene oxide (polyurethanes).
  • Benzene: styrene (polystyrene), phenol (resins), aniline (dyes, rubber processing).
  • Toluene: solvent; makes benzene, explosives and other chemicals.
  • Xylenes: terephthalic acid for PET plastics and fibres.
  • Butadiene: synthetic rubber for tyres; styrene for plastics and synthetic rubber. Methanol and ammonia are also listed as major petrochemicals.

Importance

  • Plastics and packaging: polyethylene and polypropylene for packaging and containers.
  • Agriculture: ammonia and urea fertilisers raise crop yields and food security.
  • Healthcare: pharmaceuticals, syringes, antiseptics, PVC IV bags.
  • Textiles: polyester, nylon and acrylic fibres.
  • Transport: fuels, lubricants, tyre rubber, lightweight plastic parts.
  • Construction: PVC pipes, insulation foams, paints, adhesives, sealants.

Key Points

  • Ethylene and propylene are the top building blocks.
  • Petrochemicals serve packaging, farming, health, textiles, transport and construction.
  • Butadiene is the key petrochemical for synthetic rubber.

lessons.title: Fossil Fuels: Formation, Properties, Uses, and Importance in the Modern World
lessons.notes_html:
Formation of Fossil Fuels

Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — formed from ancient plants and organisms buried and subjected to heat and pressure over millions of years; some coal is 300-400 million years old. Coal originates from plants in swampy environments; oil and natural gas come from marine organisms in ancient seas.

Properties

  • Coal: solid; properties vary with carbon content and compression; contains C, H, S, O and other elements.
  • Oil (petroleum): liquid mixture of hydrocarbons of various molecular weights, from underground reservoirs; light to heavy crude.
  • Natural gas: gaseous, mainly methane; found with oil, or from coal seams and shale. Cleaner than coal but still releases CO2 when burned.

Uses

  • Coal: electricity, industrial heating, steel, chemical feedstock.
  • Oil: transport fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel), heating, electricity, and raw material for petrochemicals, plastics, lubricants, pharmaceuticals.
  • Natural gas: heating, electricity, industrial processes, feedstock for chemicals and fertilisers.

Importance

Fossil fuels provide energy for electricity, transport, heating and industry worldwide; they drove industrialisation and economic growth, supply feedstocks for plastics, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and synthetic materials, create large employment, are major international trade commodities, and ensure national and global energy security.

Key Points

  • Formed over millions of years under heat and pressure.
  • Coal from land plants; oil and gas from marine organisms.
  • They are both fuels and petrochemical feedstocks.
  • Natural gas is cleaner than coal but still emits CO2.

Halogen derivatives of alkanes are called haloalkanes (halogenoalkanes or alkyl halides). They consist of a halogen atom covalently bonded to a saturated carbon atom within an alkyl group, with the general formula CnH2n+1X, where X is F, Cl, Br or I. They are classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°) or tertiary (3°) alkyl halides, depending on whether the halogen atom is directly bonded to a primary, secondary or tertiary carbon atom. Fluorocarbons, a type of haloalkane, are used as refrigerants and propellants, though many have been phased out because of their role in ozone depletion.

Structure of a Haloalkane

Take methyl chloride as the example. The carbon atom to which the halogen is bonded is sp3 hybridised. The halogen atom has one half-filled p orbital. The carbon-halogen σ-bond is formed by head-to-head overlap of one sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon and one half-filled p orbital of the halogen atom. Each carbon-hydrogen σ-bond is formed by head-to-head overlap of one sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon and one half-filled s orbital of hydrogen. The H-C-H and H-C-Cl bond angles are nearly 109.5°, so the arrangement of atoms or groups around the carbon atom is tetrahedral.

Key Points

  • Haloalkanes have the general formula CnH2n+1X (X = F, Cl, Br, I).
  • They are primary, secondary or tertiary according to the carbon holding the halogen.
  • The carbon bonded to the halogen is sp3 hybridised; the molecule is tetrahedral.
  • The C-X σ-bond forms by sp3-p overlap; C-H bonds form by sp3-s overlap.
  • Bond angles around the carbon are about 109.5°.
lessons.title: Structure of Haloalkanes

lessons.notes_html:
The molecular structure of a haloalkane strongly affects its reactivity. The main factors are steric hindrance, carbon-halogen bond polarity, carbon-halogen bond strength, leaving group ability and the nature of the nucleophile.

Steric Hindrance

Steric hindrance is caused by bulky alkyl groups surrounding the halogen in tertiary halogenoalkanes, making it difficult for nucleophiles to approach the carbon atom. Tertiary haloalkanes therefore react more slowly in nucleophilic substitution than primary and secondary haloalkanes.

Bond Polarity of Carbon-Halogen Bond

The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C-X bond is polarised: carbon carries a partial positive charge and is open to attack by a nucleophile. The greater the electronegativity difference between carbon and halogen, the greater the polarity of the C-X bond.

HalomethaneElectronegativity of HalogenEN Difference between C and XDipole Moment (Debye)
CH3F3.983.98 - 2.55 = 1.431.85
CH3Cl3.163.16 - 2.55 = 0.611.87
CH3Br2.962.96 - 2.55 = 0.411.81
CH3I2.662.66 - 2.55 = 0.111.62

Carbon-Halogen Bond Strength

Weaker C-X bonds are broken more easily and are more susceptible to nucleophilic attack. Bond energy measures bond strength: the greater the bond energy, the stronger the bond and the less reactive the C-X bond.

BondBond Energy (kJ/mol)
C-F485
C-Cl327
C-Br285
C-I213

The order of reactivity of alkyl halides is: RI greater than RBr greater than RCl greater than RF.

Key Points

  • Bulky groups in tertiary haloalkanes hinder nucleophilic attack and slow substitution.
  • The C-X bond is polar because halogens are more electronegative than carbon.
  • Bond strength falls C-F greater than C-Cl greater than C-Br greater than C-I.
  • Reactivity rises as the C-X bond weakens: RI greater than RBr greater than RCl greater than RF.
  • Reactivity is decided by steric hindrance, bond polarity, bond strength, leaving group ability and the nucleophile.
lessons.title: Influence of Molecular Structure on Reactivity

lessons.notes_html:
Haloalkanes can be synthesised by three main routes: free-radical substitution of alkanes, electrophilic addition to alkenes, and substitution of the -OH group of alcohols.

Free-Radical Substitution of Alkanes

A hydrogen atom in an alkane is substituted by a halogen atom (chlorine or bromine) under ultraviolet (UV) light. Ethane gives chloroethane or bromoethane:

CH3CH3 + Cl2 →(UV light) CH3CH2Cl + HCl
CH3CH3 + Br2 →(UV light) CH3CH2Br + HBr

Electrophilic Addition of Alkene with Halogen or Hydrogen Halide

A halogen (X2) or hydrogen halide (HX) adds across the double bond of an alkene at room temperature to form a halogenoalkane:

CH2=CH2 + Cl2 →(room temperature) CH2Cl-CH2Cl (1,2-dichloroethane)
CH2=CH2 + HCl →(room temperature) CH3-CH2Cl (chloroethane)

With Br2 the product is 1,2-dibromoethane, and with HBr it is bromoethane.

From Alcohols

The hydroxyl group (-OH) of an alcohol is substituted by a halogen atom. The reagent and conditions decide the product; the major product is typically an alkyl halide:

ReactionConditionsProducts
ROH + HXH2SO4 or H3PO4RX + H2O
ROH + KBrH2SO4 or H3PO4RBr + KOH
3ROH + PCl3-3RCl + H3PO3
ROH + PCl5HeatRCl + POCl3 + HCl
ROH + SOCl2PyridineRCl + SO2 + HCl

Key Points

  • Alkanes + Cl2 or Br2 in UV light give haloalkanes by free-radical substitution.
  • Alkenes + X2 or HX at room temperature give haloalkanes by electrophilic addition.
  • Alcohols give haloalkanes with HX, KBr/H2SO4 or H3PO4, PCl3, PCl5 with heat, or SOCl2.
  • In each alcohol reaction the -OH group is replaced by the halogen.
lessons.title: Haloalkane Synthesis

lessons.notes_html:
In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile replaces the halogen atom of a haloalkane. These reactions are widely used in organic synthesis.

Reaction with Aqueous NaOH

Halogenoalkanes react with aqueous NaOH on heating to produce alcohols; the halogen atom is replaced by an -OH group:

R-X + NaOH →(H2O, heat) R-OH + NaX

Reaction with KCN

With potassium cyanide in aqueous ethanol, heated, the halogen is replaced by the -CN group, producing alkyl cyanides or nitriles. This lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon:

R-X + KCN →(aq. ethanol, heat) R-CN + KX

Reaction with NH3

With an alcoholic solution of ammonia, heated in a sealed tube, haloalkanes yield a mixture of amines: the first product is a primary alkylamine, which reacts further to give dialkylamine and then trialkylamine:

R'-X + NH3 →(ethanol, heat) R'-NH2 + HX
R''-X + R'-NH2 →(ethanol, heat) R'-NH-R'' + HX

Reaction with AgNO3

In ethanol, the halide ion displaced from a haloalkane reacts with silver nitrate to form a silver halide precipitate; this is the test used to identify the halogen present. Example: CH3CH2-Br + AgNO3 →(ethanol) CH3CH2-ONO2 + AgBr. Precipitate colours: AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI bright yellow; fluoroalkanes give no visible precipitate (AgF is colourless/soluble). The rate of reaction increases down the group: iodoalkanes react fastest, then bromoalkanes, then chloroalkanes.

Key Points

  • Aqueous NaOH (heat) converts haloalkanes to alcohols.
  • KCN in aqueous ethanol (heat) gives nitriles and adds one carbon to the chain.
  • NH3 in ethanol (heat, sealed tube) gives a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
  • AgNO3 in ethanol identifies the halogen: white (Cl), cream (Br), bright yellow (I) precipitates.
  • Rate with AgNO3: RI fastest, then RBr, then RCl; RF gives no precipitate.
lessons.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions of Haloalkanes

lessons.notes_html:
When bromoethane is mixed with sodium hydroxide in ethanol and heated, a hydrogen atom and a bromine atom are removed from adjacent carbon atoms. This process, called elimination, forms a double bond between the two carbon atoms:

CH3CH2-Br + NaOH →(ethanol, heat) CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O

The carbon bonded to the leaving group (such as bromine) is called the alpha (α) carbon, and the carbon adjacent to it is the beta (β) carbon. In elimination, a hydrogen atom is removed from the beta carbon and the leaving group departs from the alpha carbon.

Note the contrast of conditions: aqueous NaOH with heat gives substitution (an alcohol), while NaOH in ethanol with heat gives elimination (an alkene). Elimination reactions of haloalkanes are important in industry because they produce alkenes, which serve as precursors for polymers like polyethylene.

Key Points

  • Elimination removes H from the β-carbon and X from the α-carbon, forming a C=C double bond.
  • Bromoethane + NaOH in ethanol, heated, gives ethene + NaBr + H2O.
  • Solvent decides the reaction: aqueous NaOH → substitution; ethanolic NaOH → elimination.
  • Elimination is an industrial route to alkenes for polymer manufacture.
lessons.title: Elimination Reaction of Halogenoalkane

lessons.notes_html:
Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. They are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary depending on the number of alkyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom. The nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons, which controls the basicity and reactivity of amines.

ClassAlkyl Groups on NGeneral FormExample Form
Primary amineOneR-NH2CH3NH2 (methylamine)
Secondary amineTwoR-NH-R(CH3)2NH (dimethylamine)
Tertiary amineThreeR-N(R)-R(CH3)3N (trimethylamine)

Amines occur widely in nature: caffeine and nicotine are alkaloids, naturally occurring amines found in tea, coffee and tobacco, and neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin and adrenaline are also amines.

Key Points

  • Amines are ammonia derivatives: one, two or three H atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
  • Primary = one alkyl group on N; secondary = two; tertiary = three.
  • The lone pair on nitrogen makes amines basic and nucleophilic.
  • Many natural products, such as caffeine, nicotine and adrenaline, are amines.
lessons.title: Amines

lessons.notes_html:
Amines are basic because of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton. Alkanamines are generally more basic than ammonia because the electron-releasing alkyl groups increase the electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more readily available for sharing with acids. In aqueous solution (about 25°C), the basicity order of aliphatic amines is 2° greater than 1° greater than 3° greater than NH3. For the methylamines: (CH3)2NH (pKb = 3.27) greater than CH3NH2 (pKb = 3.34) greater than (CH3)3N (pKb = 4.20) greater than NH3 (pKb = 4.74). The larger the pKb value, the smaller the tendency to accept a proton from water, so the weaker the base.

Basic strength in aqueous solution depends not only on the electron-releasing effect of alkyl groups but also on steric and hydration effects:

  • Hydration effect: in aqueous solution the substituted ammonium ion is stabilised by solvation (hydrogen bonding) with water molecules; as the number of alkyl groups on nitrogen increases, the capacity for hydrogen bonding of the ion decreases.
  • Steric effect: as the number of alkyl groups increases, steric hindrance increases, making it harder for the amine to accept a proton.

Reactions of Amines as Bases

With water: alkyl amines (RNH2) act as weak bases; they accept a proton from water to form alkylammonium ions and hydroxide ions. The reaction is reversible, so only a small fraction of molecules is protonated: CH3NH2(aq) + H2O(l) → CH3NH3+(aq) + OH-(aq). The methylamines are highly soluble in water and act as weak bases.

With acids: amines neutralise acids to produce water-soluble ammonium salts, e.g. RNH2(aq) + HCl(aq) → RNH3+Cl-(aq); CH3NH2 + HCl → CH3NH3+Cl- (methylammonium chloride). The reaction is reversible: treatment of the salt with a strong base such as NaOH reproduces the free amine: RNH3+Cl-(aq) + NaOH(aq) → RNH2(aq) + NaCl(aq) + H2O(l).

Key Points

  • Basicity comes from the lone pair on nitrogen accepting a proton.
  • Alkyl groups release electrons (+I effect), so alkanamines are stronger bases than ammonia.
  • In water the order is 2° greater than 1° greater than 3° greater than NH3, due to hydration and steric effects.
  • Smaller pKb means a stronger base: (CH3)2NH is the strongest of the methylamines.
  • Amines form soluble ammonium salts with acids; NaOH regenerates the free amine from the salt.
lessons.title: Basicity of Amines

lessons.notes_html:
Amines can act as both bases and nucleophiles. The main reactions of amines arise from the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom: these electrons attack the electron-deficient centres (positive or slightly positive parts) of other molecules.

Comparing Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Amines

  • Primary amines are the most reactive. The extra hydrogen atom on the nitrogen enables them to undergo reactions like oxidation and substitution.
  • Secondary amines are less reactive than primary amines but are still capable of nucleophilic substitution reactions.
  • Tertiary amines are less nucleophilic than primary and secondary amines because the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is less available to participate in reactions.

So the reactivity and nucleophilicity order is: primary amine greater than secondary amine greater than tertiary amine. Amines are also useful intermediates, for example in the production of antihistamine medications that help alleviate allergies.

Key Points

  • Amine reactions are driven by the nitrogen lone pair attacking electron-deficient centres.
  • Primary amines are the most reactive; they can undergo oxidation and substitution.
  • Secondary amines still act as nucleophiles in substitution reactions.
  • Tertiary amines are the least nucleophilic because their lone pair is least available.
  • Reactivity order: 1° greater than 2° greater than 3°.
lessons.title: Reactivity of Amines

lessons.notes_html:
Alkylation of Ammonia by Alkyl Halides

Alkyl halides react with aqueous or alcoholic solutions of ammonia in a sealed tube, when heated, to produce primary, secondary and tertiary amines. The cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond by the ammonia molecule is known as ammonolysis. With methyl iodide the sequence is:

NH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI
CH3NH2 + CH3I → (CH3)2NH + HI
(CH3)2NH + CH3I → (CH3)3N + HI
(CH3)3N + CH3I → [(CH3)4N]+I- (tetramethylammonium iodide)

The primary amine is the major product when ammonia is present in excess; conversely, the tertiary amine is the major product when the alkyl halide is in excess. The resulting ammonium salt, on treatment with a base, regenerates the amine.

Reduction of Nitro Compounds

Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4, or Zn/HCl, or H2/Ni, or H2/Pt:

CH3NO2 + 6[H] →(LiAlH4) CH3NH2 + 2H2O
CH3NO2 + 3H2 →(Pt) CH3NH2 + 2H2O

Key Points

  • Ammonolysis: alkyl halides + ammonia (sealed tube, heat) give amines step by step.
  • Excess NH3 favours the primary amine; excess alkyl halide favours the tertiary amine and quaternary salt.
  • Ammonium salts give back the free amine on treatment with a base.
  • Reduction of nitro compounds (LiAlH4, Zn/HCl, H2/Ni or H2/Pt) gives primary amines only.
lessons.title: Preparation of Amines

lessons.notes_html:
Phenylamine, C6H5NH2, is a primary aromatic amine in which an amino group (-NH2) is directly attached to a benzene ring. Its old and still commonly used name is aniline, which is also present in the names of many of its derivatives.

Reactivity of Phenylamine (Aniline)

Phenylamine shows distinctive reactivity due to its aromatic amine structure. The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is partially delocalised into the benzene ring, increasing the electron density mainly at the 2, 4 and 6 positions. This activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution, making phenylamine more reactive than benzene.

However, the delocalisation of the lone pair reduces the availability of nitrogen to accept protons. Consequently, phenylamine is a weaker base than aliphatic amines; resonance stabilisation makes aniline less basic than ammonia and alkylamines as well.

Key Points

  • Phenylamine (aniline) is C6H5NH2, a primary aromatic amine.
  • Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
  • Electron density rises at the 2, 4 and 6 positions, so the ring is activated for electrophilic substitution.
  • Because the lone pair is delocalised, aniline is a much weaker base than aliphatic amines.
lessons.title: Phenylamine (Aniline)

lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

  • Phenylamine is a colourless to pale yellow liquid with a strong, unpleasant odour.
  • It is slightly soluble in water but much more soluble in organic solvents like ethanol, ether and benzene.
  • Its melting point is approximately -6°C and its boiling point is around 184°C.
  • Its density is approximately 1.02 g/cm3 at room temperature.

Chemical Properties

Salt formation: aniline reacts with acids, such as hydrochloric acid, to form anilinium salts, showing its basic character: C6H5NH2 + HCl → C6H5NH3+Cl- (anilinium chloride).

Electrophilic aromatic substitution: the -NH2 group is electron-donating and activates the ring; substitution occurs mainly at the ortho and para positions. With bromine water at room temperature, aniline immediately forms 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine: C6H5NH2 + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3NH2 + 3HBr. Direct nitration with concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids is unfavourable because the amino group gets protonated; the amino group is therefore first protected by acylation, and then controlled nitration is performed.

Acylation (protection): the amino group attacks acid chlorides or anhydrides to form stable amides instead of the ring undergoing substitution: phenylamine + ethanoyl chloride → N-phenylethanamide + HCl; phenylamine + ethanoic anhydride → N-phenylethanamide + ethanoic acid. This acylation protects the amino group, preventing unwanted reactions on the ring.

Applications of Phenylamine (Aniline)

  • Essential precursor for synthesising azo dyes, used to colour textiles, leather and paper (the famous purple dye mauveine was accidentally discovered from aniline in the 1850s).
  • Used in manufacturing drugs such as paracetamol (acetaminophen), sulpha drugs and other medicinal compounds.
  • Used to synthesise agrochemicals, including herbicides, fungicides and plant growth regulators.

Key Points

  • Aniline: pale yellow oily liquid, mp -6°C, bp 184°C, slightly soluble in water.
  • It forms anilinium salts with acids, e.g. anilinium chloride with HCl.
  • Bromine water instantly gives 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (ortho/para substitution).
  • For nitration, the -NH2 group is first protected by acylation to N-phenylethanamide.
  • Main uses: azo dyes, drugs such as paracetamol, and agrochemicals.
lessons.title: Properties of Phenylamine

lessons.notes_html:
Azo compounds are a class of organic compounds containing the azo group (-N=N-), which connects two aryl or alkyl groups. The general structural formula is R-N=N-R', where R and R' can be aryl (aromatic) or alkyl groups. The azo group is responsible for the vivid colours (red, orange, yellow, blue) of azo compounds. When the groups attached to the azo group are aromatic rings, the colour intensifies because of the extended conjugation of double bonds, which lets the molecule absorb more visible light; hence azo compounds are used as dyes. Examples: azobenzene (yellow to orange-red) and the yellow azo dye; Methyl Orange and Methyl Red are azo compounds used in laboratories as acid-base indicators for titration experiments.

Reactivity of Azo Compounds

  • Electrophilic substitution on the aromatic rings is generally limited because the azo group is mildly electron-withdrawing. If electron-donating groups such as -OH or -NH2 are present on the ring, substitution can occur at the ortho and para positions relative to those groups, e.g. nitration of 4-hydroxyazobenzene gives 2-nitro-4-hydroxyazobenzene.
  • Reduction: azo compounds can be converted into aromatic amines. Using tin and hydrochloric acid, the -N=N- bond breaks, resulting in two -NH2 groups: azobenzene + 4[H] →(Sn/HCl) 2 phenylamine.
  • Azo compounds are largely stable under neutral and basic conditions.

Uses of Azo Compounds as Dyes and Pigments

  • Azo dyes are widely used in the textile, leather and paper industries for their vibrant and diverse colours.
  • They are also used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and food colorants, e.g. Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow (note: Tartrazine, E102, may cause allergies in some individuals).
  • Azo pigments are water-insoluble and are used in paints, plastics, rubber and printing inks because of their excellent light and thermal stability.

Key Points

  • Azo compounds contain the -N=N- group joining two aryl or alkyl groups: R-N=N-R'.
  • The azo group plus extended conjugation gives strong colours, so they are used as dyes.
  • Methyl Orange and Methyl Red are azo indicators used in titrations.
  • Reduction with Sn/HCl cleaves -N=N- to give aromatic amines.
  • Azo dyes colour textiles, leather, paper and foods; azo pigments go into paints, plastics, rubber and inks.
lessons.title: Azo Compounds

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are compounds in which a hydroxyl group (—OH) is bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Ethanol is used as a solvent, a fuel additive and in medicines; methanol and glycerol are used in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and polymer production. By number of hydroxyl groups, alcohols are monohydric or polyhydric.

Monohydric Alcohols

Monohydric alcohols contain a single hydroxyl group, e.g. ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol. They are classified by the carbon carrying the —OH group:

  • Primary (1°) alcohol: —OH on a primary carbon, bonded to only one other carbon and at least two H atoms, e.g. ethanol, CH3CH2OH.
  • Secondary (2°) alcohol: —OH on a secondary carbon, bonded to two other carbons and one H atom, e.g. propan-2-ol.
  • Tertiary (3°) alcohol: —OH on a tertiary carbon, bonded to three other carbons and no H atoms, e.g. methylpropan-2-ol.

Reactivity depends on this class: tertiary alcohols dehydrate easily at low temperatures, while primary alcohols need severe conditions.

Alcohols with Multiple Hydroxy Groups (Polyhydric Alcohols)

Polyhydric alcohols contain two or more hydroxyl groups. Two —OH groups = a diol, e.g. glycol (ethane-1,2-diol); three —OH groups = a triol, e.g. glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol); more than three = a polyol. Glycerol is used in toothpaste, moisturisers and cough syrups because it retains water.

Key Points

  • Alcohol = —OH group bonded to a saturated carbon atom.
  • Monohydric alcohols have one —OH; polyhydric alcohols have two or more.
  • Primary, secondary and tertiary depend on the carbon attached to —OH.
  • Ethanol (1°), propan-2-ol (2°) and methylpropan-2-ol (3°) are the standard examples.
  • Diols have two —OH groups; triols have three; polyols have more.
lessons.title: Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are prepared by addition to alkenes, substitution of halogenoalkanes, reduction of carbonyl compounds, acids and esters, and hydrolysis of esters.

Key Reactions

MethodReagents / ConditionsReaction
Electrophilic addition of steam to an alkeneH3PO4 catalyst, steamR—CH=CH2 + HOH → R—CH(OH)—CH3
Alkene to a diolCold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4/H2SO45CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 2H2O → 5HOCH2—CH2OH (ethane-1,2-diol) + 2MnSO4 + K2SO4
Substitution of a halogenoalkaneAqueous NaOH or KOH, heatCH3CH2Br + KOH → CH3CH2OH + KBr
Reduction of an aldehyde or ketoneNaBH4 or LiAlH4; NaBH4 needs a polar solvent (water, ethanol)CH3CHO → CH3CH2OH (1° alcohol); CH3COCH3 → propan-2-ol (2° alcohol)
Reduction of carboxylic acids and estersLiAlH4 in ether (strong reducing agent)CH3COOH + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + H2O; CH3COOCH3 + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + CH3OH
Hydrolysis of an esterDilute acid or dilute alkali, heatCH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2OH + CH3COOH; with NaOH: → CH3CH2OH + CH3COONa

LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent: it reduces carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols, unlike NaBH4, which reduces only aldehydes and ketones under mild conditions in polar protic solvents.

Key Points

  • Steam adds to alkenes with an H3PO4 catalyst to give alcohols.
  • Cold dilute acidified KMnO4 converts an alkene into a diol.
  • Aqueous NaOH/KOH and heat replace the halogen of a halogenoalkane by —OH.
  • NaBH4 or LiAlH4: aldehydes → primary alcohols; ketones → secondary alcohols.
  • Only LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols.
  • Ester hydrolysis (dilute acid or alkali, heat) gives an alcohol plus an acid or its salt.
lessons.title: Preparations of Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols undergo complete combustion in excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water and releasing heat, which makes them potential fuels: ROH + O2 → CO2 + H2O + Heat.

Examples

  • Methanol burns with a clean, nearly smokeless flame: 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O + Heat. It is used as a fuel in high-performance racing engines; its flame is nearly invisible in daylight.
  • Ethanol also burns cleanly: CH3CH2OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O + Heat. It is ideal for spirit burners and as a renewable biofuel blended with petrol.

Combustion of hydroxy compounds is a clean energy source, releasing only carbon dioxide and water while reducing harmful emissions.

Key Points

  • Complete combustion needs excess oxygen and gives CO2 + H2O + heat.
  • Methanol: 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O; clean, nearly smokeless flame.
  • Ethanol: CH3CH2OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O; used in spirit burners and as a biofuel.
  • Alcohol combustion is a clean energy source with reduced harmful emissions.
lessons.title: Combustion of Organic Hydroxy Compounds (Alcohols)

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols undergo many conversions. In substitution with phosphorus halides or thionyl chloride, the hydroxyl group is replaced by a chlorine atom, giving alkyl chlorides.

Reaction with SOCl2, PCl3, and PCl5

ReagentConditionsReaction
SOCl2 (thionyl chloride)Pyridine catalystR—OH + SOCl2 → R—Cl + SO2 + HCl; CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl
PCl3—3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3
PCl5Reacts readilyCH3CH2OH + PCl5 → CH3CH2Cl + POCl3 + HCl

Reaction of Hydroxy Organic Compound with Sodium

Ethanol reacts with sodium metal to produce sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas: 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2. In general: R—OH + Na → R—ONa + 1/2 H2.

Key Points

  • SOCl2 (pyridine), PCl3 and PCl5 all convert alcohols into alkyl chlorides.
  • SOCl2 also gives SO2 + HCl; PCl5 also gives POCl3 + HCl; PCl3 gives H3PO3.
  • Sodium reacts with alcohols to give an alkoxide (e.g. sodium ethoxide) + H2.
  • The reaction with Na shows the acidic character of the —OH group.
lessons.title: Reactions of Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Oxidation uses acidified potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4) or acidified KMnO4. The product depends on the type of alcohol and the conditions, so oxidation differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

Oxidation of Methyl Alcohol and Primary Alcohols

Methanol is oxidised first to formaldehyde, then to formic acid: CH3OH + [O] → HCHO + H2O; HCHO + [O] → HCOOH. The reaction can be stopped at the aldehyde stage by removing the aldehyde from the oxidising medium (distillation). Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes, then to carboxylic acids: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O; CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH.

Oxidation of Secondary Alcohols

Secondary alcohols give ketones, which are not oxidised further easily because that needs breaking a C—C bond; only drastic conditions give acids: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O; CH3COCH3 + 4[O] → CH3COOH + CO2 + H2O.

Oxidation of Tertiary Alcohols

Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised under acidic conditions: the carbon bearing —OH is attached to three carbons and cannot form a C=O double bond, so methylpropan-2-ol shows no oxidation reaction. Under reflux, primary alcohols oxidise fully to carboxylic acids and secondary alcohols also give carboxylic acids, but tertiary alcohols still do not oxidise.

Key Points

  • Oxidising agent: acidified K2Cr2O7 or acidified KMnO4.
  • 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; distil off the aldehyde to stop at stage one.
  • Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid.
  • 2° alcohol → ketone; further oxidation only under drastic conditions.
  • 3° alcohol: no oxidation, even under reflux.
  • Reflux gives more extensive oxidation than distillation.
lessons.title: Oxidation of Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Dehydration of alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4) gives alkenes. The —OH group is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon. The ease of dehydration follows the order 3° > 2° > 1°, the order of carbocation stability.

Key Reactions

AlcoholConditionsProduct
Primary (ethanol)Conc. H2SO4, 170–180°C (most difficult; high temperature, strong acid)CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O (ethene)
Secondary (butan-2-ol)60% H2SO4, 100°C (range 100–140°C)Butan-2-ol → but-2-ene + H2O
Tertiary (methylpropan-2-ol)20% H2SO4, 85°C (range 25–80°C, just above room temperature)2-methylpropene + H2O

Key Points

  • Dehydration removes —OH from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon, forming an alkene.
  • Catalyst: concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4; a heated catalyst such as Al2O3 also works.
  • Ease of dehydration: tertiary > secondary > primary (carbocation stability order).
  • Primary alcohols need the highest temperature; tertiary dehydrate near room temperature.
lessons.title: Dehydration of Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 (or H3PO4) as catalyst to form esters. This process is called esterification: R—COOH + R—OH ⇌ R—COOR + H2O. Example: CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 (ethyl acetate) + H2O.

Reaction with Halogen Acids

Alcohols react with halogen acids to form alkyl halides: R—OH + HX → R—X + H2O.

  • With HCl, a ZnCl2 catalyst is used: CH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O.
  • HBr and HI react in the same way, but without a catalyst: CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O.

Key Points

  • Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water, conc. H2SO4 catalyst.
  • Ethanol + acetic acid gives ethyl acetate, the standard example.
  • Halogen acids convert alcohols to alkyl halides + water.
  • HCl needs ZnCl2 catalyst; HBr and HI do not.
lessons.title: Formation of Esters

lessons.notes_html:
Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols are identified by the Lucas test and the oxidation test.

Lucas Test

The unknown alcohol is added to Lucas reagent (anhydrous zinc chloride dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid), stoppered, shaken and left to stand at room temperature: R—OH + HCl → R—Cl + H2O (ZnCl2).

AlcoholObservation
PrimaryReacts very slowly; no turbidity (turbidity only on prolonged heating)
SecondaryBecomes cloudy after a few minutes (5 to 10 minutes)
TertiaryImmediately forms two separate layers, becoming cloudy at once

Oxidation Test

With acidified K2Cr2O7, the chromium ion is reduced from Cr(VI) (orange) to Cr(III) (green). Primary alcohols (oxidised to aldehydes or acids) and secondary alcohols (oxidised to ketones) give this colour change; tertiary alcohols do not oxidise, so there is no colour change.

Key Points

  • Lucas reagent = anhydrous ZnCl2 in conc. HCl.
  • Lucas test: 3° cloudy immediately, 2° cloudy in 5–10 minutes, 1° no turbidity.
  • Oxidation test: acidified K2Cr2O7 changes orange → green for 1° and 2° alcohols.
  • Tertiary alcohols give no colour change with acidified K2Cr2O7.
lessons.title: Distinction between Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Methanol and ethanol are distinguished by the iodoform test. Ethanol reacts with iodine in the presence of NaOH to form a deep yellow precipitate of iodoform (tri-iodomethane, CHI3); methanol does not give this test.

CH3OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → No reaction (no deep yellow ppt)

CH3CH2OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa (sodium formate) + 5NaI + 5H2O

The reaction with alkaline I2(aq) detects the CH3CH(OH)— group in an alcohol: formation of tri-iodomethane confirms this group in the original alcohol, which is then oxidised to a carboxylic acid. Methanol is dangerous: in the liver it is metabolised to formaldehyde and formic acid, which can cause blindness or death, while ethanol gives the less harmful acetaldehyde and acetic acid.

Key Points

  • Iodoform test: ethanol gives a deep yellow ppt of CHI3; methanol gives no reaction.
  • Reagents: I2 with NaOH (alkaline iodine).
  • The test detects the CH3CH(OH)— group in an alcohol.
  • Ethanol + 4I2 + 6NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H2O.
lessons.title: Distinction between Methanol and Ethanol

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are acidic in nature due to the polar O—H bond; the greater the polarity of the —OH group, the higher the acidity. Acidity order: CH3OH > RCH2OH > R2CHOH > R3COH — primary alcohols are more acidic than secondary, which are more acidic than tertiary. The polarity of —OH decreases as electron-donating alkyl groups on the α-carbon increase, so tert-butyl alcohol is less acidic than methanol or ethanol. Acidic character is shown by reaction with sodium metal, releasing hydrogen: 2R—OH + 2Na → 2R—ONa + H2; e.g. 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2.

Comparison of the Acidity of Alcohols and Water

Generally alcohols are less acidic than water, except methanol, which is more acidic than water; the acidity of ethanol is nearly equal to that of water. Water dissociates as H2O(l) → OH−(aq) + H+(aq) and has a pKa of 15.7, placing it between methanol and ethanol in acidity. Longer chains and more branching lower acidity, because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilise the alkoxide ion, making it less likely to donate a proton.

Key Points

  • Acidity comes from the polar O—H bond; more polar —OH means stronger acid.
  • Order: methanol > primary > secondary > tertiary alcohol.
  • Alkyl groups are electron-donating: they lower —OH polarity and destabilise the alkoxide ion.
  • Methanol is more acidic than water; ethanol is about equal; longer-chain alcohols are weaker than water.
  • Reaction with Na (H2 evolved) demonstrates the acidity of alcohols.
lessons.title: Acidity of Alcohols

lessons.notes_html:
Carbonyl compounds contain a carbonyl group (C=O), in which a carbon atom is double-bonded to an oxygen atom. The carbonyl carbon is highly polarised: carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ+) and oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−). Carbonyl compounds include aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.

  • An aldehyde has one alkyl (or aryl) group and one hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl carbon, e.g. formaldehyde, HCHO.
  • A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups attached to the carbonyl carbon, e.g. acetone, used in nail polish removers, paint thinners and cleaning products.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain a carboxyl group (—COOH); general formula R—COOH, where R is an aliphatic or aromatic group. The name carboxyl comes from carbonyl + hydroxyl, the two groups present in carboxylic acids. Formaldehyde (in aqueous solution, formalin) is used as a preservative in medical laboratories, as a disinfectant, and in resins, adhesives and plywood; it is an irritant and a health risk on long exposure.

Key Points

  • Carbonyl group C=O is polarised: C is δ+, O is δ−.
  • Aldehyde: carbonyl carbon carries one R group and one H.
  • Ketone: carbonyl carbon carries two R groups.
  • Carboxylic acids contain —COOH (carbonyl + hydroxyl), general formula R—COOH.
  • Formaldehyde and acetone are the simplest aldehyde and ketone.
lessons.title: Carbonyl Compounds

lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones are prepared by the controlled oxidation of alcohols with an acidified solution of potassium dichromate or potassium permanganate.

  • Primary alcohols give aldehydes: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) + H2O, using K2Cr2O7/H2SO4.
  • Secondary alcohols give ketones: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 (acetone) + H2O.

Distillation is commonly used to separate and collect the desired product — the aldehyde from a primary alcohol or the ketone from a secondary alcohol — and so isolate and purify it from the reaction mixture. Distilling the aldehyde out as it forms also prevents its further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.

Key Points

  • Controlled oxidation: acidified K2Cr2O7 or acidified KMnO4.
  • Primary alcohol → aldehyde; secondary alcohol → ketone.
  • Ethanol → acetaldehyde; propan-2-ol → acetone.
  • Distillation isolates and purifies the carbonyl product.
lessons.title: Preparations of Aldehydes and Ketones

lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols and add hydrogen cyanide to form hydroxynitriles.

Reduction to Alcohols (Reduction with NaBH4)

Metal hydrides NaBH4 (sodium borohydride) and LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride) reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Reduction with NaBH4 requires polar solvents like water and ethyl alcohol: CH3CHO → CH3CH2OH; CH3COCH3 → propan-2-ol.

Reaction with HCN — Hydroxynitriles

Hydrogen cyanide (a weak acid) reacts with aldehydes and ketones, with KCN as catalyst and heat, to form hydroxynitriles (cyanohydrins): CH3CHO + HCN → CH3CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile); CH3COCH3 + HCN → (CH3)2C(OH)CN (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile).

Mechanism of Nucleophilic Addition of HCN

  • Step 1 — Ionisation: HCN ⇌ H+ + CN−. KCN is added to increase the supply of CN− ions; a little dilute H2SO4 supplies H+.
  • Step 2 — Nucleophilic attack: CN− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, breaking the π bond of C=O and forming an alkoxide intermediate.
  • Step 3 — Protonation: the negatively charged oxygen accepts H+ from the medium, giving the stable hydroxynitrile.

Key Points

  • NaBH4 or LiAlH4: aldehyde → 1° alcohol; ketone → 2° alcohol.
  • HCN adds across C=O to give a hydroxynitrile (cyanohydrin); KCN is the catalyst.
  • Mechanism: ionisation of HCN, nucleophilic attack by CN−, then protonation.
  • The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (δ+), so it is attacked by nucleophiles.
lessons.title: Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones

lessons.notes_html:
Different tests detect carbonyl compounds selectively: the choice of test depends on the information wanted.

Tests for Carbonyl Compounds

TestPositive resultDetects
2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH)Orange-yellow precipitate (a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone)Carbonyl group in both aldehydes and ketones
Fehling's testRed (brick-red) precipitate of Cu2O; aldehyde oxidised to an acidAldehydes only; ketones do not react
Tollens' test (silver mirror test)Grey-black precipitate or a silver mirrorAldehydes only; ketones generally do not react
Iodoform test (alkaline I2)Yellow precipitate of CHI3The acetyl group CH3CO— (methyl ketones and ethanal)

Fehling's: RCHO + 2Cu(OH)2 + NaOH → RCOONa + Cu2O + 3H2O; the aldehyde reduces Cu2+ ions. Tollens': RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]OH + H2O → RCOOH + 4NH3 + 2Ag + 2H2O; the aldehyde reduces silver ions to a silver mirror — always use freshly prepared Tollens' reagent. Iodoform: CH3CHO + 3I2 + 4NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H2O; CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH → CHI3 + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O.

Key Points

  • 2,4-DNPH confirms a carbonyl group: orange-yellow precipitate with aldehydes and ketones.
  • Fehling's and Tollens' tests identify aldehydes (ease of oxidation); ketones fail both.
  • Fehling's: brick-red Cu2O. Tollens': silver mirror; use freshly prepared reagent.
  • Iodoform test detects the CH3CO— group; it does not apply to all carbonyl compounds.
lessons.title: Identification of Carbonyl Compounds

lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids are prepared by oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes, and by hydrolysis of nitriles and esters.

Oxidation of Primary Alcohols

Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes, which on further oxidation give carboxylic acids, using K2Cr2O7 and H2SO4 (KMnO4 can be used instead) under reflux: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O; CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH.

Hydrolysis of Nitriles

Alkyl nitriles (alkyl cyanides) react with a hot aqueous solution of an acid or an alkali to produce carboxylic acids.

  • Acidic hydrolysis: CH3C≡N + 2H2O + HCl → CH3COOH + NH4Cl.
  • Alkaline hydrolysis: CH3C≡N + H2O + NaOH → CH3COONa + NH3; the sodium ethanoate is then acidified with dilute HCl or dilute H2SO4: CH3COONa + HCl → CH3COOH + NaCl.

Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters react with aqueous NaOH to give the sodium salt of the acid, which with dilute HCl yields the carboxylic acid: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O →(Δ) CH3COONa + C2H5OH. With dilute acid the hydrolysis is reversible: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH. Acid hydrolysis is reversible, whereas alkaline hydrolysis is not, because the alkali neutralises the acid formed and prevents the reverse reaction.

Key Points

  • Oxidation: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid (acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4, reflux).
  • Nitrile hydrolysis: hot aqueous acid gives the acid + NH4+ salt; alkali gives the carboxylate salt + NH3, then acidify.
  • Ester hydrolysis with dilute acid is reversible; with alkali it goes to completion.
  • Alkaline hydrolysis gives a carboxylate salt, converted to the acid by dilute acid.
lessons.title: Preparations of Carboxylic Acids

lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids behave as acids — reacting with metals, alkalis and carbonates — form esters, and are reduced to primary alcohols.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation (acetic acid)Products
Redox reaction with reactive metals2CH3COOH + 2Na → 2CH3COONa + H2Salt + hydrogen (metal is oxidised; H+ is reduced)
Neutralisation with alkalisCH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2OSalt + water
Acid–base reaction with carbonates2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + CO2 + H2OSalt + water + carbon dioxide (via carbonic acid, which decomposes)
Esterification with alcoholsCH3COOH + CH3OH → CH3COOCH3 + H2O (H2SO4 catalyst)Ester + water
Reduction by LiAlH4CH3COOH → CH3CH2OH (1. LiAlH4, ether; 2. H2O, H+)Primary alcohol

Esterification Mechanism

  • Step 1: the carbonyl oxygen of the acid is protonated by H+ from the catalyst, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.
  • Step 2: the lone pair on the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.
  • Step 3: a proton transfer converts one —OH group into a good leaving group (—OH2+).
  • Step 4: water is eliminated and the protonated ester loses H+, regenerating the acid catalyst and giving the neutral ester.

In LiAlH4 reduction, an aldehyde forms as an intermediate but cannot be isolated, because it is reduced more easily than the original carboxylic acid.

Key Points

  • With reactive metals: salt + H2. With alkalis: salt + water. With carbonates: salt + water + CO2.
  • Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4).
  • Esterification mechanism: protonation, nucleophilic attack, proton transfer, elimination of water.
  • LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols; the aldehyde intermediate cannot be isolated.
lessons.title: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis is a reaction in which water breaks down a molecule into smaller parts. Esters are hydrolysed by two methods — dilute acid and heat, or dilute alkali and heat; both methods require heat.

Hydrolysis with Dilute Acid

A dilute acid (hydrochloric or sulfuric acid) acts as a catalyst: the acid makes the oxygen atom in the ester more reactive, so it can be attacked by water, forming a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. The reaction can go in both directions — the products can react to form the original ester again (reversible): R—COOR + H2O ⇌ R—COOH + ROH (HCl); e.g. CH3COOCH3 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + CH3OH.

Hydrolysis with Dilute Alkali

A dilute alkali (sodium hydroxide) is used instead of acid. The alkali acts as a base and attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, forming a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. This reaction proceeds in only one direction, so complete conversion is easier and the products are easier to separate: R—COOR + NaOH(aq) → R—COONa(aq) + ROH.

Key Points

  • Ester hydrolysis needs water, heat, and dilute acid or dilute alkali.
  • Acid hydrolysis: ester ⇌ carboxylic acid + alcohol (reversible).
  • Alkaline hydrolysis: ester → carboxylate salt + alcohol (one direction only).
  • Alkaline hydrolysis gives complete conversion and products that are easier to separate.
lessons.title: Hydrolysis of Esters
Functional Group Interconversion (FGI)
lessons.notes_html:
Organic synthesis is the process of creating organic compounds from simpler starting materials through a series of chemical reactions, designing efficient pathways to produce molecules with specific structures or properties — crucial for pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, materials and other essential substances. More than 80% of modern pharmaceuticals are formed through synthetic methods designed by chemists.

Functional group interconversions (FGI) are a crucial part of organic synthesis: the transformation of one functional group into another through chemical reactions such as substitution, addition, elimination, oxidation or reduction. Functional groups are specific arrangements of atoms within a molecule that determine its chemical reactivity, so FGI lets chemists modify a molecule's structure and influence its chemical and physical properties.

Methods of Functional Group Interconversion

Reaction TypeWhat HappensBook Example
Addition reactionsAtoms or groups add across double or triple bondsAlkene + H2O —H2SO4→ alcohol (hydration)
Substitution reactionsOne functional group is replaced by anotherNH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI (halide to amine, nucleophilic substitution)
Elimination reactionsAtoms or groups are removed from a moleculeCH3CH2OH —conc. H2SO4, 170–180°C→ CH2=CH2 + H2O (dehydration of an alcohol to an alkene)
Oxidation–reduction reactionsTransfer of electrons converts one functional group into anotherSec. propyl alcohol (CH3–CHOH–CH3) + [O] —K2Cr2O7/H2SO4→ acetone (CH3–CO–CH3) + H2O
Functional group transformationA sequence of reactions changes one functional group into another; often needs multiple steps and strategic planningMulti-step routes linking the groups below

The FGI Web (Fig. 14.1)

  • Alkane ⇌ alkene: dehydrogenation / hydrogenation. Alkane ⇌ haloalkane: halogenation / reduction (Zn/HCl).
  • Alkene ⇌ haloalkane: addition of HX/X2 / dehydrohalogenation (alc. KOH, heat). Alkene ⇌ alcohol: hydration (acid catalysed) / dehydration.
  • Haloalkane → amine: substitution (conc. NH3). Haloalkane → nitrile: substitution (KCN, ethanolic). Haloalkane ⇌ alcohol: nucleophilic substitution (aq. KOH).
  • Alcohol ⇌ ketone: oxidation / reduction. Alcohol → aldehyde (oxidation); aldehyde → carboxylic acid (oxidation).
  • Carboxylic acid ⇌ ester: esterification / hydrolysis. Acid → acid halide (chlorination), acid anhydride (dehydration), amide (ammonia/amines via acid chloride); each returns by hydrolysis.

Key Points

  • FGI = converting one functional group into another by substitution, addition, elimination, oxidation or reduction.
  • Functional groups determine a molecule's reactivity and properties.
  • Hydration converts alkenes to alcohols; dehydration converts alcohols back to alkenes.
  • Oxidation links alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid, and secondary alcohols → ketones.
  • Haloalkanes are key intermediates: they lead to amines, nitriles and alcohols.

lessons.title: Functional Groups and Their Properties and Reactions in Organic Molecules (Part 1: Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes)
lessons.notes_html:
Functional groups are specific atoms or groups of atoms within organic molecules that determine the properties and reactivity of molecules. By identifying these groups, we can predict how organic molecules will react and what physical characteristics they will have.

Alkanes

Alkanes have low reactivity due to their saturated hydrocarbon structures — they lack reactive sites (reactive functional groups) and mainly participate in combustion reactions with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water vapour and energy. Examples: methane, ethane and propane, found in natural gas, petrol and diesel.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH = −891 kJ/mol

Alkenes

Alkenes undergo addition reactions, such as hydrogenation and halogenation; the double bond provides their reactivity. They may also undergo polymerisation. Examples: ethene, propene and butene. Ethylene (ethene) polymerises in the presence of a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to form polyethene:

nCH2=CH2 (ethene) —400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2/peroxide→ –[CH2–CH2]n– (polythene)

Alkynes

Alkynes are hydrocarbons characterised by a triple bond and are less reactive than alkenes. They can form acetylide compounds; for example, ethyne (acetylene) reacts with sodium amide (a strong base) to produce sodium acetylide and ammonia:

HC≡CH + NaNH2 → HC≡C−Na+ + NH3

Key Points

  • Functional groups decide both the properties and the reactions of a molecule.
  • Alkanes are saturated and unreactive, but burn completely to CO2 and H2O.
