  • Alkenes react by addition across the C=C bond and can polymerise.
  • Ethene polymerises to polythene at 400°C and 100 atm with a peroxide/O2 initiator.
  • Alkynes have a C≡C triple bond and form acetylides with strong bases like NaNH2.

lessons.title: Functional Groups and Their Properties and Reactions in Organic Molecules (Part 2: Alcohols, Amines, Carboxylic Acids, Esters, Ketones, Aldehydes and Alkyl Halides)
lessons.notes_html:
Each functional group gives its family a characteristic set of properties and reactions, summarised below with the book's examples.

FamilyProperties and Typical ReactionsBook Reaction
AlcoholsForm hydrogen bonds, which affect solubility and boiling points. Undergo dehydration to alkenes and esterification to esters. Examples: methanol, ethanol, propanolCH3CH2OH —conc. H2SO4, 170–180°C→ CH2=CH2 + H2O; CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ (H2SO4) CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (ethyl acetate)
AminesBasic in nature, accept protons, and participate in nucleophilic substitutions and addition reactions. Examples: methylamine, ethylmethylamine, anilineNH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI (primary amine); CH3NH2 + CH3I → (CH3)2NH + HI (secondary); (CH3)2NH + CH3I → (CH3)3N + HI (tertiary)
Carboxylic acidsAcidic in nature, donate protons, and undergo esterification. Examples: formic acid, acetic acid, benzoic acidCH3COOH + CH3CH2OH ⇌ (HCl + HOH) CH3COOCH2CH3 + HOH (ethyl acetate)
EstersFormed from carboxylic acids + alcohols; undergo hydrolysis to give back carboxylic acids and alcohols. Examples: methyl formate, ethyl acetate, ethyl benzoateR–CO–OR + H2O ⇌ (H+) R–CO–OH + ROH
KetonesUndergo nucleophilic addition reactions; react with hydrazine to form hydrazones. Examples: acetone, cyclohexanone, acetophenonePropanone (acetone) + hydrazine (H2N–NH2) → propanone hydrazone + H2O
AldehydesUndergo nucleophilic addition reactions; easily oxidised to carboxylic acids. Examples: formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, benzaldehydeCH3CHO + [O] —K2Cr2O7/H2SO4→ CH3COOH (acetaldehyde to acetic acid)
Alkyl halidesUndergo nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions. Examples: ethyl bromide, isopropyl chloride, chlorobenzeneRX + KOH —H2O→ ROH + KX

These properties and reactions enable us to understand and predict how organic molecules will behave in various chemical processes.

Key Points

  • Alcohols hydrogen-bond, dehydrate to alkenes and esterify with carboxylic acids.
  • Amines are basic and are built up step by step by reaction with alkyl halides (primary → secondary → tertiary).
  • Carboxylic acids donate protons and form esters; esters hydrolyse back to acid + alcohol.
  • Ketones and aldehydes undergo nucleophilic addition; aldehydes are easily oxidised to acids, ketones are not.
  • Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution (e.g. aq. KOH gives alcohols) and elimination.

lessons.title: Guidelines for Devising Multi-Step Synthetic Routes in Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
To create multi-step processes for synthesising organic molecules, a thorough understanding of the reactions of different functional groups is essential. Drug companies depend on such carefully planned multi-step syntheses for medicines such as aspirin, antibiotics and paracetamol, where each step must be efficient, selective and cost-effective. The general steps are:

Steps for Devising a Synthetic Route

StepWhat To Do
1. Identify functional groupsIdentify the functional groups present in the starting material and the desired product; this helps select the appropriate reactions
2. Plan the first stepSelect a reaction for the first step that modifies or introduces a functional group in the starting material to move towards the desired product
3. Consider protecting groupsIf reactive functional groups are present, use a protecting group to prevent undesired reactions in later steps
4. Plan subsequent stepsDesign each step to transform the starting material into new intermediates, progressing toward the desired product
5. Optimise reaction conditionsIdentify the best conditions — temperature, solvent and catalyst — for each step, to maximise product yield while minimising side reactions
6. Purify and characterise intermediatesAfter each step, purify the intermediate product and verify its structure using techniques such as spectroscopy
7. Final stepsRemove the protecting groups to get the desired product
8. Workup and purificationAfter each reaction, use work-up methods such as extraction and purification techniques (including chromatography and distillation) to obtain the final product

The specific process depends on the starting material and the target molecule.

Key Points

  • Start by comparing functional groups in the starting material and the target product.
  • Protect reactive groups that would interfere with later steps; remove protection at the end.
  • Each step converts the material into a new intermediate closer to the product.
  • Optimise temperature, solvent and catalyst for maximum yield and minimum side reactions.
  • Purify and characterise (e.g. by spectroscopy) every intermediate.

lessons.title: Synthetic Route for Carboxylic Acid from Methane
lessons.notes_html:
Methane is relatively unreactive on its own, so the route to a carboxylic acid first adds a reactive functional group by radical chlorination, then builds the carbon chain through a nitrile, which hydrolyses to the acid.

Key Reactions: Methane to Acetic Acid

StepReaction and ConditionsWhat Happens
1. Radical chlorinationCH4 + Cl2 —hv→ CH3Cl + HClMethane reacts with chlorine gas under UV light to give chloromethane, a more reactive intermediate
2. Nucleophilic substitutionCH3Cl + NaCN —DMSO, reflux→ CH3CN + NaClChloromethane reacts with the cyanide ion in a polar aprotic solvent (dimethyl sulphoxide); refluxing with sodium cyanide gives acetonitrile, adding one carbon and a nitrile group
3. HydrolysisCH3CN + 2H2O —H+, reflux→ CH3COOH + NH4+Refluxing the nitrile with dilute mineral acid converts the nitrile group into a carboxyl group: acetic acid is the main product, with an ammonium salt as byproduct

At each stage, intermediates are purified through distillation or extraction, while spectroscopic techniques confirm the progress of the synthesis: infrared spectra indicate the disappearance of the nitrile group and the appearance of acid carbonyl groups, and proton NMR and mass spectrometry confirm the structures of intermediates and the final product.

Alternative Oxidation Route to Formic Acid

Methane can also be converted into formic acid through a step-by-step oxidation: CH4 —[O]→ CH3OH —[O]→ HCHO —[O]→ HCOOH (methane → methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid). Although theoretically feasible, controlling this process experimentally is difficult because methane and its intermediates often oxidise completely to CO2 — this highlights the difficulties of selective oxidation chemistry.

Key Points

  • Route: CH4 → CH3Cl → CH3CN → CH3COOH.
  • Step 1 needs UV light (radical chlorination) because methane is unreactive.
  • The cyanide step adds the extra carbon needed for acetic acid.
  • Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile gives the carboxylic acid plus NH4+.
  • IR, proton NMR and mass spectrometry confirm each intermediate and the product.

lessons.title: Retro-synthesis in Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Retro-synthesis is a systematic and strategic method used to plan the synthesis of complex molecules. Working backwards from a target molecule, chemists identify simpler starting materials, breaking the target down into progressively simpler fragments. This aims to find easily accessible precursors, facilitating efficient synthesis planning, route optimisation and the use of established reactions and methodologies. The concept of retrosynthetic analysis was developed by Elias James Corey, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1990.

Main Steps in Retro-synthesis (Example: Paracetamol)

StepApplication to Paracetamol
1. Identification of the target moleculeExamine the target's structure and key functional groups. Paracetamol contains a hydroxyl group (–OH) and an amide group (–NHCOCH3) attached to a benzene ring
2. Strategic bond breakingDeliberately break bonds to identify potential precursors, relying on established reaction pathways. Breaking the amide bond suggests p-aminophenol + acetic anhydride as precursors; in the forward reaction, p-aminophenol undergoes acylation to give paracetamol (+ CH3COOH)
3. Functional group interconversionsConvert one functional group into another via established reactions. The amine group in p-aminophenol originates from a nitro group: p-nitrophenol + 3H2 —Pd/C, 25–50°C→ p-aminophenol + 2H2O
Repeat until simple starting materialsp-Nitrophenol is produced from phenol, which is commonly available, by controlled nitration at the para-position: phenol + HNO3 —H2SO4, 0–10°C→ p-nitrophenol + H2O

The entire forward pathway is: Phenol —HNO3/H2SO4, 0–10°C→ p-nitrophenol —H2, Pd/C→ p-aminophenol —(CH3CO)2O→ paracetamol. Retrosynthesis is not simply dividing a molecule into smaller parts without pattern; it is a systematic, logical process of strategically breaking bonds to identify simpler, commercially available precursors.

Key Points

  • Retrosynthesis works backwards from the target molecule to simpler precursors.
  • Step 1 is always identification of the target molecule and its functional groups.
  • Strategic bond breaking must follow known forward reactions.
  • FGI steps (e.g. nitro → amine by reduction) connect the fragments into a full route.
  • Working backwards stops when simple, inexpensive, commercially available materials are reached.

lessons.title: Applications of Retro-synthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Retro-synthesis is widely used wherever complex organic molecules must be planned and built efficiently — for example, antiviral drugs such as those used in HIV treatment are designed by identifying simple, readily available precursors and constructing the active molecule step by step.

Applications

ApplicationBenefit
Efficient synthesis planningProvides a roadmap for the stepwise construction of the target compound, avoiding dead ends and unnecessary steps
Economic and sustainable synthesisIdentifies efficient and cost-effective synthetic routes, minimising the number of steps and maximising the use of available starting materials
Chemical educationEnhances problem-solving skills and deepens understanding of synthetic strategies in organic chemistry
Drug discovery and developmentUsed to design and optimise synthetic routes for potential drug candidates in the pharmaceutical industry
Total synthesis of natural productsApplied in the total synthesis of complex natural products, giving access to molecules found in nature

Key Points

  • Retrosynthesis gives a clear roadmap and avoids dead-end routes.
  • It makes synthesis cheaper and more sustainable by cutting steps and using available materials.
  • It is a core tool in drug discovery and development.
  • It enables the total synthesis of complex natural products.
  • It also trains problem-solving in chemical education.
